en: Preface to the Commentary on the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, composed by the monk Jinnan, a successor to the ancestral lineage who formerly resided at Shangsheng Chan Monastery in Fuzhou.
All Buddhas appear in the world for only one purpose; what is expounded throughout the thousand sutras contains no other vehicle. It is solely to manifest the wondrous...

By clarifying the one mind through the Dharma, and by revealing the true reality (dharmatā) within illusory flowers, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the fundamental tenet of all Buddhas and the governing principle of a thousand scriptures;
it is the primordial mirror of the one mind and the wondrous gateway to true reality.

Since the translation by Master Qin returned [to China], nearly eight hundred years have passed. Throughout the generations, there have been sages who have expounded the phrasing and interpreted the meanings;

yet, as they sought perfection with critical scrutiny, their efforts were characterized by both gains and losses. Truly, even if the *Śāriputras* of this world and *Bodhisattvas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to exhaust their thoughts in measurement and deliberation, they could not know even a small fraction of its depth.
Therefore, although it has been extensively explained through many lectures, there remains that which is not fully exhausted; thus, [this work] polishes and adorns it.
This commentary does not reject those who come to it. Master Huán of Lian Temple in Wēn-líng investigated the One Vehicle deeply and explored various doctrines extensively.

Having refined the subtle points and extracted the essentials, he composed this topical analysis. In the first year of the Jǐ-hài year of the Xuānhuá era, he condescended to request me to collate and verify the text.

Subsequently, he consulted the master patriarchs extensively to ensure his understanding accorded with the Buddha’s intent. In the year Bingwu, he met me again at Nanshan, where we investigated the commentaries and sought out the scriptures, deliberating upon them repeatedly.

He discarded mere names and appearances and cut away the profuse undergrowth, ensuring that those who enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision would have no weariness of plucking leaves or tracing branches, but instead possess the perspective of splitting firewood or holding a candle. This is truly one who can illuminate the secret essentials.

It is the treasury. Someone asked the Master, "In which part of the Seven Fascicles of the Text does the correct teaching reside? The Master said, "Among thousands of sutras and myriad treatises, they all exist solely for this matter.
How could there be a different discourse in this single session? It is by means of this that the World-Honored One revealed and showed;
it is by means of this that the deluded masses awaken and enter; it is by means of this that one departs from the burning house; it is by means of this that the treasure..."
Advancing forward, they may traverse many kalpas in half a day; they manifest the great trichiliocosm within a single body.

There is the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood, the Universal Prediction of Never-Despising, King Bhaiṣajyarāja’s self-immolation by fire, Avalokiteśvara’s responsive manifestations, and Viśuddhagarbha’s conversion of the heterodox.
It is for this reason that Samantabhadra exhorts us to arouse the aspiration [for enlightenment]. If one does not understand this matter, every word before one’s eyes is but conventional discourse;
yet once the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened, what is not the wondrous Dharma? By privately observing these questions and answers, one perceives the composition of the entire sutra.

If one were to follow, examine, and savor them until reaching profound realization and attaining it for oneself, one could then sit cross-legged in the station of Immeasurable Meaning and reflect back upon the source.
The light of the ūrṇā-kośa mark opens the gate of expedient means to reveal the true reality.

To cast away the dung-basket directly and drive the white ox far along—then the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is fully present within oneself and not in the Buddha; it is fully present within the mind and not in the scriptures.
For example, although the lute, the *sīsa*, and the *konghou* possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them.
Thus, one who wishes to illuminate this matter should take this understanding as their skillful finger.

Preface to the Propagation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Written by the Mountain Recluse Ruyi, the Elder Xiangmai. Commentary on the *Saddharma*.
The commentary states: In Sanskrit it is called *sad-dharma*; here it is translated as "Wondrous Dharma" (*Miaofa*) or "Right Dharma" (*Zhengfa*).
This is because the character *sa* contains two meanings; thus, the "Wondrous Dharma" of the Qin edition and the "Right Dharma" of the Jin edition are both without error.
It possesses ten wondrous meanings and is uniquely superior to other sutras, hence it is called "wondrous. It is the true doctrine of the One Vehicle, the definitive meaning of the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is called "Correct" (Zheng). It upholds the true principle as a model for all beings; therefore, it is called "Dharma" (Fa).
The *Tiantai Xuanyi* and the *Cien Xuanzan* extensively elaborate upon these categories of meaning, which are not recorded here in full.

"Lotus flower. The commentary states: In Sanskrit, it is called *puṇḍarīka*; here it is translated as "white lotus flower. White is the source of all colors, and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the fundamental principle of the other vehicles;
therefore, it is taken as a metaphor. This is as in the passage below in the sutra where he first emits light from his white tuft of hair.
This is the meaning: at the end, he was granted the carriage of the white ox. As for the "Lotus," it dwells in the mud yet remains unstained;

its cause and effect are manifested together. This metaphor illustrates how the preceding *Saddharma* (Wonderful Dharma) reveals the provisional to manifest the real, unifying the three vehicles into one, and clarifying that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision differ from those of other sutras.
Because both the Dharma and the metaphor are presented together, it is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Preface to the Sūtra. The commentary states: In Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*; here it is translated as *qijing* (契經). "Qie" (契) means to accord with principle and to accord with the capacities [of sentient beings].

"Jing" (經) means to string together and encompass the eternal Dharma. Thus, it refers to the teaching that accords with principle and harmonizes with capacity; hence it is called a *qijing*. Here, the character "qie" is abbreviated.
The aim is to follow simplicity. To describe the profound essence of the sutra and set forth its origins is called a "Preface" (*xu*).
Thus, Tiantai said: "To reveal the secret, profound treasury is termed 'Wondrous' (*miao*); to demonstrate the correct path of the provisional and the real is thus called 'Dharma' (*fa*";
to point to the fundamental fruit of the distant past is illustrated by the metaphor of the lotus; and to harmonize the perfect path of non-duality is compared to..."
It is adorned with its blossoms; its resonance constitutes the Buddha-work, and it is titled a Sūtra. As the initial stage of perfect exposition, it is designated as the Preface.
This Sūtra sweeps away the attachment to the teaching of the "Transformation City" and discards the stagnant sentiments of the "Thatched Hut.

It opens the provisional gate of skillful means and reveals the wondrous principle of ultimate reality. It unifies the minor practices of various virtues and leads them back to the single vehicle of vastness.
Its literary elegance is vast and its meaning profound, such that no other sutra can surpass it. To explain it in detail:

there are the Ten Subtleties (*daśa-sūkṣmatā*), the Three Modes of the Dharma (*trividha-dharmamārga*), the Six Meanings of the Lotus, and the Six Explanations of the Sutra, all as set forth in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
Furthermore, there are the commentaries by Guangzhai and the *Xuanzan* by Cien; let students be aware of these.
Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain composed this commentary, stating:
"The name Zhongnan Mountain is located south of the city of Chang’an; it connects with Qinling, Taibai, and Taiyi Mountains.
It lies in Wugong County of Fufeng. The *Guangzhong ji* (Record of Guanzhong) states that Zhongnan is also called Zhongnan."
It is situated to the south of the capital within the Tian (Heavenly) Mountains; hence it is called Zhongnan (Central-South).
According to the *Sanqin ji*, Mount Zhongnan is also known as Didi, which can serve as a refuge from floods. Vinaya Master Daoxuan’s secular surname was Qian;
he was a descendant of Pengzu and a native of Changcheng County in Huzhou. He was the son of Qian Shen, the Minister of Personnel during the Sui dynasty, and was born in the Sui period.
During the Kaihuang era, he performed great Buddhist services. In the reigns of Tang Taizong and Gaozong, his literary brilliance shone forth and his moral virtue was peerless.

He composed the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*) to extensively praise the *Vinaya*, and further authored over one hundred volumes of works such as the *Hongming ji* and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
On one occasion, while practicing the Way, he stumbled and fell, whereupon he was moved by the vision of General Wei [Zhou] supporting his feet. However, he erred...
When he was cutting the sitting mat, the celestial being Huang Qiong pointed out the instructions to him. He was thus able to borrow the *śarīra* from heaven to circulate among humans.

There were further miraculous responses, as detailed in the *Account of Extraordinary Events*. His posthumous title was Great Master Chengzhao (*Chengzhao Dashi*). The *Essential Survey of the Lotus Sūtra* (*Fahua yaolan*) states:

When the Master was composing the preface, the Heavenly Lord Wei (Weitian) informed him that because the *Lotus Sūtra* is so supreme and exalted, it would not be easy to find words to crown its beginning. Thus [he submitted].
He reported this to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and all the Buddhas granted their approval; this is precisely the prologue to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Thus, the hymn by Cizhao says: "The Great Being of the Southern Mountain is most profound and mysterious; he has distilled the essential pivot and placed it before the sūtra.
The celestial general Vaiśravaṇa personally delivered the report, and the Buddhas of the ten directions approved the Master’s words."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas descend as spirits.

The commentary states: "Purpose" (*zhì*) means intent. The Buddhas appear in the world primarily to preach this sutra, opening the gate of expedient means (*upāya*) to reveal the true reality (*bhūtārtha*).
They entice the deluded children within the burning house and point out the bright pearl beneath their robes, leading them to awaken to the emptiness of all phenomena and enter [the Way].
The Buddhas possess knowledge and vision. Therefore, the sutra below states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world for the sake of one great causal matter alone.
That is to say, they appear in the world because they desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and to make it pure;
they appear in the world because they desire to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings; they desire to..."

It is because sentient beings awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world; it is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that he appears in the world.
This is what is meant by the Buddhas appearing in the world for the sake of the one great causal event.
Master Tiantai said: "One" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Great" refers to Prajñā; and "Event" refers to Vimukti (Liberation). This...
These three dharmas are inherently possessed by sentient beings as the cause; the Buddhas manifest them as the condition. The original intent of appearing in the world is solely for this purpose.
This explains the "one great causal condition" (*ekamahākaruṇā-nidāna*). The four kinds of knowledge and vision are explained through four meanings.
First, in terms of the four stages; second, in terms of the four wisdoms; third, in terms of the four gates;

and fourth, in terms of contemplating the mind—wherever it is said that "the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" are attained, it refers to the beginning of the stage of partial realization (*vibhāṣika-satya*), when the three wisdoms and five eyes are simultaneously developed, together entering the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle of all Buddhas.
Tiantang explains: "It is called 'one' because it is neither three nor five," for it is vast and expansive.

It is called "Great" because it encompasses all; it is called a "matter" because it refers to this manifestation through transformation (*nirmāṇa*). The capacity to evoke the Buddha is the cause; the Buddha responding to that [capacity] is the condition.
It is for the sake of these causes and conditions of this one great matter that he appears in the world.
Regarding "opening, showing, awakening, and entering": the former two refer to the transformer—that is, opening broadly and demonstrating in detail—while the latter two...

This refers to those being transformed, meaning beginning with awakening and ending with entry. "Knowing" is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); "seeing" is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
It is also called the wisdom of all modes of wisdom (*sarvajña-jñāna*). Master Tiantai Zhiyi of Nanyue said: "Opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision corresponds to the stage of the ten abidings;

revealing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision corresponds to the stage of the ten practices; awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision corresponds to the stage of the ten transferences; and entering [the Buddha’s knowledge and vision]..."

The Buddha’s knowledge and vision refer to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). All instances of "the Buddha knows" signify the attainment of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
all instances of "the Buddha sees" signify the full attainment of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). This is an explanation based on the stages. The *Guxiang Chao* states:
"The perfect contemplation of the three knowledges is called the Buddha’s knowledge; the perfect awakening of the five eyes is called the Buddha’s vision."
"Accumulated in the Great Mansion, it emerged after those thousand years. Transmitted East to Zhendan for over three hundred years.
The commentary states: "Accumulated" means gathered together. "The Great Mansion" refers to the Western Regions. "Zhendan" refers to the Eastern Land.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, more than a thousand years later, the teaching flowed to the East; thus, it was accumulated in the Western Regions and emerged after the millennium.
Indeed, from the time Zhu Fahu first translated this sutra during the Western Jin dynasty until the Tang dynasty, more than three hundred years had passed.
During the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin, there was the Dharma-protector Zhu Fahu, a bodhisattva from Dunhuang, residing at the Qing Gate in Chang’an.
The first translation of this sutra was titled *Zhengfahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
The commentary states: "The Jin dynasty was ruled by the Sima clan with its capital at Luoyang; because it was situated to the west of Eastern Jin, it is referred to as Western Jin.
Emperor Hui was the son of the founding emperor (Wu). Yongkang was the reign title of Emperor Hui. Qingmen is the eastern gate of Chang'an. [The original text continues: "...originally long..."
The Anba (Anxi) City Gate is colloquially called the Green Gate (Qingmen). Dharmarakṣa was originally a native of the Yuezhi people;
later, he moved his residence to Dunhuang and thus became a person of the Dunhuang Commandery. Having left home at a young age, he devoted himself to the propagation of the Way.
During the Western Jin dynasty, he came to convert the people in Luoyang and established a monastery outside the Green Gate in Chang’an, where he set up images and performed [rituals].
Dharmarakṣa assisted in guiding his later disciples, translating numerous scriptures to illuminate the Semblance Dharma; people praised his virtue and titled him a Bodhisattva.
Initially, he translated this scripture as the *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra) in ten fascicles;
all its mantra words and phrases were rendered into the Jin language.
During the Long’an era of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the Kuchean śramaṇa Kumārajīva translated this sūtra next,
under the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus Sutra of the Sublime Dharma), during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.
The commentary states: During the Western Jin dynasty, the realm fell into chaos. Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangtze River and established his capital in Jiangdong;
thus it is called Eastern Jin. Emperor An was the son of Emperor Xiaowu. "Long'an" was the reign title of Emperor An. Later Qin refers to Yao Xing. "Hongshi" was the reign title of Yao Xing.
Since the Jin occupied the legitimate position while the Qin were a peripheral usurpation, the Jin is mentioned first and the Qin afterwards.
Kumārajīva was a native of Kucha. He transmitted the teachings to the state of Qin and greatly propagated the Buddha-dharma.
He translated such sutras as the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Vimalakīrti*, and treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Śata-śāstra*.
He retranslated the aforementioned sutra, naming it the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which consists of seven fascicles; this is the version currently in circulation.
During the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, the North Indian śramaṇa Jñānagupta translated [the text] at Daxingshan Monastery.
Later translations were given the same title, *Miaofa* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
The commentary states: "The 'Sui dynasty' refers to Emperor Wen of Sui; Renshou was the reign title of Emperor Wen. Jñānagupta..."
"Tripiṭaka Dharma Master" is his title. Guptā and the Master Narendrayaśas arrived together in this land.
Emperor Wen honored them and established them at Daxingshan Temple, providing all their necessities from the state treasury. They translated numerous scriptures;
later, they translated this sūtra titled the *Aṣṭabaddhika-saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in eight fascicles. However, regarding the "Herbs" chapter...
The *Yuyi jing* (Sutra on Similes) has more than a thousand additional characters appended to it. As for the other [versions], they all agree with the version by Kumārajīva.
These three sutras overlap one another, presenting their themes and purports alternately; however, those held in high esteem at the time all propagated the Qin edition.
The commentary states: "Since the three preceding translations are versions of the same scripture, their phrasing and intended meanings overlap and vary.
Among those transmitted and read by the world, the translation by Kumārajīva is most widely propagated."
There are indeed other verses from various chapters and sections that follow this tradition; these have not been recounted here as they are fully detailed in the preface.

The commentary states: Master Xuán composed the *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù* (Record of Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang) in ten fascicles, which comprehensively encompasses the origins and developments of the various sutras and treatises.

What is mentioned here—namely, that besides the three primary versions, there are further derivative branches and separately circulated chapter-verse collections—is exactly as recorded in his compilation.

In the catalogs of the Inner Canon (*Nèi-diǎn-lù*), the matters are numerous and disorganized; therefore, they are not recounted here. The above constitutes the preface on the sources and lineages of the translations.
Below this follows the exposition of the essential purport of the present sutra.
Now, as for the descent of spiritual power upon a sacred mountain, it could not have been brought about by anyone other than a Great Sage.

The commentary states: "The descent of spiritual power upon a sacred mountain" means that when a mountain possesses the excellence of refined spirit, it gives birth to such a spiritually luminous Great Sage who transforms the world.
This meaning borrows from the line in the *Shijing*: "Only from the mountains did the spirit descend; Shu Fu and Shen Sheng were born."
This is the "Pattern" (wen). It is the numinous spirit. That refers to the descent of birth of a beautiful and worthy minister; this praises the manifestation and descent of the spirit of a sage.
Regarding the reach of such transformation, were it not for past conditions, there would be no means to guide the mind.
The commentary states: Although the Buddha is a Great Sage, he does not transform those with whom he has no karmic affinity.
Therefore, wherever his transformation reaches, there are all past affinities that open and guide their minds; thus, only upon hearing what is now being taught can they finally believe and accept it.
Therefore, when the Immortal Garden was completed, the capacities [of beings] were distinguished as small and great.
The commentary states: "The Immortal Garden is the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī. It was the place where five sages possessing the five supernatural powers fell due to hearing the voices of palace women;
for this reason, it is also called the Garden of Sages. Thus spoke the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One.

After first attaining Buddhahood, he turned the Wheel of Dharma three times within this grove. Among those who heard the Dharma, some ascended to the stage of the Mahāyāna, while others realized the fruits of the Hīnayāna.
From this point on, there were the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna in the world; these were distinguished according to the capacities of sentient beings.
Regarding the *Bequeathed Teaching at the Golden River* (*Suvarṇanadī-parinirvāṇa-saṃcodana*), the path differs according to the categories of the "Half" and "Full" [Teachings].
The commentary states: The Golden River is the Ādira-vatī River to the north of Kuśinagara;
this is translated as "Possessing the Golden River. On the bank of this river is a Śāla grove, wherein the Tathāgata entered [nirvāṇa].
*Nirvāṇa*. A "bequeathed testament" (*gùmìng*) refers to the final instructions bestowed when one’s life is about to end; thus it is called a bequeathed testament.

In the past, when King Cheng was about to pass away, he composed the *Gùmìng* (Bequeathed Testament) scripture. Now, as the Buddha is about to pass away, he preaches the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra. These are distinct cases.
Within that *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra, the Tathāgata speaks of the two characters "half" and "full," thereby distinguishing between the two vehicles of the Great and the Small.
Is it not the case that when the teachings are bestowed according to the vehicles and the times, there is no way to fully scrutinize their sublime assemblies?

The commentary states: From the initial proclamation at the Immortal Garden to the final discourse at the Golden River, the division of the Way into Great and Small—is this not because the teachings are bestowed according to the faculties [of beings] and the transformations are established according to the timing of the vehicles?
I can only regret that I lack the capacity to participate in the examination and scrutiny of these sublime assemblies.
Thus we know that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats did so for the sake of those whose pride was increasing.
The commentary states: When the Tathāgata was about to preach the *Lotus Sūtra* of the One Vehicle, the five thousand bhikṣus prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
To reveal the profound depth of this present sutra and cause those of overweening pride to advance toward seeking the Mahāyāna, five hundred [disciples] receive their predictions;
all together they honor the traces of esoteric transformation.
The commentary states: Pūrṇa and the other five hundred śrāvakas had long cultivated pure conduct under past buddhas;
all were encouraged and transformed by Śākyamuni to be reborn [in the Pure Land]. Internally they harbored the bodhisattva nature while externally appearing as śrāvakas;
now, at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, they have all received the prediction of attaining buddhahood.
Therefore, he emitted light and manifested auspicious omens to initiate the source of the teaching that invites [the Buddha].
The commentary states: "The emission of light and manifestation of omens constitute the causes and conditions for initiating the teaching.

When the Tathāgata first emitted light from the mark of the white tuft between his brows, it illuminated eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction; thereupon, Maitreya beheld seven matters and proclaimed them.
Doubt arises; Mañjuśrī responds by citing the ten causes, which constitutes the causal conditions for the teaching’s emergence.
Emerging from meditative concentration, he extols his own virtues and elucidates the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The commentary states: The Buddha arises from meditative concentration and elucidates two kinds of profundity; this is a general exposition of the Buddha’s wisdom. As for the two kinds of profundity:
first, the profundity of realization (*adhigama-gambhīrya*), as the sutra says, "The wisdom of all Buddhas is profound and immeasurable";

second, the profundity of the scriptures (*āgama-gambhīrya*), as the sutra says, "The gateway to that wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. This is the purport of the introduction.
"The decaying house is brought into the great system of tracks and models.
The commentary states: "This is the parable of the burning house. The burning house is a metaphor for the triple world; the children are metaphors for sentient beings."
The three vehicles set out outside the gate of the burning house are a metaphor for the provisional teaching of the three vehicles in the past.

Finally, the equal bestowal of the great white ox-cart is a metaphor for the present true teaching of the one vehicle. By destroying the three to reveal the one, beings are enticed to enter the Mahāyāna.
This is the fundamental intent of the Tathāgata. The Master Guangzhai established the teaching of the four vehicles; its meaning accords with this.
The "transformed city" (pariṇāmika-nagara) preserves the conditions of the past so that they do not fall into oblivion.
The commentary states: This is the parable of the conjured city. The conjured city represents the Two Vehicles, while the treasure land represents the Mahāyāna.
It encourages those of the Two Vehicles to return to the single ultimate goal, lest they remain stalled in provisional teachings as their final destination.

In the past, when he was a prince, he already transformed you; now, by preaching the Lotus Sūtra, he leads you once more into it. These three preceding lines clarify the three stages [of the teaching].
This is the essential meaning.
The "Tying the Jewel" illustrates that the rational nature is ever-present.
The commentary states: "Tying the jewel" is a metaphor. The jewel represents the Buddha-nature of the One Vehicle. It is like a jewel tied beneath the garment of a drunken man.
The jewel represents the śrāvakas who, in their dullness and torpor, do not realize [the truth] and undergo suffering in vain.

In the past, when the Buddha was a prince under the Great Universal Buddha (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū), he inspired them to resolve for awakening through the Mahāyāna Dharma. For many kalpas, they had neglected and forgotten this, remaining unaware;
having attained the state of an arhat, they were satisfied with little. Only now, upon hearing the Buddha recount these past events, do they finally remember.
He bestows the unsurpassed teaching. This is illustrated by the analogy of a close friend who points out a jewel to someone, enabling them to leave behind poverty and suffering.
The act of digging a well represents the various skillful means used to manifest and lead one to awakening.

The commentary states: "Digging a well" is a metaphor; "water" represents the One Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; and "digging and seeking it" represents hearing and understanding [the Dharma].
Contemplation and Practice: If one sees wet mud, one knows that water must be near; likewise, if one hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one knows that Buddhahood is not far off.
He reveals many expedient means to enable people to awaken and enter [the path]. Furthermore, dry soil is a metaphor for sentient beings; damp soil is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles;
mud is a metaphor for Bodhisattvas; and water is a metaphor for the Buddhas.
"The words and meanings are perfectly clear, and the metaphors presented are most profound.

The commentary states: "The Buddha’s exposition of this sutra is such that its phrasing and principles are transparently manifest. The metaphors laid out reveal its significance to be most far-reaching.
Were it not for the Buddha’s profound wisdom and deep compassion, who would be willing to act in this way?"

Were it not for Great Compassion that universally rescues those submerged in the stagnant currents, and the singular, ultimate heart of pity that saves those whose natures have become obscured by delusion—[the commentary] notes:
"Ai" means compassion; "kuang" means vast and far-reaching; "yi ji" means the ultimate limit. This refers to the manifestation through the three cycles and seven parables.
He reveals the One Vehicle; through four modes of practice and six records, he encompasses all sentient beings.
His words and metaphors are skillful and his exhortations are earnest, as he pulls them from the current of birth and death and rescues their deluded natures.
Were it not for the Tathāgata’s great compassion that reaches afar and his ultimate heart of mercy, who else could act in such a way?

From the Han to the Tang dynasties, over six hundred years elapsed. Among the total of more than four thousand fascicles of various scriptures traversed during this period, none surpassed this sutra in terms of being received and upheld.
The commentary states: "From the Han to the Tang, as the Great Teaching was transmitted to the East, among the more than four thousand scrolls of scriptures that passed through in the interim..."
The upholding and recitation of this sutra alone flourishes most brilliantly;

is this not because the capacity of the recipient and the teaching have struck one another? This is surely the lingering dust of the wisdom of Jñānabhadra, which we hear and revere deeply; it is likewise the remaining achievement of King Vīrasena.

The commentary states: "Ji" means merit; "kou" means to cast or strike. This refers to those who, upon hearing [the teaching], immediately develop reverence because their faculties and the teaching harmonize;
such people are all the lingering dust of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and the residual merit of the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.

I have therefore recorded and synthesized these at the beginning of each scripture, hoping thereby to quickly purify the six sense faculties, to look up to the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One,
to swiftly perfect the four virtues, and to follow the profound path toward the Land of Bliss.
The commentary states: "Shu" (庶) expresses a hope or aspiration. This sutra is so preeminent that those who rejoice in it obtain five blessings;

those who copy and uphold it purify the six sense faculties. "Aiming upward" means to reach out for the auspicious assembly of the Compassionate Honored One, which refers to the Dragon Flower Assembly of Maitreya Tathāgata.
"Four Virtues" refers to Nirvana being endowed with the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. "Land of Bliss" refers to the Dharma... [text ends]
The nature is the eternally quiescent land of light; it is profound and subtle. "You" (猷) means the Way (道).
Its vast praise is inexhaustible, intended to be perpetually bequeathed to future generations.
The commentary states: "Bequeath" (貽) means to leave behind. This means that by widely praising this sutra, one hopes to leave it as a legacy for posterity, so that it may circulate without end.
The End. *The Preface to the Propagation of the Lotus Sutra*.
*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle One, Part One.
Explication by the Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wēnlíng.
△ Fifth Section: Detailed Explanation of the Title. First, a general explanation of the title of the scripture:
The wondrous Dharma of the True Mark (bhūtatathatā) is skillfully likened to the lotus flower. Internally, it points directly to the one mind; externally, it encompasses all things.
Within the myriad realms, when the flower blooms it is already the fruit; amidst defilement, there is constant purity. This is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the lotus.
Sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally co-existent; their immersion in change is no different. This is the true reality of the mind.

Their form is illusory, yet their essence is profoundly real. This is the true reality of the realm. Mind and realm, in all their myriad varieties, are collectively termed "Dharma"; whether refined or coarse, they are of one consistency.
Ordinary beings and sages share the same source. Thus, within the various conventional truths, reality is encountered in every encounter with phenomena;

it cannot be demonstrated through words, nor can it be understood through conceptual discrimination. Therefore, it is designated as "wondrous. That the six realms of existence are mired in delusion is because they are confused about this;

that the Buddhas cultivate and realize their enlightenment is because they have realized this. It is for this reason that the verbal teachings were extensively expounded through countless skillful means.

It is for this reason. However, because the defilements of sentient beings are heavy and their faculties are not yet mature, [the Buddhas] first taught the provisional names of the Three Vehicles as a guidance.
Thus, it was expedient rather than real, and coarse rather than subtle.

Once the various impurities have been removed and they trust one another with the essence of the mind, [the Buddhas] then reveal the true aspect and bring them together to return to the One Vehicle; thus, it is subtle and without coarseness. All Buddhas...
The task of teaching has thus been brought to completion. Now, what is called the "Sublime Dharma" (Saddharma) does not involve discarding the coarse to grasp the sublime;

rather, it reveals the sublime by means of the coarse itself. What is called the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) does not involve departing from the three vehicles to speak of one; rather, it brings the three together to return to the one.
Revealing the sublime through the coarse is like the lotus flower, which is pure even while amidst defilement. It is the convergence of the three and the return to the one.
Just as a lotus flower naturally produces both its blossom and its fruit, so too do the Dharma and its metaphor mutually manifest, with name and reality appearing together;
thus it is titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma). Now, one who realizes this Dharma must take great wisdom as its essence and sublime practice as its function.
Wisdom is likened to the lotus and practice to the flower; only when both wisdom and practice are perfected is its wondrousness fully realized. Therefore, the text of the sutra begins with...
A single light shines eastward, fully manifesting the realm of wisdom and culminating in the four dharmas.
The accomplishment of the gates of practice is entirely contained within the beginning of the orthodox teaching. The three cycles of instruction all serve to clarify the essence (*tattva*).

Following the entrustment, the six chapters that unfold thereafter all serve to clarify the function (*prayoga*). Every trace left in the interim is none other than wisdom-practice, which incidentally reveals the essence.

This work comprehensively elucidates the full perfection of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and sets forth the authentic paradigm for awakening. It reveals how the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) brings about the fruition of enlightened virtue;
thus, should anyone hear it, there is none who shall not attain Buddhahood. All who can grasp and awaken to its meaning receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Every single phenomenon and every single characteristic is nothing other than the wondrous Dharma. From this point onward, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—
Regarding brightness and darkness, form and emptiness: if one expands and fulfills this principle, then every object becomes a lamp illuminating the essence of wisdom;

if one extends and puts it into practice, then every step is the gateway to Samantabhadra’s conduct. To directly realize the mind through phenomena, without again departing from objects to contemplate the subtle—this fully encapsulates what is called the "Great Matter" (the Great Cause and Condition).
△ Second, a general statement of his own intent:
I reverently observe that this scripture is widely circulated in the world; there are none who do not desire to recite it with deep mastery.

Yet, whenever I see those for whom it is difficult to achieve, it is not the Sūtra itself that is difficult, but rather the commentaries (zhuanji) that pose the difficulty. For the commentary exists to facilitate understanding of the Sūtra.

This is for the sake of the meaning. Once the words have conveyed the sense, they should cease. Yet, categories are proliferated, names and characteristics are falsely exalted, redundancies abound like rising smoke, and minute classifications fly about like dust.
Various arguments flow on endlessly and aimlessly, so remote that they cannot be fathomed; this is why it is difficult to master.

I have observed the style of those who clarify the scriptures in recent times: they focus solely on the essential intent of the sūtras rather than clinging to archaic phrasing, desiring to be concise yet exhaustive.
Profound yet lucid; in explaining the meaning, he did not rely on formal topical outlines, but sought instead a continuous thread in his discourse.

Brilliant in its literary elegance and clear in its ease of understanding, I now venture to compose this commentary in his style. However, while I possess the aspiration, I lack the talent; I am deeply ashamed that my abilities fall short.
At the outset of this presumptuous endeavor, I privately held the view that the *Lotus Sūtra* is the comprehensive synthesis of the Three Vehicles and the Great Matter.
A Guide. This work concludes with the *Avataṃsaka*’s ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Thereupon, for two years, he pondered deeply upon the *Avataṃsaka* sūtras and śāstras, conducting a profound investigation into the fundamental purpose of our Buddha’s descent into the world.

He further consulted the great masters to explore the mysteries within the lecture halls, exhaustively studying the extensive commentaries of Zhiyi and Ci’en, as well as the annotations by authors of both ancient and modern times. He has selected from what he heard and synthesized it with...

Having examined the essential tenets and verified the methods for realizing the correct dharma across various sutras such as the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*, and the *Vimalakīrti*, he then set pen to paper.

Although his structural divisions and explanations of meaning differ from traditional commentaries, his synthesis of the text and interpretation of its intent accord more closely with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

I have pruned away the superfluous to record only practical matters for the sake of clear exposition. Although I have realized the Buddha’s great matter of knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), I do not yet dare to claim it for myself.
If those who attain realization will not condemn the past or disparage the present by rejecting words because of their author, I ask that you examine this in detail and verify its correctness.
△ Third, the general introduction outlining the structural divisions.

In the exegesis of the sutras there are structural divisions (*ke*), and in the judgment of the teachings there are schools (*zong*). It is like grain having stalks (*ke*) to contain its sheaths and roots, or water having a source (*zong*) to unify its branches and tributaries.
I have often said that the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* constitute one single school. Why is this?
To clarify this: when the Dharma-King appears in response to the times, he manifests as a true sage for a single purpose, having no other vehicle.

Therefore, at the outset, he proclaimed the *Avataṃsaka* specifically to clarify the Sudden Teaching. Although he knew that the faculties of beings were dull, he nevertheless expressed his original intention.

When they became terrified by the Great [Vehicle] and fell into confusion, he then provisionally established expedient means. Once their resolve had become truly sincere, he returned to reveal [the ultimate truth].
[The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] speaks of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). Thus, these two sūtras—one at the beginning and one at the end—truly complement and inspire one another.

Therefore, I now take the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as my primary school and provide this commentary and exposition. Some may say that the *Avataṃsaka* discusses only the pure nature of reality and addresses exclusively those of great capacity, whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* leads those of provisional capacities into the ultimate, addressing all three grades of faculties equally;
thus, the purports of these two sūtras are far apart and do not reach one another. To address this, I cite the former to explain the latter.

I almost do not know its fundamental principle. Yet, I, a fool, have privately observed the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" (*Śraddhābhūmi-parivarta*). Therein, the father previously came seeking his son but could not find him, so he stayed in a certain city.
His household was immensely wealthy; when the impoverished son saw him from afar, he was terrified and fled quickly. This precisely illustrates the initial teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.
When [the father] was near death, he commanded his son to take charge of his wealth; the impoverished son then rejoiced and obtained great treasures.
The "Treasury" (the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*) serves as a direct metaphor for the ultimate teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Viewing it from this perspective of its traces (*jì*), those who were initially startled and terrified and ultimately became closely attached are no different from a father; that which was discarded by the impoverished and acquired by the successful is no different from a treasure.

Since there is nothing about it that differs [from the *Lotus Sūtra*], why would one not take it as the fundamental principle? Furthermore, both sūtras establish their essence through wisdom (*prajñā*).

The practice achieves virtue; the radiance emits auspicious omens, revealing the true mechanism of the entire Dharma-realm. Causes and fruits are harmonized, opening a swift path for cultivation and realization.

In all that is established as the Dharma, the underlying intent is identical. That the two sutras correspond in their essential principles is sufficient to show that the Sage’s teaching is consistent from beginning to end.
The fruit is but a single matter, with no other vehicles; the purport is slightly...

I am fortunate that there is no cause for deep reproach. Now, this scripture is divided into twenty-eight chapters, categorized into three parts: first, the Introduction (Nidāna), consisting of one chapter;
second, the Main Body (Śarīra), consisting of nineteen chapters; and third, the Dissemination (Parīndanā), consisting of eight chapters. Within the Main Body, there are two sections:

the first consists of ten chapters that reveal the Dharma through three cycles, specifically from the "Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya) to the "Record of Learning" (Śaikṣa), which comprise eight chapters, expounding the teachings of the three cycles and bestowing them upon others.

The three chapters on the prediction [of Buddhahood] span from the "Dharma Master" chapter to the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter; they bestow the extensive prediction to encompass and perfect the previous predictions, and assemble all Buddhas to perfectly realize the previous Dharma.
The two sections revealing the marvelous exhortation to uphold consist of nine chapters:
from the "Devadatta" chapter to the "Peaceful Conduct" chapter, which reveal the excellence of meritorious practice; and from the "Emergence" chapter to the "Life Span" chapter.
The four chapters from "Distinction" to "Not-Light" manifest the marvel of the fundamental and the manifested.

They cause those who have attained awakening through the preceding [sections] to rely upon these for broad propagation and maintenance, so that they do not lose the perfect school and accord with the wondrous Dharma.
The remaining six chapters, from the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" which initiates the teaching to the "Chapter on Entrustment" which confers it, constitute the entirety of the circulation.

The substance of the preceding Dharma manifests the sphere of practice; its circulation constitutes this Path. This is called "the gateway of the constant great function, wherein practice accords with wisdom.
Now, first, regarding the introductory section (*nidāna*): it opens the thread of the main teaching (*samyak-artha*). That Dharma has two parts:

from the assembly of the multitudes of humans and devas until the conclusion of the *Ananta-artha-sūtra*, when the Buddha sat in Great Samādhi and the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers. Six...
It shatters the conditions of the veil of ignorance and manifests the true reality of the realm of wisdom through a single light; this is how the World-Honored One Śākyamuni initiated its unfolding.
Subsequently, Maitreya presented his inquiries and Mañjuśrī resolved the doubts, drawing forth the fundamental light of the Lamp-Light Buddha to attest to the auspicious signs of the present Buddha;
this is how that Great Being followed the current and assisted in its unfolding.

The remaining extensive citations all provide a general overview of the beginning and end of a single sutra. To reach the orthodox teaching, one must first clarify the introductory section (*nidāna*).
Then, regarding profound sutras, it will be like finding the thread when unraveling silk—nothing will remain unexhausted;
it will be like ascending to the hall in proper order—one will surely reach its depths. △ Fourth, the time of the translator.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, by imperial decree.
Yao Qin was a usurping kingdom during the Eastern Jin; its ruler was surnamed Yao and named Xing, who served as the King of Qin.

"Kumārajīva" in Sanskrit means "Child-Immortal," signifying that he possessed the virtues of an elder despite being of childhood years. He translated [these texts] in accordance with the decree of the King of Qin.
Translation of this Sūtra.
*The Introduction to the Lotus Sūtra*, Chapter One. △ Five:
Correctly Explaining the Textual Meaning, Part Three. First, the Introductory Section, divided into four parts. One: The Time and Place of the Teaching.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.

"Thus have I heard from the Buddha regarding this Dharma"—this was the first utterance when Ānanda ascended the seat at the time of the compilation of the teachings, intended merely to testify that there was a transmission of the Dharma;
it was not meant as a profound exposition. The phrase "at one time" refers to the Buddha.
"Bequeathed words. Because they are commonly used across various sūtras, they do not point to a specific location. Rājagṛha is the city adjacent to Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa);
it belongs to the territory of the kingdom of Magadha and is situated among the human realms of the Western Regions. Gṛdhrakūṭa means "Vulture Peak" in Chinese;
it is named after its shape and was the dwelling place of ancient Buddhas, as it was where those ancient Buddhas resided.
Therefore, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Now, the locations upon which the preaching of the Dharma relies vary according to their respective thematic intentions (*abhiprāya*).

In the *Avataṃsaka*, ten successive sites are established to perfectly manifest the *dharmadhātu*. In the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Śūraṅgama-samādhi*), reliance is placed on the Great Luminous Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) to directly reveal the primordial arising.
This reliance on a city in the human realm is intended to clarify the meaning of the lotus through the identity of defilement and purity, and it accords with the dwelling place of ancient Buddhas.
This indicates that he followed the patriarchs to continue the way of the lamp’s light. △ Second, the audience at the Dharma assembly, in two parts:
first, the heading and enumeration of the categories;

second, the audience at the Dharma assembly, in three parts: first, the śrāvakas; next, the bodhisattvas; and finally, humans and devas. This assembly of the sutra represents the provisional [teachings].

Returning to the reality [of the text]: the Śrāvakas are listed first because they were the primary audience (*pratyadhikaraṇa*). The Bodhisattvas constitute the assembly of the principal and the retinue;

the humans and devas constitute the assembly of external protectors. △ Second, listing the assemblies according to the topical outline, in three parts: First, the assembly of Śrāvakas, in two parts. First, the assembly of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus (up to: ... whose minds had attained mastery).
The Buddha usually followed an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people; that the present number is stated as twelve thousand includes those gathered from other regions.
The meaning of *arhat* is translated as "slayer of thieves" (*zhai-ze*), also called "one worthy of offerings" (*ying-gong*), and also called "non-arising" (*busheng*).

Furthermore, the mind of the "Good Abyss" (Śubhākara) cannot maintain its singular unity. When it clings to stillness and gives rise to consciousness, which flows out and rushes toward objects, it is called "outflow" (*āsrava*).

These various outflows refer to the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). All of them take the deluded consciousness that clings to stillness as their essence.

They are the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. These afflictions—namely greed, hatred, delusion, and the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—serve as the conditions for the outflows (*āsrava*).

They ravage the *dharmakāya* and oppress the true nature; thus they are called "affliction-thieves. To speak of the exhaustion of outflows and the absence of affliction means that because the root has been exhausted, the conditions no longer exist;
this is what is meant by "slaying the thieves. One's own benefit consists in the realization of wisdom and the abandonment of delusions.
Regarding this matter, the words and phrases mean that the causes and effects of the three realms are all matters for others, whereas the merit of wisdom and abandonment is called one’s own benefit.
Only upon attaining one’s own benefit does one become fit to serve as a field of merit for humans and devas; therefore, one is titled "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

In the Vinaya texts, whenever it concerns being "worthy of offerings," one must reflect upon whether one's own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient; this is what is meant by reflecting upon one's own benefit. Indeed, [The text continues: ...for indeed...
They afflict their bodies, sit upright while eating, prostrate themselves with raised knees, and receive offerings while standing in a contrarian posture.
If one lacks the virtue of self-benefit, the harm is no small matter; let those who practice the Way recognize this.

For all those with fetters, the karma of deluded habits serves as the cause for birth within the twenty-five realms of existence. Since the cause is exhausted, the fruit perishes; this is called "non-arising."
Furthermore, in the Hinayana, having concentration without wisdom constitutes a partial bondage and a lack of mastery;

that it is now said "the mind has attained mastery" indicates one who is fully endowed with both concentration and wisdom and is thus liberated in both ways— this clarifies that the Great Arhats are merely appearing as manifestations for the sake of the assembly.
Their names were Ājñātakauṇḍinya (and so on), up to these great Arhats renowned by the multitude.
This passage cites the leaders among the twelve thousand [monks], who belong to the ranks of the ten great disciples.
The Buddha had ten great disciples who, as Dharma-kings and Dharma-ministers, each possessed a multitude of virtues; they provisionally manifested specialization to assist [the Buddha].
They assisted in the great transformation. Thus, Mahākāśyapa was foremost in *dhūta* practices; Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyāyana in supernormal powers;
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra in debate; Aniruddha in the divine eye; Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra in preaching the Dharma; Subhūti in understanding emptiness;
Ānanda in extensive learning; Upāli in upholding the Vinaya; and Rāhula in secret conduct—each occupied the first place, just as there were ten disciples in the school of Confucius.
Their inclusion among the ranks of the Sages is their constant number.

That there are now twenty individuals, from Kauṇḍinya to Rāhula, is because they concurrently possess manifold virtues that fully manifest the transformation of the Dharma. Each of them also possesses a foremost virtue.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Kauṇḍinya was the first to attain awakening; Uruvilvākāśyapa [gathered] a multitude through offerings; Gayākāśyapa subdued all fetters; Nadīkāśyapa..."
Śāriputra was skilled in teaching and transforming others; Kapphiṇa understood the stars and constellations; Gavāmpati received celestial offerings; Revata was free from confusion and disorder;

Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was able to practice ascetic sitting; Bakula lived out his full lifespan without an untimely death; Kuṭhivīra excelled at answering difficult questions; and Sundara was preeminent in his physical appearance.

Each is foremost. As for those well-known to the assembly, their virtues are so manifest that there is no need for elaborate explanation of the various names and their etymologies, as these are not the essential points of the sutra.
△ Second, the assembly of those still in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, there were two thousand persons, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), who had arrived together with their retinues.
This assembly of lesser *śrāvakas* consisted of those still on the stage of training and those training toward the state beyond training.
Mahāprajāpatī—here translated as "Great Path of Love"—was the head of the community of nuns; she and Yaśodharā both manifested traces among the mundane world to act as guiding influences.
The Assembly. △ Second, the Assembly of Bodhisattvas:
"Eighty thousand Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas... able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
Regarding "Bodhisattva-mahāsattva": this refers to the great bodhisattvas among bodhisattvas, namely those on the stages (bhūmi) and those who are equal to enlightenment (samyaksambuddha).

This places them in the same category [as those beyond the stages]. This excludes those prior to the [first] stage. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Universal Enlightenment.
*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "Total Retention," meaning that one attains all-knowledge and retains all phenomena.

*Pratibhāna* (eloquence) is the general term for the four types of analytical eloquence. From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are called the stage of non-retrogression. At the fifth and seventh stages, they attain...
The *dhāraṇī*. To speak of the definitive Dharma is called the "Non-retrogressive Wheel. All [beings] extol its virtues.
Those who abide in the stage of non-retrogression have attained this Path and established themselves therein; those who turn the non-retrogressive wheel employ this Path to benefit others.
This is the virtue of awakening oneself and awakening others. One who cultivates the body through compassion intends to provide universal succor.
"Skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom" means being able to employ *upāya* (expedient means). "Thoroughly penetrating great wisdom" means that what is realized is luminous.
"Reaching the other shore" means that what is accomplished is substantial. These are internal virtues. Because they are thus fulfilled and manifested, one's reputation spreads.
His external virtues are universally renowned. As for his internal virtues, those who have attained thorough penetration are transformed upon seeing him;

as for his external virtues being universally renowned, those who hear of them are transformed. Thus, the number of those he delivers reaches hundreds of thousands, none of which exist prior to the stages [of the Bodhisattva path];
these are all the virtues of a great Bodhisattva.
Their names were: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva (and so on), totaling eighty thousand people.

Because this sutra establishes its essence through wisdom (*jñāna*), Mañjuśrī is placed at the head. Indeed, Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom and sublime virtue as the embodiment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
he is the teacher of all Buddhas and the eye of the world. In opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), none precedes him.
These [names] each represent a single virtue of this sutra. Avalokiteśvara assists with wisdom and practices compassion; Mahāsthāmaprāpta possesses great virtuous function;
Vīrya-dhara (Diligent Mind) does not regress in his recollection, tirelessly practicing with diligence for billions of kalpas; Ratnapāṇi (Jewel Hand) holds the Dharma-jewels in his grasp;

Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King) dispenses medicine according to the capacity of beings; Viśvada (Courageous Giver) is able to relinquish everything; and Ratnacandra (Jewel Moon) awakens to the luminosity of the essence.
Vimala is pure; Candraprabha can dispel the darkness of delusion; Pūrṇacandra possesses both of these virtues; Mahāsthāmaprāpta bears the great Dharma;
Amitabha remains unmoved by objects despite his immeasurable power; Trailokyavikrama does not manifest body or mind; Bhadrapāla skillfully protects right view;
Maitreya continues the Buddha’s work through compassion; Ratnākara is able to gather and benefit others; and Śāstṛ leads those who go astray into [the path].
Correct. These eight thousand [verses] represent the manifest dharma of the foremost sutra.

It is because Great Wisdom opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, while Compassion assists that wisdom to cultivate all virtues through successive stages, even leading the heterodox into the correct path;

thus, the essence of the One Vehicle is complete and the function of the ten thousand practices is perfected. The reason Puṇyaprasava (Samantabhadra) is not listed here is that, from the perspective of Avalokiteśvara onwards...
The following sections all concern the practices of Samantabhadra. However, at the outset, one first establishes the fundamental nature through wisdom to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
finally, one perfects virtue through practice, thereby manifesting the specific representations of Samantabhadra. [Section on] the Threefold Assembly of Gods and Humans, Part Two: 1.
The Heavenly Beings and the Eight Classes of Spirits (Ṣaḍ-devanikāya-aṣṭa-graha). 6. First, the Assembly of Various Heavenly Beings.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, together with his retinue of twelve thousand devaputras, was present.

Śakra Devānām-indra is the same as Indra. Also present were the devaputra Candraprabha (Moonlight), the devaputra Samantagandha (Universal Fragrance), and the devaputra Ratnaprabha-sūrya (Jewel Light Sun).
The six heavens of the desire realm are called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, and the Tuṣita Heaven.
[The heavens] leading [to] Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmita-vaśavartin: Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Lord of Nirmāṇarati is titled Īśvara;
the Lord of Paranirmita-vaśavartin is titled Maheśvara. The reason Yāma and Tuṣita are not mentioned is that by citing the upper and lower extremes, the middle ones are included.
Within the four dhyānas of the Rūpadhātu, there are eighteen heavens. In the first dhyāna, there are three Brahmā heavens, whose king is...
He who is the lord of the Sahā world is named Śikhin Mahābrahmā; the Heavenly King of the Three Radiances in the Second Dhyāna is named Ābhāsvara Mahābrahmā.
As for the omission of other devas, the term "etc. is used to include them. △ Second, the assembly of nāgas.
There were eight dragon kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

Nanda is translated here as "Joy" and Upananda as "Worthy. Because they bring joy to all things with their timely rains and possess the virtue of worthiness, these two dragons are those who were subdued by Maudgalyāyana.
Sāgara means "Ocean"; Vāsuki means "Many-Headed"; Takṣaka...
*Kāyūna* means "manifesting poison. *Anavatapta* is the name of a lake. *Mānasa* means "large-bodied. *Utpala* means "blue lotus pond.
*Saṃkhyeya* refers to an indefinite number; that is to say, an incalculable number. △ Third, the assembly of *kiṃnaras*.
There were four Kinnara kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
"Kinnara" is translated here as "Doubtful Deity" (*yishen*); they resemble humans but have horns, making them suspect.

They are also called "Singing Deities" (*geshen*), for they can sing along with whatever the Buddha preaches; thus, they are all named after the Dharma. Dharmakinnara sang the Four Noble Truths; Sukumārakinnara sang...
The twelve links of dependent origination; the six perfections of the Great Gāndhārī; the one vehicle of upholding the Gāndhārī. △ Fourth, the assembly of *gandharvas*:
there were four *gandharva* kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
Gandharva is translated here as "Fragrance-Sniffer. They are able to seek out fragrances and perform music. "Music" refers to arts such as singing and dancing;
"musical sounds" refer to drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments. "Exquisite" refers to the most superior among these arts; "exquisite sound" refers to the most superior among musical sounds.
△ Fifth, the assembly of asuras.
There are four asura kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundred thousand retinues.
Asura is translated here as "non-deva" (fei-tian), because they possess much anger and lack the conduct of devas. Vemacitra is translated as "having bonds," for he is fond of fighting.
Because of his combat, Khara-vāman (佉羅云) has broad shoulders. Regarding "surging ocean waters": Vemacitra (毗摩質多) refers to the sound of waves on the ocean.
Regarding "striking the ocean waves": Rāhu (羅睺) means "obscuration," for he is able to obstruct the sun and moon. △ Sixth, the assembly of Garuḍas.
There are four *garuḍa* kings (up to), each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
*Garuḍa* is translated here as "Golden-Winged Bird" (*jīngì niǎo*). They constantly devour dragons; they possess great majesty that terrifies dragons, and their massive bodies surpass all others.

The Great Dragon King is always satisfied with his desires; he possesses this jewel upon his neck. Among the eight classes of divine beings, all are able to manifest transformations and attend the assembly;
the yakṣas and mahoragas are not listed here, as they are omitted. △ Second, the assembly of kings and others.
King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī (up to: withdrew and sat to one side.
The queen of King Bimbisāra of Magadha was named Vaidehī; her son was named Ajātaśatru. Regarding the phrase "not raising the people":
it is understood that when the king went out, the people followed him. Each paid homage at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
On one side, although his words were many, they were not hurried; instead, they were solemn and orderly. △ Third, the Great Enlightenment Perfectly Gives Rise to Six:
these are called the six auspicious omens. First, the omen of preaching the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly... [the teaching on the Dharma for enlightening beings, which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind].
△ Second, the auspicious sign of entering meditative concentration:
After the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra... [his body and mind were unmoving].
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "Immeasurable meanings arise from the single mark of reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa*), giving rise to immeasurable dharmas.

That the assembly first hears the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and, upon its conclusion, enters the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings is for the purpose of initiating the sequence of the *Wonderful Dharma*.
It demonstrates that within a single phenomenon, a single principle, a single movement, and a single stillness, there is nothing that does not fully possess [all meanings].
After [the teaching of] the Immeasurable Meanings, one may then enter the Subtle Dharma. △ Third, the auspicious omen of the raining of flowers:
At that time, the heavens rained *māndārava* flowers (extending to) which were scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
*Mahā* means "great. *Mandārava* means "pleasing to the mind. *Mañjūṣaka* means "soft and supple. These are all exquisite celestial flowers.
Flowers symbolize the direct cause (*nidāna*), for a cause must inevitably lead to its fruit.

That they were scattered upon the Buddha and also reached the great assembly demonstrates that those present in this gathering shall attain the direct cause. △ Fourth, the auspicious sign of the earth quaking.
The worlds of all Buddhas shake in six ways. These six shakes consist of:

moving, rising, surging, trembling, roaring, and crashing. Explanations such as "rising in the east and sinking in the west" or "shaking everywhere and shaking universally" do not depart from these [six].
The reason for the six shakes is to symbolize the overturning and breaking of the six consciousnesses.

[The text] clarifies this. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the mountains, rivers, and great earth are all produced by the coagulation of ignorance (*avidyā*), while their fundamental basis is solely the One True Reality.
Therefore, it says, "Throughout the Buddha-worlds. △ Fifth, the auspicious omens of the assembly’s joy.
At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly (up to) rejoiced, joined their palms, and with single-minded devotion gazed upon the Buddha.

Delighted to behold the preceding auspicious omen, they stood poised and waited for the sublime response. △ Sixth, the threefold auspicious sign of emitting light: First, the radiance of the light extended everywhere.
At that time, the Buddha emitted from the white tuft between his eyebrows a light (extending until) it reached everywhere without exception.
A single ray of light pervaded all, fully manifesting the wondrous essence. The white tuft is the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).

The eastern direction represents the realm of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). The "eighteen thousand worlds" refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses. Sentient beings...

Deluded regarding this fundamental luminosity and fundamental wisdom, one forms the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). Because these act as self-imposed limitations and obstructions, it is difficult to realize the wondrous essence.

Therefore, prior to preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he first manifests these auspicious signs, causing the practitioner to directly and spontaneously awaken their own fundamental luminosity and clearly perceive fundamental wisdom.
Thus, the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses all become the realm of wisdom; no longer subject to limitations or obstructions, they are vast, penetrating, and perfectly interfused.
Therefore, it is said that there are eighteen thousand worlds. △ Second, the complete manifestation of the phenomena and characteristics of the Dharma-realm:
from below, down to the Avīci Hell (up to) and hearing the sutras and teachings preached by all Buddhas.
*Avīci* is translated here as "Uninterrupted" (*mujian*); it is the lowest level of the hells. *Akaniṣṭha* is translated as "Ultimate Limit of Obstruction";
it is the highest pinnacle of the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). The reason the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not mentioned is that formless states cannot be seen.
From the upper limit of the heavens down to the depths of the hells, one sees all those lands within this world; this is what is meant by "manifesting completely."
The three [visions] fully manifest the beginning and end of the Buddha’s life:
first, seeing those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs (up to) erecting stūpas of the seven precious substances for the Buddha’s relics;
second, seeing the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus practicing and attaining the Way; and finally, seeing the modes of conduct of the bodhisattvas and buddhas.
Reaching Nirvana and erecting a stupa—this manifests the beginning and end of all Buddhas for sentient beings.

That a single ray of light shines eastward, pervading everywhere and appearing in its perfect entirety, is shown in such detail precisely because it reveals the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena based upon the realm of wisdom.
When the myriad phenomena of the world are observed from the perspective of the objective realm of consciousness, they are all illusory and deceptive, and their reality cannot be grasped.

When observed from the perspective of the objective realm of self-aware wisdom, such natures and characteristics, causes and conditions, and such fruits and retributions—both in their origins and their conclusions—are all one wondrous luminosity;

there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). If sentient beings were to have this fundamental luminosity fully manifest and their fundamental wisdom appear before them, then they would illuminate everything with vast clarity.
The perfect manifestation is no different from that of the Buddha; the wondrous essence, the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), is vividly manifest within the mind and eyes.
Thus Mañjuśrī said: "Now the Buddha emits radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true reality. From this point onward, the entire text of the sutra fully reveals this principle;

therefore, the introductory thread is set forth as follows. Part Two: The Four Great Beings Assist in Bringing Forth [the Meaning]. Section One: Maitreya Presents the Question. Subsection Two: [Maitreya’s Question].
