First, the general inquiry into the reason for the six auspicious omens.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
"Mañjuśrī... [you have] attained what was never before."
This question concerns the four auspicious omens of the emission of light, the raining of flowers, the shaking of the earth, and the joy of the assembly;

it does not inquire about the two omens of preaching the Dharma and entering meditative concentration, because these are things commonly seen. II. A detailed inquiry into what was seen within the light, in two parts: 1.
An inquiry into the phenomena and characteristics of the Dharma-realm manifested in their entirety.
Light radiates from between his eyebrows (extending) so that all this is seen.
This verse describes the phenomena ranging from the highest heavens above to the hells below.
Furthermore, he beholds the various Buddhas (extending) as they preach the path of purity for him.
The verse describes seeing and hearing the various sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Buddhas. The Holy Lord, the Lion, fearlessly speaks the Dharma;
he expounds the sūtras as the most subtle and supreme, such that people delight in hearing them. He teaches the bodhisattvas through the One Vehicle.
He preaches the True Dharma with its various causes and conditions, even teaching the path of purity. That is to say, by means of the Three [Vehicles]...

This refers to the vehicle for awakening sentient beings. If a person encounters suffering and reaches the ultimate limit of all suffering, this is the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths of the Hīnayāna.
The four phrases correspond respectively to the vision of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, the cultivation of the path, and the realization of cessation.

If a person possesses merit, one explains the Pratyekabuddha vehicle to them; this is the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination of the Madhyayāna. The Śrāvaka plants the seeds over three lifetimes.
Practicing merit is for the sake of wearying of suffering; practicing merit for a hundred kalpas is for the sake of seeking the Way.

Therefore, if there is one who possesses the merit to make offerings to the Buddha and whose resolve seeks the supreme Dharma, they may be granted the Middle Vehicle. If there is a son of the Buddha, one should proceed to explain to them the Pure Path, which is the Dharma of the Six Perfections of the Mahāyāna.
The Six Perfections take various practices as their function and take unsurpassed wisdom as their essence. Practice...

Attaining the wisdom of deliverance is itself free from defiled attachment; therefore, it is called the "Pure Path. Regarding those who speak of the two vehicles as "persons," and those who speak of the Mahāyāna as "sons of the Buddha":
while they may dwell in grass huts and identify themselves with common laborers, once they have accomplished their great resolve, they are then designated as "sons."
"Mañjuśrī, from now on I shall briefly explain.

[This marks] the conclusion of the preceding section and the opening of the subsequent one. △ Second, the question concerning the beginning and end of the manifestation of Buddhas and sentient beings in the perfect realm:
"I see that land... [up to] "...and strike the Dharma drum."

This verse marks the beginning of practice; the subsequent verses mark the end in Nirvana. These represent the various signs of faith and understanding through diverse causes and conditions, yet their essential core does not transcend the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
From "There may be those who practice giving" up to "seeking the wisdom of a Buddha" refers to the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
From "I see various kings" up to "donning the dharma robes" refers to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). [The section on] the bhikṣu’s dwelling...

Reciting the sutras in leisure is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). The bodhisattva’s courageous striving for the Way is the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Detaching from desire to cultivate dhyāna up to the praise of the Dharma-kings is the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Profound wisdom and firm resolve up to the striking of the Dharma drum is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). There are three aggregates of precepts (*śīla-skandha*):

namely, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), the precept of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of gathering ethical discipline (*saṃvara-śīla*). All...
The King’s inquiry concerns the inclusion of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*); the dismissal of ministers and concubines concerns the inclusion of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka*);

and donning the Dharma robes concerns the inclusion of ethical discipline (*saṃvara-saṃgrāhaka*). There are three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*): namely, patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*), patience toward suffering (*duḥkhakṣānti*), and patience regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthakṣānti*).

When a bhikṣu dwells in seclusion reciting the sūtras, the presence of wicked people and fierce beasts in the quiet forests and secluded valleys constitutes patience toward living beings; the sharpening of the bhikṣu’s moral conduct constitutes patience toward suffering.
Patience in suffering and delighting in the recitation of the sūtras constitute the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). There are three kinds of detachment from desire:

namely, detachment from the desires of the five sensory objects, detachment from the desires of the two vehicles, and detachment from the desire for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). Those who attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) do not possess the five powers of ordinary worldlings;
rather, they are distinguished as being with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*) based on whether they are beginners or have attained the stage of a Buddha.

Furthermore, seeing the Bodhisattvas (up to) seeking the unsurpassed path—this extensively praises the characteristics of the causes and conditions for the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Way. That devas and nāgas pay him homage without feeling pride is the Bodhisattva’s self-respect.
That he dwells in the forest, emits light, and relieves the sufferings of those in the hells is the Bodhisattva’s great compassion.
The "affinities of delusion" refers to those who merely indulge their passions and are unable to transform toward the good.

From never having slept to being joyful without satiety—these constitute the six perfections. The various practices do not follow a fixed sequence; rather, they are undertaken according to what one encounters.
Some may speak of the Dharma of quiescent extinction (*śānti*), while others seek the Way through the teachings. As for "contemplating the nature of all phenomena," etc.:

Some seek the Way through applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). As for the phrase "the mind has no attachments," it means seeking the Way by departing from doctrinal contemplation and forgetting the traces of the mind.
Although various causes, conditions, and appearances differ, they are none other than the wondrous practice of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, it is clearly manifested within the light.
From "Mañjuśrī" until "its flowers bloomed," this verse marks the conclusion of the *Nirvāṇa*.
"Straight" refers to length, while "horizontal" refers to breadth. Forty *li* constitute one *yojana*.

"Ten days. Regarding the "King of Heavenly Trees": this is the *pārijāta* tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When its precious flowers bloom, the celestial realm is naturally adorned with exquisite beauty;
this is the karmic fruit of making offerings to the śarīra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the sons of the Buddha adorn [the stūpa] for the offering of the śarīra in such a manner. △ Second, the request to resolve doubts.

△ II. Mañjuśrī Resolves Doubts (in four parts). 1. Responding through Reflection: At that time, Mañjuśrī...
[omitted] ...therefore manifests this auspicious sign. The rain falls with a single flavor to moisten and saturate;
the conch shell sounds with a single voice to penetrate everywhere; the drum beats with a proclamation to gather the multitude. This is the meaning.
This is the section on "Revealing according to what is appropriate. △ Second, citing scriptural evidence, which has two parts. First, citing the original beginning of the Lamp-Light [Tathāgata]:
"O sons of good family... (up to)... the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

" asaṃkhyeya " means incalculable; "kalpa" means a period of time. To trace the original source and initial beginning of this radiant auspiciousness back through incalculable and inconceivable kalpas—this light and this Dharma truly begin in the beginningless, transcending all measure and number.
As for the Buddha’s title, "Sun, Moon, and Lamp": the sun illuminates the day, the moon illuminates the night, and the lamp illuminates even during the day.
Where the moon does not shine, it penetrates the way of day and night, continuing without end.

Because that Buddha’s wondrous wisdom and true illumination possess the virtues of these three, they are taken as his title. Of the ten titles, the first refers to the root and the last refers to the trace.

The "Middle" refers to the root of virtue, which is the true nature that is identical to all suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. The "Trace" refers to the transformation through the Path;
because humans and devas revere him, he is called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavat*). Virtue is the matter of the myriad virtues and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);

because he is a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), he is worthy of offerings. Because he perfectly possesses the four wisdoms, he is able to achieve correct and universal knowledge. The true illumination of the myriad practices is called...

One who is perfected in knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*). One who skillfully enters into the afflictions of the world and exhaustively masters all phenomena is called the "Well-Gone One who Understands the World" (*sugata lokavidū*).

One who has realized that which is unequaled is called the "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*). One who transforms sentient beings without violence and remains steadfastly unbending is called the "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*).

He who serves as a model for the three realms is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). One whose self-enlightenment and enlightenment of others are perfected is called a Buddha (*buddha*).
In brief, these are titles for one who has come from the path of suchness, is endowed with all virtues, responds to sentient beings, and is honored by the world.
He expounds the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, culminating in the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This passage describes how the Lamp-Lightener (*Dīpaṃkara*) likewise taught the Three Vehicles according to what was appropriate for the One Vehicle. Regarding "beginning, middle, and end," this refers to the teachings of the Three Vehicles;

they are all "not not-good" because they accord with the capacities of beings and harmonize with the Path. Since the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) is revealed by means of provisional skillful means (*upāya*), such is their significance.

Profound and far-reaching; because it employs skillful means according to the capacities of beings, its language is subtle and ingenious. Because it is rooted in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it is pure and without admixture.

Although the three vehicles are taught, they all ultimately return to the single reality. △ Seven: Verses on the identity of the paths of the three periods of time. One verse on the past.
The departure from the Way is the same for both. First, all Buddhas are equal;
from "countless kalpas in the past" up to "causing them to enter the Buddha-way," it is said that they all rely on skillful means (*upāya*) to expound the reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, from "the various great holy lords" (up to) "to assist in manifesting the ultimate truth," this extensively elaborates upon the differences in the Buddhas' skillful means according to the capacities of sentient beings; these words are numerous.

That is to say, by means of many skillful means, they assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the wondrous Dharma, as set forth in the following text, reaching upward to the Bodhisattvas and downward...

This refers to the fact that even the minor good roots and subtle causes of humans and devas all lead to the attainment of Buddhahood. In the following text, four categories are presented as side-issues.
△ Second, the Bodhisattvas and others are equal to the three [vehicles]. First, a verse on the practice of the Bodhisattva.
"If there are any classes of sentient beings... (up to) "...have all already attained the Buddha-way.

Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The first four constitute merit (*puṇya*), while the latter two constitute wisdom (*prajñā*).

Therefore, it is said: "Practicing various kinds of merit and wisdom. From here below, all practices are exhaustively and minutely enumerated; this is precisely the manifestation of assistance through manifold means.
If one takes that which is revealed as the primary meaning, then every single practice and every single characteristic is nothing other than the wondrous Dharma;

every raising of a hand and every lowering of the head is nothing other than wondrous conduct. This is why all attain the Buddha-way; even if they have not yet perfected it, the Way is already complete within them.
△ Second, the verse on the practices of the śrāvakas.
After the various Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, those sentient beings who possess a virtuous and gentle mind have all already attained the Buddha-way.

Those who practice as śrāvakas through virtue and gentleness are praised for having minds that are well-tamed, supple, and soft, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Abiding in a tamed mind is the practice of the noble ones. △ Third, the verses on the practices of humans and devas, in four parts. First, the composition...
The Stūpas of Good Conduct.
After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas—[up to] all have already attained the Buddha-way.

As for the "ten thousand billion kinds," these consist of either the seven treasures, fragrant wood, or tiles, stones, sand, and earth; they vary in quality according to whether they are noble or humble, and whether they are of superior or inferior substance.
The various forms are the wondrous land; the expressions of earnest sincerity and playful laughter are the wondrous mind.
Thus, all attain the Buddha-way. △ Second, the virtuous practice of creating images.
If a person, for the sake of the Buddha, [creates] various images—
whether carved from wood or lacquered on cloth, molded from clay or inlaid with jewels,
cast from gold, silver, or even tin and iron, or painted with various colors or even with fingernails— the essence of these forms or their shadows...
The "marks" (lakṣaṇa), such as those of the Buddha, are the wondrous form. The "mental activities" (citta-karma), such as performing them oneself or directing others to do so, are the wondrous mind.
As for the gradual accumulation of merit and the perfection of great compassion—such various phenomena are none other than the true mark (dharmatā); they are all the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Therefore, they all attain the Buddha-way. However, this is not something that can be reached by those of the Two Vehicles; hence it is said, "He transforms only the Bodhisattvas.
△ Third, the good practice of making offerings to the Buddhas.

If a person, at a stupa or temple (up to the point where it is like a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted), offers incense, flowers, banners, or canopies out of a heart of reverence; or plays various drums and music out of a heart of joy;
or offers a single color or a single fragrance out of a distracted mind; or even [offers] the faint sound of a hymn or the slight bowing of the head—
It is well that all shall attain the Buddha-way. This is because the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is free from reverence and negligence, and transcends joy and aversion;

for both stillness and agitation, the small and the great, are all universally integrated into one. If one were to regard reverence and joy as correct and negligence and agitation as incorrect, [one would not realize this truth].
Thus, one would dwell for a lifetime in the realm of right and wrong and the field of likes and dislikes;

even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, with body shattered and life ground to powder, there would still be no time for attaining the Way—let alone in the brief moment of raising a hand or lowering the head.

That he "crossed over the multitudes and entered extinction" is a detailed account of his attainment of Buddhahood and his transformative activities. A *śaṅkha* is a conch shell; the large variety is coiled and curved.
Because it resembles a horn, it is called a "horn-shell. △ Fourth, regarding scattered wholesome deeds:
If a person with a distracted mind enters a stupa or temple and recites "Namo Buddha" even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.

The various practices begin by citing the six perfections; among these, merit and wisdom are the most difficult. At the end, it cites the distracted mind and states that invoking the Buddha's name is the easiest.

Yet, since all achieve the path to Buddhahood through these means, one can truly believe that the Way has neither difficulty nor ease. Whether in times of upheaval or in moments of haste, there is nothing that is not the wondrous Dharma;
there is nothing that is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding all the Buddhas of the past, whether they were in the world or had already entered parinirvāṇa, if there were those who heard this Dharma, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood.
This concludes the section on the commonality of the past path. △ Second, the verse on the commonality of the future path.
All future World-Honored Ones (up to and including this point) shall likewise attain this path.
This is identical to Śākyamuni’s original establishment of his vow. Next, it clarifies how [the path] assists in manifestation according to the capacities of beings.
Although the Buddhas of future ages may preach hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates, in reality they constitute but a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is similar to the Buddhas of the past who, through various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), assisted in manifesting the same intent; this passage merely simplifies the wording.
"The Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings" (up to) "the Guide’s skillful means of teaching.

This again clarifies the Buddha’s intention in preaching the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Since phenomena are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), words and signs are quiescent and cannot admit of verbal expression.
It is solely for the sake of initiating the Buddha-seed that the One Vehicle is taught. This is the same as what follows in the subsequent text.

First, regarding "extinction," it is taught through the power of skillful means. As for "this Dharma abides in its own station": the myriad phenomena of the universe are all, in their very essence, the true mark (*dharmatā*).
As for "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding": mountains, rivers, and the great earth are, in their actual substance, truly constant.
Because the Three Vehicles eliminate appearances to clarify the truth, the Dharma does not abide in a fixed station; because they seek stillness by rejecting movement, they perceive existence.
As for the flux of conditioned phenomena: in the One Vehicle, reality is encountered in every event because one does not give rise to emotional attachments or intellectual interpretations.

Thus, each phenomenon abides in its own station, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant; this is precisely what is realized at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Therefore, it is for the sake of sentient beings that these teachings are expediently expounded.
△ The three verses concerning the present path are the same [as those for the future].
From "Worshipped by devas and humans" up to "its reality is the Buddha-vehicle," it next clarifies how [the teaching] assists and manifests [the truth] according to the capacities of beings.
"Knowing the various conducts of sentient beings... (up to) "...teaching through appropriate skillful means.
This is also the same as the preceding supplementary explanation for the *Jianwen* (Explanatory Text). △ Eighth: Verses on the Identity of the Path of Self-Cultivation.
Now I am likewise; for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings, I proclaim and reveal the Buddha-way through various Dharma-gates.
Next, it clarifies how [the teaching] assists manifestation according to individual capacities.
"By the power of my wisdom, I know the dispositions and desires of sentient beings; through skillful means, I preach all dharmas so that they may all attain joy.

This also serves to clarify and supplement the prose text. The reason for citing these supplementary clarifications at each section is to demonstrate that the ritual protocols for preaching the Dharma are identical for all Buddhas of the three periods of time, from the past up to Śākyamuni.
△ Ninth: Verses on the Original Beginning and the Opening of the Provisional.
Śāriputra, you should know... [up to] ...and give rise to the mind of great compassion.

The verses concerning the Buddha’s appearance in the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) state: "Exhausted in merit and wisdom" refers to the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). "The cycle of birth and death is not severed" refers to the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

The turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). To be blinded by attachment to desire is the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Not seeking the Buddha-dharma is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

To enter deeply into false views is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Using suffering to abandon suffering—claiming not to know the essential way out—is why the Sages give rise to compassion for them and reveal provisional means (*upāya*).
Among the five eyes, the physical eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is obstructed and does not penetrate; the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*)... [text continues]

While the *sāmānyajñāna* (penetrating knowledge) remains obstructed by marks (*nimitta*), the *prajñā-cakṣus* (wisdom eye) directly destroys these marks; the *dharma-cakṣus* (dharma eye) directly contemplates the conventional (*saṃvṛti*);

and the *buddha-cakṣus* (Buddha eye) penetrates everything without exception, skillfully observing the conditions and karma of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that "one observes with the Buddha eye.

The yak is a beast of the southern barbarians who, being blinded by its attachment to its tail, thereby brings harm upon itself. Sentient beings are likewise blinded by their attachment to the five desires.

The harm remains the same. As for the Buddha of Great Power (*mahāvega*): when sentient beings, destitute of merit and wisdom, fall into peril and encounter suffering, only the Buddha possesses great power capable of rescuing them from the treacherous path;
the Dharma possesses great power capable of severing all sufferings.
"From the time I first sat at the site of enlightenment (until) how can they be delivered?

Regarding "first sitting at the site of enlightenment": following the *Avataṃsaka*, the body of Vairocana was concealed and a manifestation of great expedient power appeared, demonstrating the beginning of the attainment of perfect awakening.
He contemplated the tree and practiced walking meditation, intending to provide the shade of the Way for all beings. For twenty-one days he engaged in contemplation.

"Contemplation" refers to opening up the three [vehicles] to propagate the transformation [of beings]. Sentient beings are immersed in the five desires and have lost their way on the right path; this is called being blinded by the pleasure of delusion.
At that time, the various Brahma Kings (and so forth) requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Just as I was contemplating how to propagate the transformation [of sentient beings], the Brahmā deities happened to request it; thus, the Way of the world flourished in tandem with a silent resonance of karmic conditions.
I then reflected upon myself... [until] I quickly entered into nirvāṇa.
Because their capacities were dull and their thoughts deep, they could not decide whether to advance or retreat.
He then recalled the skillful means employed by past Buddhas and reflected: "The path I have now attained should likewise be taught as the three vehicles."
This was done to emulate the ritual for preaching the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods.

When he engaged in such contemplation (up to the point where it says) "merely for the sake of instructing bodhisattvas," these were all the words of the Buddhas of the ten directions praising Śākyamuni’s excellence of thought and his harmony with the skillful means of all Buddhas.
"Śāriputra, you should know... I also practice in accordance [with this].
In the past, Śākyamuni heard the words of the Buddhas of the ten directions consoling him; he then invoked their names and took refuge, practicing in accordance with their words.
This was done to accommodate the capacities of sentient beings. *Namo* is a term for taking refuge."
Having reflected on these matters [up to] the distinction between the Dharma and the Saṃgha, he contemplated what would be appropriate;
he then proceeded to the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). This represents the reliance on the provisional based on the ultimate.
Vārāṇasī is the name for the region of the Deer Park; it is the place where the Four Noble Truths were first taught. The five bhikṣus were Kauṇḍinya and the others.
[The others], such as [Ājñātakauṇḍinya], had studied the Way under Kāśyapa Buddha but had not yet attained realization.

[The Buddha] vowed that they would be the very first to attain awakening within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, and therefore he delivered them first. It was because of this that the names of the Triple Gem emerged: the name "Buddha" arose because he first sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
the name "Dharma" arose because he turned the wheel of the Dharma and preached *nirvāṇa*; and [the name "Saṃgha" arose] because he delivered Kauṇḍinya and established him as an arhat.
The names "Buddha," "Dharma," and "Saṃgha" all arise from a single path and yet possess distinctions.
If one knows that the Buddha is itself the Dharma and the Dharma is itself the Saṃgha, entering thus into the gate of non-dual dharmas, then what distinction could there be?
"Since time immemorial, I have praised and revealed the Dharma of Nirvana, stating that the suffering of birth and death is forever extinguished;

I have always spoken thus. This marks the beginning of the provisional intent. By praising and revealing the Dharma of Nirvana, he declares that the suffering of birth and death is forever extinguished;
that is to say, he speaks of the path for exhausting all suffering and points toward Nirvana. This is merely a skillful means to accommodate the capacities of beings. (Ten Verses)
To bring matters to their conclusion and reveal the ultimate truth:
Śāriputra, you should know that now is precisely the time.
It was only because he saw that the faculties [of sentient beings] had matured that he finally thought to reveal the ultimate truth.
"Śāriputra, you should know" (up to) "only speak of the unsurpassed path.
"Those of dull faculties and small wisdom" refers to the assembly that has withdrawn from their seats; they are now glad to have withdrawn, and thus there is no need for expedient means.
Upon hearing this Dharma, the Bodhisattvas have all cast off the net of doubt. The twelve hundred Arhats shall likewise all become Buddhas.
Having encountered the Tathāgata’s path of correct practice, those whose faculties are neither great nor small shall all attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Just as the Buddhas of the three periods of time have employed the ritual protocols for expounding the Dharma, so do I now likewise expound the non-discriminative Dharma.
This concludes the intended meaning of the final summary. △ Eleven: Extensive Praise of the One Vehicle.

The appearance of the Buddhas in the world—up to the point that it is rarer than the udumbara flower—is a praise of how difficult it is to encounter and hear the One Vehicle. For example, prior to the Great Penetration [Samādhi], one hundred and eighty kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha;
thus, a Buddha is difficult to encounter. Śākyamuni appeared in the five turbidities and waited for his time for forty years; thus, the Dharma is difficult to expound.

It is because of these two factors that it has been difficult to hear for vast eons. Furthermore, because there are those who withdraw from their seats, it is also difficult to receive and uphold [the teaching].
These four difficulties coincide, which is why such occurrences are as rare as the *udumbara* flower. Moreover, one who can praise the Dharma upon hearing it surpasses even the aforementioned four;
this is because this Dharma is exceedingly profound and subtle, and few are able to believe in it. To be able to praise it is...
The Dharma is for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddhas, because all Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge from it.
△ Twelfth, comforting and exhorting to faith:
"You should not have any doubts" (up to) "there are no śrāvaka disciples."

Having first expounded the One Vehicle, fearing that they might be startled or alarmed, he comforts them by telling them not to doubt, so that they may know that within the Dharma of the Dharma-King, there has never been a second vehicle.
△ Thirteen: The Circulation of the Dharma-Exposition.
"O Śāriputra, you [should] extensively praise the path of the One Vehicle.

You must know this secret essence and cause it to be protected and circulated. [He spoke thus] regarding the five turbidities and the wicked people of the future, so that [the teaching] may be circulated after discerning the capacity of the recipients.
[He spoke thus] regarding those who possess shame, remorse, purity, and so forth, so that [the teaching] may be applied accordingly.
...it is circulated according to the capacity [of beings]. △ Fourteen: Conclusion of the Teaching by Dharma.
Śāriputra, you should know: [from "you should know" to] "knowing for yourself that you shall become a Buddha.
Knowing that the past expedients were employed according to what was appropriate, and believing in the present reality without delusion—this is the true wisdom of all Buddhas.
"You have already attained it; you should rejoice and know that you shall become a Buddha. Śāriputra, having realized this, spoke in verse:
"Abiding in the midst of true wisdom, I shall certainly become a Buddha. This was his realization of these words.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll One, Part Three;
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Scroll Two, Part One.
By the Bhikṣu Jiéhuán of Kāiyuán Lián Temple in Wēn’lǐng. Commentary.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Three: The Parable. △ Second:
The Exposition by Way of Parables, which in one session reaches those of medium capacity. Part One: The Title and the Outline of the Meaning.

"Parable" (譬) means to cite the shallow to illustrate the profound; "analogy" (喻) means to rely on words to instruct and enlighten. Following the preceding exposition of the Dharma, various methods were shown.

All are, in fact, of the One Vehicle. Because those of superior wisdom have already awakened while those of middling faculties have not yet understood, [the Buddha] employs the shallow analogy of the three carts at a single gate to illustrate the profound reality of the three vehicles as one path, thereby instructing and enlightening them. For this reason, it is called the "Parable Chapter."

The sutra contains nine parables: namely, the Burning House, the Poor Son, the Medicinal Herbs, the Phantom City, the Hidden Jewel, the Well-digging, the King’s Topknot, the Father, and the Junior Physician.
Formerly, only seven parables were mentioned, omitting the two parables of the Well-digging and the Father;

these were considered secondary digressions, yet they are not actually so. The textual exposition of these parables consists of two parts: first, the introductory discourse on the Dharma; second, the formal exposition through parables.
The prose section: Now, the supplementary discourse on the Dharma is joined to the end of the preceding chapter, while the title of the parable is placed after the supplementary discourse.
As for the apparent overlap in the division of chapters:

since Śāriputra had already personally realized the Dharma-discourse and, wishing to awaken others, expressed his joy at this realization, he gave rise to doubt among those with the appropriate capacity and thus elicited this parabolic discourse. Thus it is that...
The intention of Wuxi and others is the reason for providing this illustrative explanation; it is appropriate to include it here so that the text does not become confused.
△ Second, the explanation of the text according to the topical outline, in two parts. First, the four introductory sections of the Dharma-exposition. First, Śāriputra’s realization, in four parts.
First, there was the joy of awakening.
At that time, Śāriputra leaped for joy (until) he attained what he had never experienced before.
Having understood the teaching on the Dharma, Śāriputra realized for himself that he would become a Buddha; thus, he leaped for joy and celebrated this unprecedented realization.
Why is this? (Up to: "I am deeply moved by grief that I have lost the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision.
This explains the superior [joy]. It means that in the past, during the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, we heard this Dharma together; yet while they received their predictions, I was not included.
This was to lose the Tathāgata’s immeasurable knowledge and vision. Now that I have finally attained it, I leap for joy.
Joy. Immeasurable knowledge and vision is precisely the correct wisdom of the One Vehicle. △ Second, the expression of remorse:
"World-Honored One, we have always dwelt alone in mountain forests and beneath trees... (up to)... this is our own fault, not that of the World-Honored One."
In my daily conduct, I have always followed the principle of "recording what I hear and noting what differs. It is not that the Buddha holds me in private favor; rather, the fault truly lies with me.
To say we "enter the same dharma-nature" means we claim to have realized the same truth.
Why is this so? (Up to: When first inquiring about the Buddha-dharma, one encounters it and immediately believes and accepts it, contemplating it until realization is attained.
This is Śāriputra’s self-reproach. That which served as the cause was precisely the true wisdom of *prajñā*, which is the direct cause for Bodhi.

Although the Buddha was certainly about to explain it, I failed to wait with earnest expectation. Instead, upon first hearing the Four Noble Truths, I immediately believed and accepted them, swiftly attaining the minor fruit [of Arhatship].
This was truly my own error. △ Third, rejoicing in oneself.
“World-Honored One, from the past until now, I have attained a portion of the Buddha-dharma;
I rejoice in what I have realized. That which is born of the mouth arises because of hearing a single sound; that which is born of the Dharma is the realization of such a Dharma.”
Regarding "the portion of the Dharma": it is the attainment of one's share of the Tathāgata’s precious treasury of knowledge and vision. △ Fourth, the fourfold repetition in verse.
First, the verse on the joy of awakening.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"I have heard this sound of the Dharma" (up to) "hearing it also removes sorrow and affliction.
"Sound of the Dharma" refers to the teaching of the Dharma. One whose outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted should naturally be free from sorrow and affliction;

yet, the text says "also removes" because although their outflows were previously exhausted, residual habits (*vāsanā*) had not yet been eliminated. Now, having attained ultimate realization, they remove the sorrow of having lost the Mahāyāna, as well as other [afflictions].
To practice until afflictions are exhausted. △ Second, the verse on repentance and reproach:
"I dwell in mountain valleys... how can I deceive myself?
This verse concerns the constant self-reproach of one's habitual state.
"We too are sons of the Buddha" (up to) "I have deceived myself.
This verse concerns the fault of not receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and the loss of the Buddha’s merits.

The thirty-two marks begin with the feet being flat and firm, and end with the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) being high and round like a celestial canopy. The ten powers (*daśabala*) begin with the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*).

The powers (*bala*) range from the power of knowing the cessation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) to their ultimate eradication, and from the eighty minor marks—beginning with the narrow and long fingernails—to the *śrīvatsa* mark on the chest.
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) are those not shared with the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
They range from being free of faults to the unattached and unimpeded knowledge of the events of the past, present, and future.
Day and night, I have constantly deliberated upon these matters.
Seeing that the Bodhisattva praised [others] and recognized my faults, I have therefore weighed my own failings. △ Third, a verse on self-congratulation.
Now I hear the Buddha’s voice, preaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate. It is untainted and inconceivable, leading all beings to the site of enlightenment.
Only now do I realize that these teachings given according to what is appropriate are all untainted dharmas, which can directly lead one to realize the Way.
"I originally adhered to false views... (until) they were forever extinguished without remainder.
This was his expression of realization and self-congratulation. In the past, Śāriputra served Sañjayin as a teacher of the non-Buddhist Brahmins.
Because the Buddha extracted them from error and preached the Dharma for them, they entered the Buddha-way. Their prior realization of emptiness was not yet the ultimate cessation;
only through the perfect realization of marks (lakṣaṇa) is it called the eternal extinction of the remainderless, which is *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha, amidst the great assembly, declared, "I shall become a Buddha. Having heard such a sound of the Dharma, all doubts and regrets were completely eliminated.
This restates the opening words of the verse to provide a general conclusion. The preceding verses, which corresponded to the prose, have now ended.
IV. A Separate Explanation of One's Own Doubts (in two parts): A. Raising the Doubt and Explaining It Oneself.
From "First hearing what the Buddha taught" to "I heard and my web of doubt was severed":
upon first hearing that the three vehicles were unified into one—that śrāvakas would attain Buddhahood—he doubted it because he considered it beyond the scope of his own wisdom.

However, as he carefully examined the Buddha’s teaching, his mind became like the ocean; the deeper he explored it, the more profound it became, and the further he measured it, the more remote it proved. Only then did he believe it.
The true Way is beyond further doubt. △ Second, citing evidence to resolve doubts:
"The Buddha spoke of past ages... [until] Pāpīyān has no such thing.

This cites the passage from the "Expedient Means" chapter concerning the identity of the Way across the three periods of time and the identity of the Way of one's own practice, thereby providing a self-explanation.
"Pāpīyān" is the name of Māra.
By this, I definitively know that [the Buddha] teaches and transforms all bodhisattvas;
this restates and resolves the previous doubt because of his realization. "True wisdom" (*bhūtajñāna*) is precisely the correct wisdom of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As for the body...

Your great wisdom should have allowed you to understand the Dharma heard from the Buddha without needing further explanation; yet, you became entangled in doubts and suspicions, even to the point of regarding the Buddha as a demon.

This was likely because the Way is vast while your capacity was small; upon first hearing such teachings, few do not experience inner conflict and mental confusion, leading them to slander and revile them.
It is like hearing the description of Mount Gushan and deeming it a mere delusion, refusing to believe it, and looking toward it with disdain.
"Aidai’s (Aide) manner was considered so loathsome that it startled the world. Those of later generations and vulgar customs who hear of the Buddha-way are for the most part like this;
thus, the Great Wisdom [of the Buddha] established [the teachings] out of a concern for such circumstances. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra... (up to) "...I have used skillful means to guide you so that you were born into my Dharma.
This recounts his original cause, clarifying the reasons for his realization and receiving the prediction.
The statement "spoken among the assembly of devas and humans" is intended to clarify that the distant cause and the distant prediction are not false. As the *Śīla-sūtra* says: "Śāriputra once..."
Having cultivated the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas, the phrase "now at the abodes of twenty thousand koṭis of Buddhas" refers to that period.
It means that throughout the long night, he followed and studied [the teachings], yet his correct wisdom had not yet become clear.
Śāriputra (up to) the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
Previously he was bound with a jewel; now the jewel is shown to him again. △ Third, the best faculties receive their prediction, in two parts: first, the granting of the prediction.
Śāriputra... [up to] the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Men.
Having already awakened to the wondrous Dharma and being destined to achieve the Way of the Buddha, he thus received the prediction (vyākaraṇa) of his future Buddhahood.

All texts concerning such predictions consist of two parts: first, the causal prediction based on his offerings to the Buddhas and his practice of the Path; second, the resultant prediction regarding the ten titles, the eon, and the land. This is that prediction.

"Great cause, great fruit": this is intended to urge those of the Lesser Vehicle forward. He is titled "Flower-Light" (*Huaguang*) because "flower" symbolizes causal practice while "light" signifies the ability to bring forth illumination;
this is because he was the first to realize and illuminate this Way. Although he has received the Buddha’s prediction, he must still pass through many kalpas before attaining the fruit.
This is because Buddhahood is attained through wisdom, whereas the fruit [of the Lesser Vehicle] is attained through practice. Although the Lesser Vehicle...
Having awakened to true wisdom but not yet cultivated the great practices, this is called the "original dharma-body Buddha" (*dharmakāya-buddha*).

This vehicle severs the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms, which is the same as that of the *śrāvaka*.
