Śāriputra [and the others] bestowed great carts upon the sons.
This summary shows that the sons emerged from the open space and sat down; they thought to themselves that their wealth was infinite, and thus he did not give them small [carts].
The passage on the "chariot" and so forth. △ Next, the synthesis:
"The Tathāgata is likewise thus" (up to) "all are brought to extinction by means of the Tathāgata’s own extinction.

This may be clearly understood as synthesizing the above: escaping the suffering of the triple world and attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa refers to the provisional vehicle and its minor fruits. The Tathāgata...
To bring about extinction through extinction is the ultimate fruit of the Mahāyāna;
it is that by which all sentient beings who have escaped the three realms [attain] the ability to give rise to the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss.

The commentary and other such works accord with the intent of the Mahāyāna. This means that although those who have escaped the three realms may attain the meditative concentrations and liberations of the Hīnayāna, they still harbor a distaste for existence and an attachment to emptiness;
thus, it is not the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). It is split into two vehicles rather than being of one kind.
Since their attachments have not been eliminated, it is not pure. Since emptiness and existence have not yet been harmonized, it is not wondrous. Therefore, it differs from...
These are the implements for the enjoyment of the meditative concentrations and liberations of all Buddhas; they are the singular, uniform, pure, and wondrous bliss.
They are like that great chariot, fully equipped with every excellence. △ Ninth: A combined examination to produce firm faith.
Śāriputra, it is like that elder... (up to) ...yet that elder is without the fault of falsehood.
First the premise, then the conclusion. △ Tenth: The combined conclusion answers that there is no falsehood.
The Tathāgata is also like this (up to) "distinguishing and preaching three within the single Buddha-vehicle.
This summarizes the preceding text. As for "not being able to receive it all," it is because their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) are not uniform.
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Volume Two, Part One;
Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, Volume Two, Part Two.
Expounded by the Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Wenling Kaiyuan Lian Temple.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Three: The Parable, Part Two. Section Four:
Versification in Five Parts. First, the versification of the ten parables. First, the versification of the fundamental parable.
The Buddha, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"For example, there was an elder who had a large house;
this is a metaphor for the Buddha reigning over the three realms. (2) The second [section] is the verse on the dilapidated house and the multitude of people.
That house is ancient (up to: they dwell within it).

The great house is a metaphor for the triple world (*tridhātu*). The hall and chambers are metaphors for the human body. The characteristics of the triple world have come from a beginningless past; therefore, it is said to be "ancient.

Because the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) converge therein, it is said to be "suddenly dilapidated. The hall and chambers of the five aggregates (*pañca skandhāḥ*) are constructed of emptiness and illusion.
It is precarious and easily toppled; its life-force is not firm or strong. Like a pillar-root that has rotted away, its substance is not solid;
like a ridgepole that has tilted, it leans. Ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as its foundation, thereby forming this hall; the remaining conditions serve as its steps.

The reason for entering this hall is that these twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) undergo transformation and decay from moment to moment. Therefore, it is said that the foundation and steps have collapsed;
the crumbling walls and fissures represent the decline of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The peeling of the plaster represents the wrinkling of the skin;
the thatching represents the hair; and the rafters and eaves represent the skeletal frame. "That" (*shān*) refers to the thatching grass; "ruined" (*chě*) refers to its falling apart.
The chaotic falling and disordered scattering are all signs of ruin; these are its external characteristics.
Internally, the gates, membranes, organs, and viscera are obstructed and convoluted, filled everywhere with pus, blood, excrement, and filth.

Such is the extent of its decay and impurity, yet worldly people remain especially deluded, attached, and greedy for it; therefore, this detailed analogy is provided. As for the "five hundred people," they represent the five realms of existence.

This is that which all sentient beings share in common. The rafters (*chuán*) and the ridge-poles (*lǚ*) belong to the same category: those at the eaves are called rafters, while those at the ridge are called ridge-poles.

"Rafters" follows the radical for "to depend on" (*yuán*); they depend upon one another and are mutually connected. "Ridge-pole" follows the radical for "backbone" (*lǚ*); it is like the backbone itself. △ Third, the verse on the four marks of fear.
First, the metaphor for the marks of the three poisons.
The concluding passage states: "That house was thus terrifying and transformed; such was its state.
From "owls, crows, eagles, and vultures" [to] "running about in all directions":

the body is the vessel of suffering. The primary [actions] of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are called the three karmas. The mind is the root of suffering, primarily characterized by greed and anger.
Delusion is said to consist of the three poisons. The three [actions] of the body and the three of the mind support one another and are mutually complete.

Now, the eight birds beginning with the hawk serve as metaphors for the poison of greed, yet they possess all three types of karmic action. The hawk devours living creatures; the earth-owl preys upon its own kind;

these possess both the karma of killing and the poison of greed. The eagle is skilled at seizing rabbits; the vulture feeds on corpses; these possess both the karma of stealing and the poison of greed. The crow, the magpie, the pigeon, and the dove transmit saliva.
"Self-movement" refers to being fully possessed by lustful greed; the rest may be inferred accordingly. The six types of insects, such as the *yuán* (viper), are metaphors for the poison of anger.

*Yuán* means "original," as it is the foremost among poisons and belongs to the same category as snakes, whose nature is predominantly prone to anger. The *fù* (adder) means "repetition"; it cannot see during the day.
When touched, it returns to sting the person; once the person has returned [to its place], it kills them. Scorpions mostly dwell in the shade and are difficult to perceive.
Centipedes and millipedes are adept at hiding and harbor poison. All categories of anger are like this: some possess the innate poisonous nature of a venomous snake;
some become angry with others only after being provoked, like a viper; or some are not [visible] in form.
They manifest as resentful beings; they merely harbor malice to provoke others' anger and lie in wait to poison them, such as the species of scorpions and centipedes.
The six types of insects, including the *śakragopaka* (gecko-lizard), are metaphors for the poison of delusion. The *śakragopaka* resembles a lizard or scorpion and mostly dwells in dark rooms.
The *śatapadī* (centipede) is a type of millipede; though it has many legs, it moves slowly and cannot advance. The *nakula* (mongoose) and its kind are capable of... [text truncated]

The weasel and fox catch mice by entering their burrows; when these animals grow old, they become malevolent spirits (*piśāca*). The *kṣveḍa* (the "sweet-mouthed" mouse) is so enamored with its own taste that it does not realize it is being injured when encountered by others.
Mice are cunning and skilled at hiding; likewise, the state of the foolish is one of hidden obscurity, lingering stagnation, and secret injury, where their treachery lies latent—such is their nature.
The various evil insects running about crosswise are like the three poisons (*triviṣa*) agitating one another.
They struggle and contend without ceasing. △ Second, the analogy for the characteristics of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*).
"A place of excrement and urine stench" (up to) "bones and flesh strewn in disorder.
Regarding the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*), losing correctness constitutes perversion. "A place of excrement and urine stench" refers to impurity overflowing.
It is like an inverted body. One contemplates the impurity of the body in this way, yet the world regards it as fragrant and clean;
dung beetles and various other insects swarm upon it. It is like an inverted feeling. One contemplates that feeling is suffering in this way, yet the world regards it as sensual pleasure;
consequently, they give rise to notions of beauty toward this leather bag of manifold filth, becoming deluded and attached to it without relinquishing it. This is truly like...
The gathering of dung beetles upon filth, and the gnawing and trampling of foxes, wolves, and jackals, are metaphors for the inverted mind.
The fox is full of doubt, the wolf harms things, and the jackal is a creature of strange transformations; the inverted mind is like them.

When one contemplates the impermanence of the mind, one realizes that all phenomena are not worth clinging to. Yet, one still gnaws and tramples them with attachment—is this not indeed an inversion? To chew and bite [upon them].
The corpse’s flesh and bones are scattered in disarray; this is a metaphor for the inversion of the Dharma.

To contemplate the selflessness of phenomena as being like a corpse, yet through the mind inverted by doubt, to engage in false conceptualization and exhaustive scrutiny—this is called "gnawing. That these inverted and deluded views proliferate is what is meant by "scattered in disarray.
The *ya-jian* (jackal) is a species of fox; it nests on perilous cliffs and high trees, moving in packs and howling at night—a strange beast. Its teeth are decisive.
It is said: "To taste" means to bite through the bone. △ Third, the analogy for the characteristics of the six consciousnesses.
From this point [where it says] "a pack of dogs" up to "snarling and barking," the nature of dogs is to be hasty and prone to stubbornly guarding what they hold;
this is an analogy for the attachment of the consciousnesses to objects. The "pack of dogs" is an analogy for the six consciousnesses.

"Grasping and seizing" means to take hold of. All illusory phenomena are devoid of anything worthy of attachment, yet the six consciousnesses falsely cling to them without distinction, like a pack of dogs vying to seize a corpse.
As for the phrase "arising from this," it means that the four inversions give rise to the six consciousnesses, and the six consciousnesses give rise to the three poisons;
they mutually support one another in a continuous cycle. The frantic search for food is a metaphor for consciousness.
To fall into inversion and give rise to greed is like this; to fight, quarrel, seize, and snatch is a metaphor for consciousness falling into inversion and giving rise to hatred;

to snarl, howl, and bark is a metaphor for consciousness falling into inversion and giving rise to delusion. Thus, the six consciousnesses and the three poisons arise from inverted and false conditions.

Regarding these illusory objects, they compete to grasp and crave them, their manifestations being as described. "Seizing and snatching" refers to pulling and plundering one another; "snarling" refers to resisting objects.
Such is its evil reputation. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the various signs:
"That house is terrifying; its transformations are like this.
△ Fourth, the verse on the difficulty of fear (the fifth). First, the verse on the difficulty of delusion.
The concluding text states: "Such various difficulties as these exist everywhere.
'Chi-mei and Wang-liang' refers to the fact that the house abounds in monsters.
By analogy, the nature of awakening is fundamentally luminous; when it is separated from this luminosity and becomes obscured, it is called 'chi-mei'."
The mind is fundamentally the One True Reality, yet it is deluded into duality, which is called *wangliang* (phantoms).

As for the phrase "in every place," this means that the nature of every person is like this; this serves as the starting point for raising the objection, and thus it is mentioned first. △ Second, the objection regarding ignorance and the three poisons.
From delusion arises ignorance; from ignorance arise the three poisons.
The yakṣas and evil spirits are most terrifying. "Yakṣa" translates here as "living in suffering.
This is a metaphor for the seeds of consciousness of ignorance, which grasp at manifold sufferings to sustain themselves, thereby inflicting harm.
Because they harm the Dharma-body, it is like devouring human flesh. Poisonous insects and beasts collectively represent the three poisons.

Their mating, nursing, and giving birth signify that their kind increases day by day; their respective hoarding and protection signifies that they accumulate the venom of anger and resentment, which cannot be transgressed.
When yakṣas compete to come and seize them for food, this represents the mutual arising of ignorance and the consequent affliction and injury of one another. To eat [them]...
Once they have eaten their fill, their evil hearts burn even more fiercely.
This is like using the three poisons to fuel ignorance, or like adding grease to a fire, which causes it to blaze up all the more. The sound of their quarreling and strife is truly terrifying;
it is like ignorance and the three poisons attacking one another, or like the chaotic battle of yakṣas—truly fearsome. As for those belonging to the category of hatched eggs...
"Jiǎobǎo" (爪保) means to protect and preserve. "Rǔtāi" (乳胎) refers to the nurturing provided by breastfeeding. Furthermore, "fú" (孚) and "rǔ" (乳) both convey the sense of nourishing and sustaining.
△ Third, the difficulty regarding impermanence:
The *kumbhāṇḍa* ghosts... [down to] ...terrifying dogs for their own pleasure.
*Kumbhāṇḍa* means "the Terrifying" in this [language]; it is likened to the demon of impermanence that kills. The earthen mound represents the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) where beings dwell;
one *chi* represents the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and two *chi* represent the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). All three realms cannot escape impermanence.
Therefore, the spirits who kill by slaughter travel back and forth between these realms. Recklessly committing murder, they regard killing as a mere game.

As for the statement that they "sit upon mounds of earth," and the statement that "at times they leave the ground": because the lifespan of those dwelling on earth is short, the spirits who kill by slaughter habitually remain upon the ground;
because the lifespan of those dwelling in the heavens is long, the spirits who kill by slaughter go there only occasionally. They seize the two hind legs of the dog.
Regarding the term "etcetera": the dog is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*). The two legs are a metaphor for formations (*saṃskāra*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*).

This illustrates that from consciousness itself arise formations and perceptions, through which there is movement; yet consciousness, by means of these formations and perceptions, grasps at impermanence and suffering, just as one might seize its two legs and strike it down.
When consciousness is afflicted by impermanence, formations and perceptions become inverted; therefore, they are compared to placing the feet upon the neck.
Furthermore, regarding "fearing the dog while delighting in oneself": consciousness is terrified by impermanence, yet the murderous demon delights in it and remains fearless.
This is what is meant by "being killed by decay" rather than "killed by non-decay. △ Fourth, the hardships of the three evil realms.
Furthermore, there are various ghosts (up to) those who even devour dogs.
Their bodies are large and naked, resembling the torments of the hells. A sutra states: "The Avīci Hell is thirty-two thousand li in length and breadth.
By the karmic power of the offenders, their bodies are like iron flowers that fill the entirety of the hell. Thus, one may say their bodies are long.
It is vast. To fall into this sutra means to pass through eighty-four thousand great kalpas; therefore, it is called "eternally abiding.
Within it, being naked and wailing represents the state of suffering in hell. Having a throat like a needle illustrates the hardship of the hungry ghosts (preta).
Having a head like an ox’s head illustrates the hardship of the animals (tiryagyoni). Eating human flesh or devouring dogs illustrates the three evil realms. It is not...
They merely injure the Dharma-body and likewise torment the conscious spirit.
Their hair is disheveled and matted; they are cruel and fierce, driven by hunger and thirst, crying out as they run about.
The description of the various terrifying forms of the ghosts serves as a metaphor for the physical appearances, behaviors, and karmic actions of the three evil realms.

Their disheveled hair represents their ugly appearance; their ferocity and danger represent their evil conduct; and their hunger represents the evil of their past karma. These three—cause and effect—summon one another and arise in alternation;
therefore, they are likened to crying out and running about. △ Fifth, the conclusion of the section on the characteristics of suffering.

From "yakṣas and pretas" up to "immeasurable terrors," this collectively clarifies that ignorance and the three poisons, along with their evil habitual tendencies, are fiercely blazing. Pursuing sense objects without satiety, they emerge whenever they find an opening;

thus, they are likened to one who, driven by hunger and urgency, peers out in all four directions through windows and casements. There is an ancient parable of the six-windowed monkey; its meaning is as follows:
It is like this. △ Fifth, the verse on being oppressed by fire and revolving in saṃsāra, in five parts. First, the destruction of the burning house:
"This dilapidated old house... [they] cannot escape by themselves."
The three realms offer no peace, like a dilapidated and decaying house. Only the Buddha can transform them; therefore, they belong to him alone.

When his connection with sentient beings is exhausted, the Buddha subsequently manifests extinction. Were there no longer skillful transformation, afflictions would blaze forth even more intensely. Thus it is said: "That person has recently departed.
Thereafter, fire breaks out, blazing fiercely on all four sides," which is a metaphor for birth, aging, sickness, and death—the four marks—pressing in from all directions.

The bursting and collapsing of the ridgepoles and beams is like the affliction of the four limbs; the crumbling and falling of the walls is like the dissolution and scattering of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The various ghosts and spirits raising their voices in loud cries is like the panic-stricken consciousness at the time of death, when the agony of suffering presses in and one groans and screams wildly.
The inability of the eagles, vultures, and *kumbhāṇḍas* to escape is like the karma and fruits of the three poisons having no end.
They are constantly tormented by the convergence of bitter retributions and cannot find a way to escape them. △ Second, their karmic consciousness does not cease;
fierce beasts and venomous insects fill the four directions.
When the fire has reached its extreme intensity, insects and beasts flee and hide, while ghosts and spirits remain concealed;
this is like the state after the body has perished, when the three poisons are not yet extinguished and merely reside within the cave of birth and death—the *ālayavijñāna*.
The *piśāca* is a ghost that causes affliction and harm, referring to those who torment people; this is analogous to the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*), which likewise dwells therein.

It lurks hidden within the *ālayavijñāna* and does not perish. As for the phrase "because their merit is meager, they are oppressed by fire," this refers to those who do not cultivate merit while alive and thus return to places of suffering upon death;

furthermore, they prey upon one another within the hollows, which is analogous to how the *karmic consciousnesses* (*karmavijñāna*) pursue one another in the dark and obscure realms, becoming mutual enemies.
The jackals and their ilk are likened to the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). It is said:

Regarding those who have already died: the actual karma rooted in the three poisons does not perish; it is only the branches and tips of the four inversions that arise and cease according to illusion.

Because they arise and cease following illusion, they are likewise swallowed by the four marks [of conditioned existence]. Hence it is said: "Various great beasts of prey compete to come and devour them.
"Foul smoke and flames choke the air" refers to the state of extreme torment and oppression caused by the convergence of the karmic forces of death. △
Third, regarding the continuity of birth and death:
centipedes and millipedes (up to) are seized and eaten at will.
Then, the aforementioned venomous insects hide and scurry into a hole, but are driven out by fire; they struggle to emerge from the hole only to be devoured again by the ghosts.
It is like the three poisons following consciousness as it departs; having received the retribution of death, one is reborn again into the various realms of existence.
Before one’s life must be renewed, one is again slain by impermanence; therefore, it is said that they are "eaten" as soon as they are taken up. Thus, being oppressed by suffering, they die.

Furthermore, they are born oppressed by suffering, and before even a moment has passed, they again encounter the suffering of death. Such is the nature of birth and death within the six realms of existence.
How tragic! Now, birth and death have consciousness as their seed, yet it is said that they depend upon the three poisons.
The suffering of birth and death that oppresses all beings is brought about precisely by the three poisons. These four are the root of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, as for the various hungry ghosts, fire burns upon their heads; tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat, they run about in frantic agitation.
The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states: "Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have all derived their very life and nature from lustful desire.
One should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root; lustful desire is the cause; and clinging to life is the fruit.

Because one gives rise to delusion and creates karma due to objects of desire, one is consequently reborn in the realms of hell or hungry ghosts. Here, the realm of hungry ghosts is cited to demonstrate the fruit of lustful desire.

The flames burning on his head signify the cause of sensual desire (*kāma*). Since the blazing of desire is the foremost of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), it is likened to flames burning on the head.
His frantic wandering in distress due to hunger, thirst, and the heat of affliction is a metaphor for being oppressed by the karma of desire.
Furthermore, driven by craving for life, one transmigrates through the various realms of existence without end. △ Fifth, the summary of the preceding parable:
Such is that house; it is truly terrifying, filled with poisonous harms and fires, and its manifold calamities are not just one.
Indeed, the cycle of birth and death is oppressed by manifold sufferings; it is truly like a burning house, a state to be feared.
Yet the worldly, with their inverted minds, are self-deluded and merely confused by sensual desires, unaware that karmic causes and the fruits of suffering all arise from this.

Immersed therein, one is as if in a profound dream; thus I have attained Great Awakening. Relying upon this body as a vessel of suffering, I first clarify the painful manifestations of the three poisons and the six consciousnesses;
next, I clarify the hardships of impermanence and the three evil realms; and finally, I clarify the fundamental source of suffering:
the cycle of karmic consciousness. By means of these metaphors, I demonstrate [this truth], so that through the experience of pleasure, one may awaken to suffering and dread its consequences.
If the causes are severed, the rapid wheel of birth and death will perhaps come to a halt; one will emerge from the firehouse of suffering and reach the place of fearlessness.
This is truly the supreme virtue of the Compassionate Father, the Great Teacher. △ Sixth: Verses on the Elder’s Compassionate Rescue.
At that time, the owner of the house (up to) "let alone the great fire" stands outside the gate.
This is like the Tathāgata, who has already departed from the burning house of the triple world, yet out of alarm enters the burning house.
This is like the manifestation of birth through the power of great compassionate vows; "just as appropriate" refers to skillful means (*upāya*). △ Seventh: Verses on the folly of the sons.
Deluded.
The sons were ignorant; although they heard their father’s instructions, they remained as before, delighting in and attached to their play, never ceasing.
△ The eighth verse describes the elder’s skillful means.
At that time, the elder [arrives] so that they may play;
he skillfully speaks of the three carts to save his young children. This is analogous to how, for the sake of those with limited wisdom, he expediently teaches the three vehicles (*tripravāṇika*).
Since these expedients are not the ultimate reality, they are said to be "constructed. "Mien" (湎) means to be deeply immersed or infatuated. △ Ninth: A verse on the children exiting the house.

When the sons heard this teaching [up to] "I am now happy," it is like the Two Vehicles who delight in the small and quickly realize emptiness. The phrase "the four crossroads" signifies that the sons have escaped from danger;
the "lion throne" symbolizes that the father has attained fearlessness. This is what is meant by: "If the son’s illness is cured, the parents are also cured. [This refers to] procreation.
It is extremely difficult, like a human body being hard to obtain; fearing that they might again lose it through delusion and confusion, he therefore urgently rescues them.
At that time, the sons... (until)... "I only pray that you will deign to grant [this] to me."
The verse describes the sons requesting the vehicles. △ Ten verses describe the elder bestowing the vehicles.
The elder is immensely wealthy (up to) bestowing [vehicles] equally upon his sons.
Having constructed great vehicles from a treasury of abundant jewels, this is an analogy for manifesting the One Vehicle through immeasurable knowledge and vision.
Nevertheless, even the One Vehicle has not yet transcended conditioned activity. Since it is already called "one," one should know that in the wondrous Dharma, even "one" is not maintained as fixed.
The metaphors of "adornment," "arraying," and "ornamentation" illustrate that the fruit-dharmas of the One Vehicle are fully perfected with myriad virtues.
That those of great capacity can "mount" it refers to its assistance in aiding the Right Path. The expedient means for benefiting sentient beings are all to be understood as previously explained.
At this time, the sons [of the Buddha] attain mastery and unimpededness.
Having realized the wondrous function of the One Vehicle, they do not stagnate in any single corner; hence it is said they "wander in the four directions.
Being unbound by all phenomena, it is called "sportive play and happiness. For one who plays with objects, there is neither preconceived intention nor compulsive necessity.

Adjusting to accord and meeting in harmony, they are never bound by attachment. When a practitioner of the Path treats all phenomena as if in play, they are thus able to act with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
△ Second, the ten verses on the application of the Dharma to the analogy; first, one verse applying the analogy to the original theme.
He addressed Śāriputra: "I am also like this. Among all the noble ones, I am the most honored; I am the father of the world.
(2) Second, the combination of the dilapidated house, the people within it, and all sentient beings—up to the point where [the house] is like a burning house.
△ 3. The third is the aspect of the fear of convergence:
filled with manifold sufferings, it is truly terrifying.
△ 4. The fourth is the fear of the difficulty of convergence.
There are always birth, old age, sickness, death, and the anxieties of suffering.
△ Fifth, being pressed by the conflagration of the cycle of rebirth:
such fires as these blaze fiercely and without ceasing.
△ 6. The Elder’s Compassionate Rescue:
The Tathāgata has already transcended [all afflictions]... and is able to provide protection and refuge.
△ 7. The Sons’ Delusion and Confusion.
Although he was thus instructed and exhorted, he did not believe or accept it, because his attachment to the defilements of desire was so deep.
△ 8. Combining the Householder’s Expedient Means:
By means of these expedients, [he leads them] to the supramundane path.
The supramundane path merely enables one to escape the suffering of the triple world; it has not yet opened up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
△ Ninth, the collective emergence of the sons from the house:
these sons (up to) non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
These are the causes by which those of the three vehicles attain the supramundane. "Non-retrogression" refers to bodhisattvas prior to the stages (bhūmi);
these are all provisional fruits. Regarding the "three knowledges" (trividyā): they are knowledge of past lives, the divine eye for the present, and the exhaustion of outflows regarding the future.

They are called "knowledges" because they eliminate ignorance concerning the three time periods; they are three of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā). To the six supernormal powers, the divine ear and knowledge of others' minds are added.
The Supernatural Power of the Realm. △ Ten: The Elder’s Gift of the Chariot.
"You, Śāriputra... shall attain the Buddha-way.
Because he took provisional results to be definitive, [the Buddha] preached the One Vehicle to advance him.

"This vehicle is subtle and wondrous" (extending to) "directly reaching the site of enlightenment" praises the virtues of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Because it perfectly accords with the Buddha's mind, it brings joy to all sentient beings.
"Reaching the point of making offerings and prostrating" causes one to revere the One Vehicle. "Immeasurable billions" (extending to) "and the remaining teachings of the Buddha" refers to—
This is what is possessed by the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). "The various powers and liberations" refers to the ten powers and the various liberations.

Attaining such a vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); this demonstrates the benefit of the One Vehicle. Those who attain this vehicle obtain the sun of wisdom that illuminates the night of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and so forth.
Whether for a brief moment or across many kalpas, they transcend the limits of conceptual thought and calculation, moving with ease and self-mastery amidst all phenomena.
Because he dwells therein, it is said that he constantly enjoys his play through days, nights, and kalpas, until he reaches the site of enlightenment—
meaning that he directly sits beneath the Bodhi tree and attains perfect awakening.
For this reason, if one searches truthfully throughout the ten directions, there is no other vehicle to be found, except for the skillful means of the Buddha.
This concludes the summary that reveals the One Vehicle. △ Third, restating and clarifying the three [aspects]. First, restating the parable to admonish the assembly:
"Addressing Śāriputra... causing them to emerge from the triple world."
△ Second, citing and clarifying the provisional and the real:
"Although I previously taught [that they] are all bodhisattvas" (up to this point) cites the former provisional teaching.

"What is now to be done is only [to become] a Buddha"—this is the real. This concludes the citation of the former provisional [teachings]. Regarding "although I previously taught" up to "but in reality they do not perish," this cites the former provisional [teachings]. What is now to be performed is solely [the attainment of] Buddhahood.
"Wisdom" clarifies that what is real is present now; it does not mean that the teaching of non-extinction is not the true realization. "If there are bodhisattvas...

and so forth means that those who can listen to this true Dharma with a great mind will know that although the Buddhas speak of the three vehicles, they do so entirely for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas.
△ Third, reiterating and clarifying the Four Noble Truths.
"If a person of small wisdom... is called one who has attained liberation.

This restates the reason for teaching the Four Noble Truths. At the beginning of the Four Truths, the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) is taught in order to remedy the craving and desires of those with small wisdom, so that they may come to know revulsion toward suffering—that is, birth, old age, sickness, and death—which arise from craving and desire.
Second, because sentient beings are deeply attached to the causes of suffering, the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is taught so that they may know how to suppress and sever it;

that is, afflictions, delusions, and karma are the causes of suffering. Because their attachment is profound, the Truth of Origination is taught through skillful means to guide them toward knowing how to abandon them.
Third, the "Path" (*mārga*) is pronounced as "Guide" (*dǎo*); it is the root for extinguishing suffering, cutting off its basis of reliance.
Therefore, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is taught, which brings about the extinction of craving and all the sufferings of birth and death; this is the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna.

Fourth, for the sake of seeking to realize cessation, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is taught, so that those who practice the Way may know how to progress. Briefly stated, this consists of morality, concentration, and wisdom;
in detail, it comprises the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. These methods of contemplation and observation are the path for departing from suffering and being liberated from bondage.
Regarding the statement that these four dharmas are all called "truths" (*satya*): their meaning is that they are real and accord with principle without deviation. Thus, the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* says:
"The sun might be made cold and the moon might be made hot, but what the Buddha has taught regarding the Four Truths cannot be made otherwise."
"Regarding this person, from what [point] until they reach extinction (nirvāṇa)...
This restates the previous point that liberation is not yet ultimate. To be free from delusion is liberation; this refers to one who still feels aversion toward existence and attachment to emptiness.
One who has attained all liberations is one who neither feels aversion nor has attachment. This is because such a person still possesses aversion and attachment.

Therefore, it is said that such a person has not yet truly attained *parinirvāṇa*. Because they still possess weary attachment and lack the Unsurpassed Way, [the Buddha] does not wish for them to realize it.
△ Fourth, the verse concludes with an announcement.

"I am the Dharma King" (up to "for the sake of the world, I have preached it") concludes the address to the great assembly, so that they may know the Buddha’s intent in appearing in the world and preaching the Dharma, seeking their peace, security, and benefit.
The "Dharma Seal" refers to what is called the Seal of the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇamudrā*). △ Fifth, selecting the appropriate recipients and proclaiming [the teaching] has three parts.
This is a matter of supreme significance.
Wherever you travel, until you have reached the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), do not proclaim this recklessly;
it is not something that can be endured by those of inferior wisdom. Those who are able to rejoice in and accept it should be known as great Bodhisattvas.
*Sat*. *Abhijiti* (阿鞞致) is translated here as "non-retrogression" (*avivarti*). This refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). △ Second, the capacity for faith:
"If there are those who believe and accept... [up to] ...beyond the reach of power."
To offer to the Buddha is said to be the result of profound past merit; to hear the Dharma is said to be the result of deep past causes. Thus, one is able to believe this.

When I say, "You, O bhikṣus and bodhisattvas"—referring to the assembly at the Dharma-gathering on Vulture Peak—I mean that wherever the teaching is proclaimed, if you can believe what you have heard, you will see the Dharma assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were vividly present right now.
If those of deep wisdom verify this through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [they shall likewise see it].
If one acts thus, then every encounter with phenomena is the truth. Those of shallow understanding use emotional views to discriminate, and therefore remain deluded and fail to understand.
You, Śāriputra, [up to] this is not within the scope of your own wisdom.
Although the power of the śrāvakas does not reach this level, it is nonetheless admitted that they enter by means of faith.

Generally speaking, whatever can be followed that lies beyond the capacity of one's own wisdom is entirely due to the power of faith; therefore, one must carefully discern the capacity for faith before proclaiming the teaching. As stated previously: "This Dharma cannot be shown;
its verbal expressions are quiescent. Yet it is specifically permitted that those whose power of faith is firm and stable can understand this.
Furthermore, considering Śāriputra and others, who entered the path through faith and followed it through faith—how should they have believed?

It is said in tradition: "Heaven is that which is believed without being spoken. It is also said: "To possess [the truth] within oneself is called faith. Now, wishing to understand the dharma in which words and signs are quiescent, one should rely on the faith of non-speaking; believing in what is already within oneself is sufficient. Thus, it is said: [The original text continues with a verse:

"Without speaking, there is belief; this is Heaven. To have it within oneself is called faith. Now, wishing to explain the dharma where words and signs are quiescent, One should rely on the faith of non-speaking; Believing in what is already within oneself is sufficient. Thus it is.
The initial stage among the five ranks of the *Avataṃsaka* is the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Therein, one establishes the substance of faith based on the immovable wisdom of self-nature (*svabhāva-acala-jñāna*), causing one to believe that one’s own mind is no different from the Buddha. Through this, the characteristics of awakened wisdom remain immovable;

the myriad dharmas do not shift, and cause and effect do not deviate. The holy and the ordinary are non-dual, and the mind and its objects are profoundly serene, sealing in accordance with true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

All things are in accord; this is called the faith that is beyond words. One who can give rise to this faith will suddenly overturn the karmic consciousness of ignorance, and seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing will become the wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

Thus, those who enter this sutra through faith and follow it in accordance with faith do so in this manner. △ Third, those who are not the intended audience (a-kalpa-pudgala), in three parts: first, the person who is not the intended audience.
Furthermore, Śāriputra... (up to) "do not speak for them either.

Those who are arrogant, indolent, and conceited with a sense of self are those without faith among the non-Buddhists; those who are vulgar, shallow, and attached to desire are those without faith among the ordinary worldlings—all such persons are to be excluded.
△ Second, those who are not suitable vessels [for the teaching].
If a person does not believe [this], up to harboring doubts and suspicions—what this sutra elucidates is precisely the wondrous nature of every person;
this is called the Buddha-seed. To disbelieve and disparage it is to sever and extinguish the Buddha-seed.
When the seeds of karma increase and blaze, it is better not to speak of it than to do so. One should indeed believe first before speaking.

If one has not yet gained faith, they will think that [the teaching] is an affliction to themselves; hence, they frown. Furthermore, if one has not yet gained faith, they will think that it is a slander against themselves;
hence, they harbor doubt and confusion. △ Third, the non-conformity with the capacity for response, in two parts. First, the general heading.
The mind is the mold for all forms; karma is the shadow and echo of the single mind. The good and evil of the three periods of existence are created solely by the mind.

Just as objects produced from a mold are invariably similar to it, and just as a shadow follows a form, escaping nowhere regardless of its location, so too do the retributions for the sin of slandering the sutras follow their respective categories, as listed below.
"You should listen to this" (up to) "you should now listen again.
△ Second, the detailed explanation has four parts. First, the retribution of the hells:
When that person's life ends... (up to) ...for incalculable kalpas.
This is the retribution for severing the seed of the Buddha. Because they have themselves severed the seed of the Buddha, they sink forever into the dark realms of existence.
Even when a kalpa ends, they remain; that is to say, when the lifespan of one kalpa is exhausted, they are reborn again in hell. Such is the length of time for their retribution in hell.
Losing their original nature and following their karma, they are like stones thrown into water: it is easy for them to sink but difficult for them to float; such is the nature of their momentum.
△ Second, the retribution of animals.
From emerging from hell... (up to) receiving this karmic retribution.
The dog [suffers] because it harms the upright through its casualness; the jackal [suffers] because of its doubt and lack of faith. These are the retributions for slander and skepticism.

Furthermore, it is afflicted by the diseases of scabies and leprosy, and suffers the harm of being provoked and harassed, even to the point of being subjected to agonizing pain, flogging, and being struck with tiles and stones.
These are the retributions for contempt and hateful jealousy. *Qiē* (pronounced like "qu") means bald and white; it refers to a dark, tawny complexion.
Black and variegated in color; it is a state of agitation and mockery.
If one acts as a camel [and so forth], one incurs such transgressions.
Because of slandering the True Vehicle, one incurs the retribution of being summoned to carry loads on camels and donkeys. Because of doubt and biased views, one is summoned to the wilderness.
To receive the retribution for a single eye is to enter a village driven by the power of one's karma, seeking only to be beaten and struck.

The nature of the great python-like serpent is prone to much anger; this is the retribution for harboring malice, jealousy, and resentment. To be deaf is to lack hearing, and to be dull-witted is to lack understanding.
They are likewise of the class of those who do not believe. △ Third, the retribution among humans:
if one is born as a human (up to) being crossly beset by calamity;
because they despised the light of wisdom, their six sense faculties are dark and dull; because they slandered the body of the True Dharma, they are stunted, short, and ugly. Their hands...
"Being cramped, limping, or lame" refers to physical deformities. "Whatever one says," and so forth, refers to the retribution for the karmic action of verbal abuse and slander.

To be "attached yet not intimate," or even to "unjustly encounter calamity and guilt," is because one has failed to accord with correct principle; thus, the retribution is entirely contrary [to one's desires].
The above clarifies the retribution of karma; next, the retribution of difficulties is clarified.
Such a person of sin (up to) incurs such retribution as this.
Not seeing the Buddha and not hearing the Dharma—both are difficult to repay. Gardens, pavilions, and dwellings are like places of recreation;
they are not left for even a moment. This is called being constantly born in difficult circumstances.

If one obtains a human form (up to) incurs such transgressions as these, taking illness as one's clothing, it is said that all forms of decay are difficult to cast off. The body is constantly impure; lust is fierce and makes no choice.
Because they have abandoned pure karma and increased their evil habits. △ Fourth, the general conclusion in three parts. First, regarding those who are not suitable vessels:
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra, saying, "Do not preach this sutra."
△ Second, the proper recipient:

If there is one of sharp faculties (up to) who may be taught, they will investigate with precision and venerate [the teaching] as if seeking śarīra relics. △ Third, the conclusion regarding the proper recipient.

[The text] from "Addressing Śāriputra" up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains examples of the correct objective and the correct practice that are too numerous to cite in full. I have merely indicated the general outline here,
so that one may select and bestow the True Dharma according to its kind.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Two, Part Two;
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Two, Part Three.
Expounded by the Bhikṣu Jiéhuán of Kāiyuán Lián Monastery in Wēnlíng.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Four: The Parable of the Faith and Understanding (Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta).
Part Two: The Realization of Those of Middle Capacity. First, the outline and meaning of the section.

Regarding "Faith and Understanding" (*śraddhādhimukti*): it refers to entering through faith and attaining realization and understanding of the essential points of the Dharma by virtue of hearing the parables. This follows the preceding "Dharma-exposition" (*dharmadeśanā*).
The first cycle: Śāriputra attained realization at the beginning of the Parable Chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*); the Buddha confirmed this and bestowed a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in that same chapter.
This constitutes the first cycle of parables. The four great disciples attained realization in this chapter;

the Buddha confirmed this in the Herbs Chapter (*Oṣadhī-parivarta*), and bestowed predictions in the Prediction Chapter (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*). However, although Mahākāśyapa was the foremost disciple, he attained realization only after [the others].
Regarding Śāriputra: this sutra synthesizes the two wisdoms (*jñāna*). Because Śāriputra was the primary recipient of the teaching, he was the first to attain realization.

Although all the great disciples secretly maintained their inner realization while manifesting outwardly, their faculties were neither middling nor inferior, and thus there was no sequence in their awakening.
Nevertheless, they were presented in succession to assist in the propagation of the Dharma transformation. △ Second, explaining the meaning according to the text, in five parts: First, hearing.
Rejoicing in the Joy of the Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti (up to the point of) giving rise to a rare mind, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.

Because Subhūti’s years and virtue were senior to the assembly, he is called an "Elder" (*sthavira*); alternatively, he is called "Endowed with Longevity" (*āyuṣmat*) or "Life of Wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*).
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "Such a person is able to obtain the life-force of wisdom within the Buddha-dharma. This refers to that very point.

Although Mahākāśyapa should have been listed first, Subhūti is mentioned first because he was the primary recipient of the teaching (*yathābhavyatā*). Subhūti was foremost in the realization of emptiness;
however, as a śrāvaka, he contemplated only partial emptiness and did not find joy in the Dharma of the bodhisattvas. Now, he has [abandoned that].
Because the Dharma of emptiness realizes the true path, it is expressed through those who understand emptiness. When the verses are recited below, they correspond to Kāśyapa;
furthermore, the prediction of enlightenment is also given first to Kāśyapa. This is the formal introduction. △ Second, the description of the state of faith and understanding, in two parts.
First, he recounts his former error.
He immediately rose from his seat (until) no longer seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He bared his right shoulder by turning to the right, demonstrating his humble resolve and reverence for the Dharma; he knelt with his right knee on the ground, demonstrating his submission of his limbs and profound veneration.

Baring one shoulder and kneeling is not a custom exclusive to the Western Regions (India). In this land, during the Spring and Autumn period, Duke Zheng of Zheng bared his flesh when descending before the state of Chu to signify his submission as a servant.
Furthermore, in matters of prayer one kneels before the incense burner, and in sacrifices one kneels to present the offerings; these are all expressions of profound reverence.

The passage from "Having addressed the Buddha" onwards describes how [the author] was initially immersed in the Hinayana and later heard of the Mahayana; this serves as the general heading, which will be explained in detail below.
The World-Honored One had long been preaching the Dharma in the past (until his mind was no longer joyful).

This refers to the period of forty years when he preached the Hinayana teachings. Because of weariness and indolence, he merely contemplated the emptiness of the Hinayana and no longer sought further progress.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are the three gates of liberation of the Hinayana.

This is the gate of liberation. The wise say that by relying on the Four Noble Truths to contemplate all phenomena as being without self or what belongs to a self, it is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
Because they are empty, the characteristics of all phenomena—such as unity or difference—cannot be found in reality; this is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).
Knowing that all phenomena are signless and unattainable, one has no further aspirations or seeking within the three realms and no longer engages in the three types of conditioned activity.

There is the karma of birth and death, which is called "non-action" (anabhisaṃskāra) and also termed "wishlessness" (apraṇihita). By means of this, one leaves behind all bonds of suffering and attains liberation.
However, this is merely a minor teaching and not worth dwelling upon. The Dharma of the Bodhisattvas is precisely the Mahāyāna Dharma;
their playful mastery of supernormal powers and so forth constitutes Mahāyāna practice. Those [followers of the former] only delight in the small, sinking into emptiness and pursuing quiescence.
Therefore, they do not find joy or delight in the Great Dharma or the Great Practice.
Why is this? (Up to: they do not give rise to even a single thought of fondness or pleasure.
This is because the aforementioned faults have become minor obstructions. △ Second, rejoicing in what has now been attained.
We have now, before the Buddha, [attained] immeasurable precious treasures without seeking them and receiving them spontaneously.
△ Third, the explanation of metaphors to express self-congratulation, in two parts. First, the metaphor of past loss, in four sections. First, the metaphor of deluded wandering.
“World-Honored One, we now wish to speak by way of a parable... gradually traveling on, they encounter their way back toward their native land.
‘Infant’ refers to being ignorant and lacking understanding; ‘abandoning his father’ refers to turning one’s back on original enlightenment;

‘another country’ refers to being mired in the five realms of existence. Therefore it is said, ‘reaching fifty years. Or ‘ten or twenty’ refers to the successive stages of sinking [into delusion]. Age...”

Long enduring poverty, he wandered in all four directions seeking food; this is like being distressed within the five realms of existence and passing through the four modes of birth to sustain one's life.

Gradually heading toward his native land is like encountering the Buddha’s teaching and subsequently becoming capable of self-reflection; yet, though he is headed in that direction, he has not yet arrived.
His father had previously come seeking his son but could not find him (until) there were also a great many merchants and traders.
His father is like the Buddha, the King of Dharma. Seeking him first but not finding him is like having previously taught and transformed him, yet later he fell back into decline.
Stopping at a city along the way is like the Avataṃsaka Dharma and the Bodhimaṇḍa. His family was immensely wealthy, with abundant treasures and riches.

"Treasures" (zhen) are a metaphor for the dharmas obtained at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), which possess immeasurable merit. The granaries are filled with the food of Dharma-joy (dharmaprīti), and the treasuries overflow with the wealth of all dharmas.
The servants by whom one serves oneself and the ministers by whom one governs the people are metaphors for the acts of benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
Elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep serve as metaphors for the five vehicles (pañcayāna); they represent the flourishing and expansion of the teachings.
It covers the great trichiliocosm; hence it is said that "the profits from their coming and going extend throughout other lands.
Because of this, all living beings seek the benefits of the Dharma; hence it is said that "the merchants are numerous. This collectively illustrates the giving forth of benefit and grace.
A *shang* (merchant) moves goods to exchange what they have for what they lack; a *jia* (peddler) conceals goods to await their price. "Shanggus" refers to merchants.
At that time, the impoverished son wandered through various villages and passed through kingdoms and cities until he eventually reached the city where his father resided.
The impoverished son is like one who is distressed within the five realms of existence and lacks the wealth of merit. The villages and hamlets are like the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna;
the flourishing and magnificent kingdoms and cities are like the gradual teachings of the Madhyamaka-yāna; and the place where his father resides is like the true teaching of the Mahāyāna.
The meaning is that in the past, while [the son] was lost in delusion, he was gradually led by means of the teaching and thus entered the Right Path.
The father constantly thought of his son (until... he became serene and joyful, no longer having any further anxieties.
"When the father constantly thinks of his sons" is a metaphor for the Buddha thinking of the sons of the two vehicles who have long been submerged in the five realms of existence;

their natures and habits are dull and shallow, and they are not yet fit to be taught the Mahāyāna. "Reflecting with regret and resentment" means he regrets that his past teachings were not profound enough, and he resents that their present capacities have regressed from the Great Vehicle.
"Thinking of his own old age and infirmity" means he grieves that there is no one to continue the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is destiny. △ Second, the parable of delighting in the small.
"World-Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate."
To work for others is called "hireling" (yōng); to labor for profit is called "renting" (chén). A city is like a sudden entry;

a house is like a deep penetration—meaning that one relies upon expedient vehicles to gradually advance toward profound realization. Yet, working as a hireling or a renter merely secures small profits; the merit does not belong to oneself.
This is like relying on expedient teachings while ultimately lacking actual realization. Only when one reaches the house and dwells there is true attainment.
Standing at the side of the gate, although they encounter the Buddha-way, they cannot enter it directly; they remain instead relying upon the pervasive void because they delight in the small.
△ Third, the analogy for those who are timid regarding the sudden [path].
Seeing his father from afar, he thought thus and fled away;

this is like the followers of the Two Vehicles who, upon first hearing of the Buddha’s fruition—the myriad virtues and the wisdom of all modes—become confused by the Lesser Vehicle and terrified by the Greater.
To see his father from afar is like being unable to realize [the truth] through direct personal witness. His sitting upon a lion throne symbolizes the virtue of fearlessness.

The jeweled footstool supporting his feet signifies that he honors the root of the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*). Because the root of the myriad practices is the true reality yet he is able to engage with the mundane world, the *kṣatriyas* and householders all surround him;
the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) are unable to engage with the mundane world in this way. By means of these myriad...

Because practice brings all myriad virtues to completion, his body is adorned with necklaces of true pearls; the followers of the Two Vehicles lack such adornment. Just as officials govern and subjects serve—wherein the tasks of the young servants are light and those of the male servants are heavy—so too within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, there is not a single subtle or detailed method for governing and serving that is not fully provided. Worldly speech, the arts of livelihood, and so forth, all accord with the True Dharma; yet, non-attachment and impartiality are held as supreme.
Therefore, he holds a white fly-whisk while attending at his left and right.

For a whisk can remove dust, "white" signifies non-attachment, and "left and right" symbolizes the removal of the dust of emptiness and conventionality to return to the Middle Way. The jeweled canopy is a metaphor for the vast pervasiveness of compassion.

Therefore, it is called "covering. The flowers and banners symbolize the various virtues that descend to transform sentient beings; thus, they are called "hanging down. Water symbolizes wisdom, and the flowers symbolize causes.
As for sprinkling fragrant water upon the ground, it represents purifying the mental ground of sentient beings through sublime wisdom. As for scattering various named flowers, [it represents...]
Adorning the minds and lands of sentient beings with wondrous causes; arraying precious objects to display their delights;
and bestowing, taking, and giving according to their desires and inclinations—this is like bringing those who have achieved great roots to the Small Vehicle in order to further encourage them.
All that precedes is the matter of the myriad virtues and the wisdom of the Buddha-nature. From the point where "the impoverished son saw his father" onwards, it concerns delusion.
The phrase "fearing great matters" refers to the King; "the King and his peers" refers to the royal clan, which serves as an analogy for the two bodies:

the Dharma-body and the Reward-body. "Living in poverty in the alleys" is an analogy for the narrow path of the Two Vehicles. "Having a place to exert one's strength" is an analogy for having a method for progress and cultivation.

"Not obtaining a place to acquire goods" is an analogy for the difficulty of realizing the Great Dharma. "Food and clothing are easily obtained" is an analogy for the ease with which minor fruits are sought.
Or they may see themselves being pressured by the thought that the Buddha-way is long and distant, requiring them to undergo diligent suffering for a long time—
“inner sound” (*nai-yin*) refers to either exhaling or inhaling.
At that time, the wealthy elder, from his lion throne, immediately dispatched attendants to pursue and bring [the child] back quickly.
Seeing the son and immediately recognizing him is like the maturation of past conditions; the entrusting of wealth and goods is like the transmission of the Dharma.
Although I am advanced in years, I still cherish it—this is like that which has been cultivated over kalpas of eons, not to be given away recklessly.
Sending someone to pursue him in haste is like causing the Bodhisattva to preach the Sudden Dharma; thus, all the dharma-gates of the five stages of the *Avataṃsaka* are for Bodhisattvas.
As it was said:
At that time, the messenger ran swiftly to seize him; [the son] became even more terrified, fainted, and fell to the ground.
The father’s command to pursue his son was truly out of a desire to be close to him, yet the son, in his startled fainting, abandoned himself. This is like the second [simile].

When first hearing the *Avataṃsaka*, one may feel intimidated by its sudden teaching. This is because the Sudden Teaching holds that afflictions are identical to bodhi, whereas the followers of the Two Vehicles regard afflictions as enemies;
thus [the former] speaks of them as "enemies. Furthermore, the Sudden Teaching holds that birth-and-death is identical to nirvāṇa.

Because the followers of the Two Vehicles regard birth and death as the bondage of suffering, they cry out loudly. Being seized without having committed an offense is likened to being forcibly constrained when one does not seek it.
Being urgently grasped and forcibly dragged along is likened to being compelled against one's will.

Although Bodhisattvas manifest birth within the triple world, the followers of the Two Vehicles regard the triple world as a prison; therefore, it is said that they are imprisoned without guilt. Bodhisattva...

The Bodhisattva enters and emerges from the dust and toil of the world (*saṃsāra*), yet the followers of the Two Vehicles fear they will lose the fruit of their meditative concentration; thus they say, "This one will certainly die.
Consequently, like the deaf or the mute, they remain dazed and fail to understand. Therefore it is said: "They become even more terrified, faint away, and fall prostrate on the ground."
The father saw him from afar and told his attendants not to speak with him further.
Seeing that he was terrified, frantic, and had fainted, he ordered them to provide him with comfort. This is like abandoning the sudden [teaching] to employ expedient means (*upāya*).
Just as cold water can revive one who has fainted, so too can the provisional teachings cure the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is this? (Up to: He goes to the poor quarters to seek food and clothing.

This is because he knows their resolve is inferior and they find it difficult to bear the Mahāyāna; thus, he provisionally suspends [the teaching] for them. It is not said, "My son, I shall not yet reveal the reality.
Sending the messenger away is a metaphor for abandoning the sudden [teaching]. "Proceeding according to one's inclination" is a metaphor for opening up the provisional.
Furthermore, "rising from the ground" means awakening from delusion.

"Going to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing" means relying on the impoverished dharmas favored by the Two Vehicles as provisions for entering the Way. △ Fourth, the parable of being stalled in the provisional.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, first related the aforementioned matters to explain the employment of skillful means.
By "secretly dispatching two men," he meant to cause the practitioner of the Bodhisattva path to manifest the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
As for their "haggard appearance and form," this refers to what is called concealing the power of one's sovereign mastery. "I will give you double the price" means...

This is like using a small cause of pleasure to indicate a proximate fruit. Employing you to remove filth is what is meant by "delivering them through the Dharma that accords with what the poor delight in.
Removing filth is a metaphor for severing afflictions (*kleśa*). Afflictions, delusions, and karma are the filth that defiles the ground of the mind.
While those of the Two Vehicles employ various contemplations to remove them, for a Bodhisattva, afflictions and nirvāṇa do not obstruct one another. Yet it is said:

"Furthermore, by working together with you, he employs the means of *samānārthatā* (common purpose). He related the aforementioned matters in detail, just as one who follows the Buddha extols his transformation.
At that time, the impoverished son first took the wages [and so forth], and through such skillful means, he was able to draw near to his son."

First taking the price is like being fond of the small and longing for the fruit before cultivating the cause; this is why, within the Dharma of the Four Truths, the fruit comes first and the cause later.
His father felt pity and wonder, wondering at his preference for the small while abandoning the great.

Furthermore, on another day, by means of the windows and so forth—this is a metaphor for employing many skillful means to follow along with his narrow views and secretly bestow [the truth] in a hidden manner.

The transformation causes them to aspire to the Great [Vehicle]. Being emaciated and covered in dust is a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who, though they subdue and sever afflictions, fail to grasp the essential method and are consequently disturbed by those very afflictions.
"Going left in opposition and right in compliance," with the right hand holding a vessel, is a metaphor for guiding them by conforming to the path of skillful means.
Later, he spoke to him again, saying: "Do not worry or be anxious anymore.
He used skillful means to reprimand and examine him, treating him with intimacy and kindness so that he might be at ease and free from fear. He told him:

"I shall increase your wages, which is like progressing from the stage of Stream-entry (srotāpanna) through to the four fruits of arhatship. The basin and vessels are like the auxiliary dharmas of the path; the rice and flour are like the provisions for the journey."
These dharmas are like salt and vinegar, which serve to harmonize flavors, causing all dharmas to be balanced, adjusted, and moderate.
The aged and decrepit servants are likened to the exhausted teachings of the Two Vehicles, just as it is said that "old straw dogs" have lost their utility.
Why is this so? [From "Why is this so? to] "he is called a child.
This deprecates his own senescence while praising the mental power of his son; it is like disparaging the great to praise the small, a skillful means to advance his merit.
By saying, "From now on, those such as you, my sons," he increases their intimacy and promotes them. "Child" (*er*) is a term of affectionate pity. Furthermore, he grants them...

The act of writing characters is a metaphor for transforming the stage of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and advancing toward subsequent fruits. The preceding sections were all metaphors for establishing provisional means (*upāya*).
At that time, although the impoverished son rejoiced at this encounter, [the father] for twenty years constantly had him clear away dung.
This is precisely an analogy for being stalled by provisional means. It means that although one rejoices in the Buddha’s transformation, one’s aspirations remain base and inferior;
therefore, one is first led to eliminate the filth of the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) within the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
After this period has passed, [until] he still remains in his original dwelling place.
For twenty years, the impoverished son gradually becomes more intimate with his father, yet he still stays by the side of the gate.

This is analogous to how, after severing the fetters by relying on the teachings of the Two Vehicles, one hears the Vaipulya (Universal) teachings; one extols the Great [Vehicle] without slandering it, and does not disparage the Small [Vehicle] without harboring doubt.
This is called the mind’s essence being fundamentally trustworthy. Advancing, one may discourse on the Great; retreating, one does not stagnate in the Small.
This is called having no difficulty in entering or emerging. Yet remaining in its original place, it is like being unable to enter all at once.
"World-Honored One, at that time the elder fell ill... (up to) "...you should embody this meaning.
This is like explaining the *prajñā* for the sake of gradually leading [beings] into the reality. The elder's illness is a metaphor for the period following the Vaipulya [sūtras].

As long as names and signs have not been discarded, most people suffer from the malady of clinging to dharmas. The Buddha, likewise afflicted by this, spoke of the "Treasury" (Ratnakoṭa) as he was about to pass away;
this is because his transformative conditions were nearing their end, and thus he taught the *Prajñāpāramitā* as the precursor to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

It is like a local saying that the treasury has not yet been handed over. Within the teachings of the *Prajñā*, the six perfections and myriad practices are fully contained; therefore, it is likened to a granary.
The storehouses overflow; yet, as this is not yet the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the treasures therein vary in quantity.
One may take them for one's own benefit or give them away to benefit others. Such is the mind of the Sage; one should accordingly embody this Dharma.
This is an analogy for the transmission of the teaching to bodhisattvas. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* tells Subhūti:

"You should expound the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattvas. The subsequent passage states: "We, moreover, through the wisdom of the Tathāgata, shall expound it for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
This refers precisely to the act of transmitting the teaching.
Why is this? Now I and you are no different. You should apply yourself with diligence so as not to let anything slip away.
Harmonize the feelings of father and son so that there is no room for doubt, and joyfully receive the treasure-store.

That "I and you are not different" and so forth is an analogy for the principle of Prajñā: all things are thus, non-dual and without distinction. This is the entry into the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
Therefore, one should apply oneself with diligent care.
At that time, the impoverished son accepted the instructions (until: "even his base mind had not yet been abandoned").

Having taken charge of the treasure storehouse, he did not hope to take even a small portion from it. This is like receiving an edict to propagate the Mahāyāna through further teaching, yet [failing to do so] oneself.
In this regard, there is no aspiration; even the inferior mind has not yet been abandoned. It is like merely contemplating emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The above is a general metaphor for what was lost in the past. △ Second, the metaphor for what is now attained.
After a short time had passed, [the father] first permitted the son to manage the household's income and expenditures; this is what the son understood.
Once the son’s resolve was great, the father then assembled the clan and finally established their relationship as father and son, entrusting him with the entirety of the family estate.
Again, after a short time—this serves as a metaphor for when, following the *prajñā*, the great capacity has matured and one may reach the Way through a single transformation.
To disparage one's former mind is like abandoning the small vehicle for the great. When the time of death approaches, one summons one’s sons and assembles the clan.

As it is said regarding the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*): when the Tathāgata knew that the time for his parinirvāṇa had arrived, he gathered the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached this sutra for them;
thus, the śrāvakas are the sons and the bodhisattvas are the clan. Having assembled the clan, he proclaims: "This is my son."
This refers to the parable of how he spoke among the assembly of devas and humans, saying, "In the past, I transformed [them] so that they were born within my Dharma.
This refers to the parable of how he said, "Those who abandoned us in such-and-such a city—you have now completely forgotten this from long ago."
It is because at that time their faculties were not yet determined; later, they fell back and wandered through the five realms of existence. Hence it is said:

"For over fifty years, they have been solitary and endured hardships. Regarding the phrase "their original names were such-and-such," this refers to their original names to verify the certainty of their relationship as father and son.
That "original name was such-and-such" refers to those who were transformed [by the Buddha] when he spoke of the "Transformation City," namely you, the assembly.
These are my bhikṣu śrāvaka disciples. As for me, named [so-and-so], I am the sixteenth, namely Śākyamuni.
Seeking him from our original city, we have encountered him here. This is like the ancient reliance on one's fundamental nature to propagate the teaching;
arriving now at this Sudden Gate, there is a spontaneous and perfect accord. This is truly the proof that confirms us as his children. All.
The analogy of entrusting the family estate refers to the bestowal of the prediction of Buddhahood and the succession to the position of the Dharma Lord.
When it is said, "Whatever wealth and property I have, all belongs to my son," this one great matter is inherently possessed by every person; it is not obtained from without.

"What was previously managed in terms of income and expenditure is what the son knows" refers to the ordinary application of the dharmas of seeing and hearing, and is not something else that exists separately now.
Indeed, it is by seeking within oneself that one realizes the awakening of the primordial source. This is the functioning of the true father-son nature;
this true treasury is innate and inherent. Who, then, could be without it? Alas, how can one lose oneself through running counter to this truth and become deluded by external objects?
Therefore, the Buddha’s compassionate concern urges us to urgently pursue its restoration. If you can accord with and trust this in your heart, then you may encounter it.
Had they understood this, there would have been no difficulty at all; yet they were instead struck with astonishment and lost their way, voicing grievances and harboring doubts toward the Buddha.
Had it not been for his true compassion and manifold skillful inducements, they would ultimately have wandered aimlessly and suffered in the four modes of birth and five realms of existence.
This is truly a cause for a long sigh. At that time, the World-Honored One [said]: "When this poor son heard these words of his father... until now this treasure-trove has come of its own accord.
This concludes the analogy for what has now been attained. △ Fourth, the comprehensive synthesis of the two preceding analogies. First, the synthesis of the former loss. First:
The analogy for the root:
The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata. [From "is the Tathāgata" to] "the Tathāgata always says that we are his sons. Subhūti is a true son of the Buddha;
it is for the sake of conforming to the analogy that he is said to be "like" one. △ Second, conforming to the delusion of wandering in saṃsāra and delighting in the small [vehicle].
“World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we have been deluded and ignorant, taking pleasure in and clinging to inferior dharmas.

As for the three kinds of suffering: first is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). This refers to the discordance and oppression of the sense faculties and their objects, as well as the manifest aspects of suffering such as birth, old age, sickness, and death.

Second is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). This refers to the various sorrows and afflictions arising from the transformation of pleasure; that is to say, while pleasure has not yet ended...”

Sorrow follows upon this; that is, the suffering of separation from the beloved and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. Third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which is the characteristic of momentary flux and transformation.
The suffering of the aggregates within the five destinies is all subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations. △ Third, combining timidity with sudden stagnation in the provisional.
"Today, World-Honored One... you shall have a share in the treasure-store of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

This passage describes the lingering of provisional means. To say "today" is in contrast to many lifetimes; it means that although for many lifetimes they delighted in the Lesser Vehicle, they still remain mired in delay.
Regarding all phenomena, they falsely give rise to delusive defilements and engage in various conceptualizations and frivolous play.

The treatise discusses the defiled state of mind, which is called the "filth of conceptual proliferation. The price of a single day is likened to the profit from a small fruit, which is not much obtained.
By the power of skillful means, the World-Honored One speaks of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; yet [these beings] have no aspiration for this Mahāyāna.
To speak of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is precisely the teaching of Prajñā.
Furthermore, it is because of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that we did not know we were truly the sons of the Buddha.
This means that by means of *prajñā*, he transforms and instructs the bodhisattvas, while he himself does not seek [the fruits thereof]. △ Second, the present attainment.
Now we only know (up to) "The Buddha then preached the Mahāyāna Dharma for me."
Now that I have obtained the Lotus Sūtra, I finally know that at the time of the Prajñāpāramitā, he already intended to entrust [the Dharma] to me in its entirety.
It was only because I delighted in the Lesser Vehicle that I remained deluded; had I delighted in the Great Vehicle, he would have entrusted it to me long ago.
In this sutra, it is said that there is only the One Vehicle (up to the point where it says): "However, the Buddha has in fact taught and transformed beings through the Mahāyāna.

By observing the present teaching of the One Vehicle and viewing it in light of his past censure of the partial, one can sufficiently know that the Buddha’s fundamental intention was always to transform beings through the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, we say that originally there was no mind that harbored any aspiration (up to) "all have already attained it.
This is the celebration of what has now been attained. That which a Son of the Buddha ought to attain is the Dharma of cultivation and realization of the One Vehicle.
△ Fifth, the repeated verses on the preceding meaning, in five parts. First, the verse on the joy and exultation upon hearing the Dharma.
