At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching; with great joy and exultation, we have attained what we never had before."
△ Second, two verses describe the state of faith and understanding:
The Buddha says that the śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood; this unsurpassed mass of jewels is obtained without seeking.
△ Third, two verses present a parable, the first of which illustrates the former loss in four parts; the first verse describes the state of delusion and wandering.
It is like a child (up to) searching in the four directions.
It is like being exhausted by wandering through the five realms of existence and undergoing the four modes of birth.
Having grown weary from seeking, (up to) what should one do about it?

This verse rescues those who are deluded regarding specific matters. A single city is a metaphor for the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). A residence is a metaphor for compassion. The five desires are a metaphor for the joy of the Dharma.
The family’s wealth of various treasures and so forth is a metaphor for the immeasurable merits of the dharmas obtained at the site of practice.

The increasing anxiety and concern for one's children and so forth is a metaphor for when the conditions for transformation are nearing their end while the treasury of the Dharma has not yet been transmitted; it expresses the worry that there may be no one to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom.
...Thus it is. △ Second, the verse on delighting in the minor [vehicle].
At that time, the impoverished son (until) he eventually arrives at his father’s house;
from the village to the kingdom, this is a metaphor for following various teachings in succession and gradually entering the Right Path. Because the power of the Dharma has not yet become strong.
"Sometimes they obtain it and sometimes not; because the joy of the Dharma has not yet sufficed, they suffer from hunger and emaciation, and sores and scabs break out upon their bodies.
This means that they have not yet been able to skillfully enter the Buddha’s wisdom, and instead have wounded their own bodies which were originally free of sores.

"They wander through various forms of hired labor until they eventually reach their father’s house," which is a metaphor for relying upon provisional teachings to gradually penetrate deeply. △ Third, a verse on those who are timid regarding the sudden [teaching].
At that time, the elder (up to) recorded the documents and notes.
He prepared various arrangements within the gate, desiring to lead [the guest] inside. "Documents" (券) refer to the recording of the receipt and disbursement of wealth;

"notes" (疏) refer to clearly detailing and recording specific matters. This is analogous to measuring the magnitude of one's roots of merit and clarifying them through detailed notes. "Sū-míng" (疏明) means to clarify through detailed exposition.
Bestowing the prediction of enlightenment upon one at the stage of practice is intended to entice and advance those of the Hīnayāna.
When the impoverished son sees his father, he asks, "Why have you come here?
because he fears that the phenomena of the Dharma-body and Reward-body are beyond the scope of his own intellectual capacity.
He then thought to himself: "I wish to go and work for hire, yet I fear the long distance;
I should instead take small fruit. At that time, the elder [thought]:
"[It was he] who caused me to come here."
This is like the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s sudden teaching: they are "startled" because they fear the enemy of afflictions; they "cry out" because they dread the bonds of birth and death;

they "fall prostrate on the ground" because they are distressed and cannot understand; and they "fear being killed" because they worry about losing the fruit of the Path. △ Fourth, the verse on lingering in the provisional.

The elder knowing his son [and so forth] up to "he gave you double the price" is a metaphor for abandoning the temporary and revealing the provisional (*upāya*). "Blind in one eye" is a metaphor for the partial views of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
"Dwarfish, short, and ugly" all refer to the practice of concealing the superior and manifesting the inferior.
When the impoverished son heard this, he followed along with joy to clear away filth and purify the various rooms and dwellings.

This is an analogy for delighting in the small and lingering in the provisional. The "rooms" represent the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the "dwellings" represent the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The elder [approached him] at the window (and so forth), speaking to him and urging him to work diligently.
Following his limited perspective, he concealed the superior and manifested the inferior, employing various means to encourage and advance him.
Having increased your wages (and so forth), [he said]: "You shall be like my own son."
This means to treat them with increasing intimacy and kindness while guiding them. Having increased your price is like advancing through the four fruits of the path.
Applying oil to the feet so that a hired laborer’s feet do not crack is like the dharmas of guarding the precepts and meditative concentration that assist the Way.

The mats and bedding are like the provisional methods of the various concentrations of the Hīnayāna. If it refers to the method of the Great Concentration of the One Vehicle, it is likened to fine silk and padded wool.
The padded mat (*yinru*) is not comparable to a simple reed mat (*jianxi*).
When the elder possesses wisdom, [he realizes] "I do not have this object.

Although his mind gradually expands, he still lags behind in terms of expedient means (*upāya*). Gradually causing him to enter and exit is a metaphor for entering through the large and exiting through the small. (End of Fascicle Two).
The ten years are a metaphor for traversing the teachings of the Two Vehicles; the display of gold and silver is a metaphor for the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
The father provides a precious canopy within the gate and beckons him in, while the son remains outside the gate in a grass hut and does not enter.

This illustrates how those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are thus at odds with one another. Consequently, the nature (xìng) and characteristics (xiàng) schools harbor mutual suspicion, and Chan and Vinaya practitioners mutually disparage each other, throughout both past and present.
It does not cease. When will there come a time when father and son are settled, fully preserving the family estate, and both forgetting the distinction between self and other?
The above is a general verse summarizing past losses. △ Second, a verse praising present attainment through analogy.
The father, knowing his son’s mind (up to the point of) attaining what he had never before experienced, recounts his past losses in verse to celebrate his present gain.
△ Fourth, the verses that comprehensively synthesize the two [sections]. First, one verse synthesizes the past loss;
second, the first verse synthesizes the delight in the small [vehicle].
"The Buddha is also like this" (up to) "the śrāvaka disciples.
Regarding "The Buddha is also like this": it is as when an elder knows his son is foolish and inferior, yet does not yet acknowledge him as a son;
he says, "I am equal to you," merely advancing him with small fruits so that he may achieve accomplishment. △ Second, the verse on the convergence and lingering in provisional means.
"The Buddha commanded us... [up to] "...is likewise. "The Buddha commanded us...
up to preaching the Unsurpassed Way" refers to the recitation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the purpose of transmitting the teaching.
"O sons of the Buddha... up to you shall attain Buddhahood" means that those who transmit the teaching each obtain great benefit. (1)
All Buddhas have come to proclaim this essential truth. It is lamentable that although they hear of Prajñā, they do not seek it for themselves, just as was said of that impoverished son and so forth;

all of this is because they are hindered by the provisional and thus deluded regarding the ultimate. Hereafter, the text revisits the preceding passage to extensively describe the meaning of being hindered by the provisional.
"We have attained internal cessation (up to: we do not give rise to joy or delight.

This cites the passage from the beginning of the chapter stating that they claimed for themselves to have already attained *nirvāṇa* and no longer sought progress toward *bodhi*, having no joy or delight in the *bodhisattva*-dharma, and so forth.
This is because they were stalled by expedient means (*upāya*) and took only the internal cessation of afflictions as their goal.
Taking the minor fruits as the foundation, one regards the task of purifying Buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings as external.
Why is this so? It is because the text merely mentions the contemplation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness to explain the intention of being entirely without longing or delight.
"For a long night we have [regarded this] as the ultimate.
This passage refers to the fact that upon hearing the Prajñāpāramitā, they lacked any aspiration or seeking.
"For a long night we have [regarded this] as the ultimate" [extends through to] "repaying the Buddha's kindness."
This refers to the notion that by applying diligent effort, one can attain Nirvana for the price of a single day;
to consider this sufficient is a state of mind rooted in delusion and stagnation, remaining in profound darkness without understanding. Thus, it is repeatedly described as the "long night.

To exit the three realms and realize the small fruits [of the śrāvaka] and then consider oneself to have attained the Way or to have repaid the Buddha’s kindness—all such views are instances of delusion and stagnation.
"Although we [have practiced], [it was only] to teach them great wisdom.

This passage records the intention of the bodhisattvas who transmit the teaching—that they themselves lacked aspiration—and the Buddha’s likewise permissive abandonment. To clarify the Buddha’s permissive abandonment:
it was because he wished to subdue them and await their turning of the mind that he taught them great wisdom, just like the wealthy elder.
...and so forth. This constitutes a dual citation of both the Dharma and the analogy to summarize the stagnation in provisional [teachings].

The reason for this repeated citation is that the error of the followers of the Two Vehicles in cherishing a mind for the Lesser Vehicle over vast eons has been profound; now that they have entered the Great [Vehicle], they realize it and feel deep regret.
Therefore, I have set forth my past errors in succession and spoken of them repeatedly to vent what I harbor in my breast. It is like a person whose indignation is extreme;
they must raise a harsh voice and utter bitter reproaches before they find relief. Thus, while the text may appear redundant, it actually possesses profound significance.
△ Second, the verse on the present attainment.
Today we have arrived at the point where we ought to receive offerings.
We celebrate that today we have finally attained the fruit of the true Path. We know that what was previously attained was not truly real.
That which is called attaining the Path and attaining the fruit is this: obtaining the pure eye regarding the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). As for these untainted dharmas, they are all...
The "Dharma" refers to the supreme and wondrous Dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*). The "pure eye" is the eye of the correct Dharma known and seen by all Buddhas.
Although you previously maintained pure precepts and thereby obtained karmic retribution, this was not the fruit of the true Path; it was merely a practice performed in the darkness.

Therefore, it is said that while you maintained the precepts for a long night, it is only from today that you have truly obtained their fruit. Although you previously cultivated the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) and obtained minor fruits, [it was not the ultimate realization].
This is not true outflow-free realization; it is merely a provisional skillful means to bring [the afflictions] to rest. Therefore, it is said:
"Having long cultivated the pure conduct, one now attains the unsurpassed great fruit of outflow-free realization. Only after this can one resound the voice of the Way as a true Śrāvaka;
only then can one universally receive offerings as a true Arhat. These are all the great graces of taming and guidance. Thus, below—
Chanting praises for his great kindness, he reflects upon repaying it. △ Fifth, reflecting on repaying the Buddha’s kindness has three parts. First, reflecting on the inability to repay:
"The World-Honored One’s great kindness... [up to] ...nor can I repay it."
To compassionately instruct [beings] through rare and marvelous skillful means is called "great kindness. Previously, one practiced the dharma of emptiness and realized the small fruit;
thus, one considered oneself to have repaid the Buddha’s kindness.

Yet, since that was insufficient as a repayment, one now wishes to exhaust all internal wealth—the hands, feet, shoulders, and head—as well as all external wealth—the most exquisite food, clothing, and jewels—to offer as long-term sustenance throughout kalpas.
One cannot repay it. Why is this? Because all internal and external wealth consists of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and is therefore not commensurate with such great kindness.
△ Second, the debt of gratitude for the kindness of compassion.
"The Buddhas are rare and marvelous" (up to) "teaching according to what is appropriate" praises the ultimate height of their magnificent virtue.
"The Buddhas are rare and marvelous" up to "the Kings of all Dharmas" praises the ultimate height of their magnificent virtue.

"They are able to act for those who are base and inferior" up to "teaching according to what is appropriate" evokes the depth of their compassion. Because of the ultimate height of their magnificent virtue, they adaptively [act]...
The inferior classes endure this fundamental matter because they follow the teachings of ordinary people who grasp at signs and speak according to their inclinations.
That is to say, [the Buddha] conceals his immeasurable power of mastery and instead delivers sentient beings through the Dharma that the poor delight in.
This is a rare and profound virtue, a great kindness of compassion, which truly cannot be repaid. △ Third, the gratitude for the grace of skillful means.
"The Buddhas, regarding the Dharma... (up to) "...teach the three according to what is appropriate.
This praises the virtue of skillful means (*upāya*), as the Buddhas have attained supreme mastery over the Dharma. "Knowing all sentient beings... (up to) "...preaches the Dharma for them.
This praises the power of skillful means. "According to all sentient beings... (up to) "...teaches the three according to what is appropriate."
This is to express gratitude for the grace of skillful means (*upāya*).

Since the Great Benevolence of the World-Honored One fundamentally arises from the two practices of compassion (*karuṇā*) and skillful means, although the aforementioned matters cannot fully repay it, one can ultimately only feel a profound sense of gratitude.
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Two, Part Three;
Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Fascicle Three, Part One.
By the Bhikṣu Jiéhuán of Wēnlíng Kāiyuán Lián Temple. Explanation.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs. △ Part Three:
The Tathāgata’s Confirmation. Section One: Analysis and Exposition of the Meaning.
This chapter serves to confirm and bring to completion the realization of those of middle capacity. Although Mahākāśyapa and the others had previously attained understanding...

The provisional skillful means that accord with circumstances ultimately converge upon the reality [of the truth]. Yet, it has not been clarified how the single sound secretly reveals true knowledge and the merit of its subtle transformation.

Just as a great cloud rains upon all things, and the grasses, trees, and forests receive moisture according to their respective capacities, the Buddha uses this analogy to further elaborate and confirm [the teaching], thereby manifesting the impartial compassion of the Sage, which is like that of Heaven and Earth.
This lack of self-interest arises from the self-interest of all things. Therefore, it is named the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.
The capacities of the three vehicles are likened to various plants and trees; the Dharma-transformation of the Buddha, the King of Awakening, is equal to a single rain.

Although the rain is of one flavor, the species differ; thus, there are variations in roots and stems, large and small. Likewise, although the Dharma has but a single characteristic, the dispositions of sentient beings vary.
Because of dullness, the paths and the realization of the fruits differ from one another. This compassion is without partiality, whereas all things are selfish.

Grass that can cure diseases is called "medicinal herb"; this serves as a metaphor for the seeds of goodness in humans and devas—the causes of wisdom of the Three Vehicles—which can distance one from harm and extinguish evil.
However, if they are the seeds of evil in the four miserable destinies—the causes of karma within birth and death—they serve only as useless weeds and filth.
It is not merely medicinal herbs. This parable concerns the three vehicles;

while the text also includes trees, the chapter is titled "Medicinal Herbs" specifically to provide a definitive exposition for those of middling faculties, establishing the name according to their immediate capacity. As the verse says:

"The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who hear the Dharma and attain its fruits are called medicinal herbs; each attains growth. This refers to them. If, however, there are bodhisattvas, they are called "Great [Herbs]."
[This is] not appropriate for the intended recipient. △ Second, the formal explanation according to the text, in six parts. First, restating and establishing the preceding meaning:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] "it is truly as you have said."
Kāśyapa, having realized the meaning of the parable, immediately established the analogy of the wealthy elder.

He praised how the Buddha concealed his excellence and manifested inferiority to entice the vulgar and base, thereby enabling them to obtain the great benefit of the Dharma. Furthermore, at the end of the verse, he marveled at the great kindness of the Buddha’s compassionate skillful means.
This is a sublime exposition of the Tathāgata’s true merits. △ Second, showing what was not yet fully expressed.
2. First, the heading indicates that it is inexhaustible:
"The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits (up to) which cannot be fully described.
This clarifies that through a single sound, he secretly reveals true knowledge and the compassionate transformation of equality; this is especially an immeasurable merit.
Although Kāśyapa has eloquently explained this virtue, his words have not yet reached its full extent; therefore, it is shown once more.
△ Second, explaining the reason for this, in two parts. First, showing the subtle revelation through the single sound.
Kāśyapa, you should know that all the teachings he expounds reach the ground of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

Expedient means (*upāya*) constitutes the ground of provisional wisdom, while wisdom (*jñāna*) constitutes the ground of reality. By employing expedient means to teach all phenomena, they all reach the ground of wisdom;
this is what is meant by "profoundly revealing. To reach the ground of omniscience is to accord with the realm of the wisdom of true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa-jñāna-viṣaya*).
△ Second, showing that true knowledge is a subtle transformation.
The Tathāgata contemplates and knows [up to] "manifesting all wisdom to all sentient beings.

That to which all dharmas converge is the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle. That which the minds of the multitude engage is the disposition and capacity for the Three Vehicles. The Buddha...
The teaching that all phenomena are for the purpose of liberating all minds is profound: if one does not know the ultimate destination of phenomena, it is difficult to liberate the mind;

if one does not know the movements of the mind, it is difficult to teach the Dharma. Now, having attained unimpeded mastery in both of these, he may be called one who truly knows the subtle transformation.
Furthermore, he has thoroughly investigated and clarified all phenomena in order to reveal and instruct all sentient beings.
Wisdom. To cause them to awaken and enter [this truth], all that is called the boundless *asaṃkhyeya* merits.
△ Third, the clarification through parables regarding what is shown has four parts. First, the basis for establishing the analogy.

Kāśyapa, it is like this: for example, in a trichiliocosm, although there are various distinct names and forms, the great trichiliocosm is uniformly a single earth, yet within it there are heights and depths such as mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys.

This is like how a single true realm contains the distinctions of the three realms and the various destinies. Just as plants and trees grow from the same earth, they nevertheless differ according to their species.
The distinctness of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is like the differentiation within a single dharma-nature into the three vehicles and the distinctions between the Great and Small [vehicles].
"Herbs" (*huì*) is the general term for various grasses; among these herbs there are thickets, and among trees there are forests. △ Second, the analogy of the single voice’s secret revelation.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system. At once, they pour down rain equally, and their moisture universally saturates all.

The cloud is a metaphor for the mind of compassion; the moisture is a metaphor for the rain of Dharma. As for the term "dense clouds," if the clouds were not dense, they could not pour down rain equally;

if compassion were not dense, it could not bring about universal benefit. That the rain from a single cloud universally saturates the great thousandfold world-system is an analogy for a single [instance].
The esoteric nature of the sounds reveals that both the Great and Small Vehicles are equally encompassed. △ Third, an analogy for true knowledge and subtle transformation:
"The various flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs of the forests and groves... (up to) "...the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit."

The analogy illustrates that through true knowledge, beings are transformed in accordance with their nature so that each achieves its own fulfillment. The distinction between roots, stems, and sizes collectively clarifies the differences among plants and trees, thereby elucidating the diversity of spiritual capacities (*indriya*).
The summary of all trees, large and small, as being "plants and trees" collectively demonstrates that the single rain is the same for all.

Now, with but a single cloud and a single rain nourishing myriad things, each according to its size and nature without ever being stunted or obstructed—causing those destined to be flowers to bloom and those destined to be fruits to ripen, each achieving its own fulfillment—such is the profound, mysterious transformation of the Buddha’s true wisdom.
That which is of wooden substance is called a trunk; that which is of grassy substance is called a stem; all depend upon the root to stand.

The roots are likened to the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); the trunk is likened to the arousal of the bodhicitta; the branches and leaves are likened to the teachings and principles that have been cultivated;

and the flowers and fruits are likened to the fruits of the practices performed. This means that while the lineages of the three vehicles differ in their arousal of the mind and their cultivation, they are equally moistened by the single voice of the teaching, each attaining its own respective accomplishment. △ Fourth, the analogy for the differences in the completion of the work.
Although they are born from the same earth and moistened by the same rain, the various grasses and trees each have their own distinctions.

Grasses and trees are all of the same category; they share the same earth as their ground and the same rain as their moisture. Yet, that there is a difference between the large and the small is due to the inherent diversity of their roots.
Sentient beings are likewise of the same category: what is bestowed upon them is the same nature, and what they are transformed by is the same.

Although the Way is one, that there are distinctions among the three vehicles is simply due to the differences in the capacities [of sentient beings]. △ Fourth, the application of the Dharma to the analogy, which has four parts.
First, the application of the basis for establishing the analogy.
Kāśyapa, you should know that—up to—"just as that great cloud completely covers the trichiliocosm, so too does the appearance of a Buddha extensively cover all sentient beings.
The arising of the cloud without intention is a metaphor for unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*).
The "great sound" refers to the voice of the mark of the broad and long tongue. "Devas, humans, and asuras" refers to the three wholesome realms of existence; it is not mentioned [otherwise].
The three evil realms constitute heavy obstacles and are not suitable vessels [for this teaching]. △ Second, the secret revelation in a single voice:
amidst the great assembly, he utters these words (extending to): "May those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa attain nirvāṇa."

This passage describes the Buddha’s initial sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), his proclamation of his transformative traces, and his declaration of the work of delivering sentient beings;

it serves to make known the intention behind the appearance of a Sage. To transcend and realize *bodhi* is called "deliverance" (*du*). To thoroughly comprehend all phenomena is called "liberation" (*jie*).
To be free from all fetters and bonds is called "peace" (*an*). To reach ultimate and eternal stillness is called "nirvāṇa" (*niepan*).
"One knows the present life and future lives as they truly are" (extending to "all should come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma").

This demonstrates that one possesses correct knowledge and vision (*samyagjñānadarśana*) in order to bring about broad awakening. Regarding "knowing the present life and future lives as they truly are":

it means comprehending the three periods of time through the wisdom of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇajñāna*), just as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* describes universally observing all things in a single thought-moment as being without coming, going, or abiding.
"One who knows all and sees all" means that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have thoroughly penetrated all phenomena.
"One who knows the Way" means that he has already attained prior knowledge and prior awakening. "One who opens the Way" means that he is able to use this Way to awaken those who come after him.
"One who speaks the Way" is one who can expound this Way through skillful means (*upāya*). One who proclaims it in this manner does so to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings;
thus, they summon devas and humans to cause them to listen and receive the teaching.
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma;
they had been gathered there by his summons. △ Third, the union of true knowledge and subtle transformation.
At that time, the Tathāgata observed these sentient beings (up to: and caused them all to rejoice and quickly obtain wholesome benefit.
The faculties and dispositions of the assembled multitude were diverse; the Buddha transformed each according to what they were capable of bearing.

For those capable of [attaining] the human or celestial realms, he taught the ten wholesome paths of action. For those capable of the Two Vehicles, he taught the Truths and Dependent Origination. For those capable of the Mahāyāna...
He preaches the Six Perfections for them. For those of determinate or indeterminate nature, as well as non-human beings, he teaches the Dharma according to what each can bear.
Although their faculties are infinite, he causes them all to become sharp and joyful; this is called "mysterious transformation.
△ Fourth, the combination of factors results in different outcomes.
When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma (up to) being fully moistened and each attaining growth, this clarifies the benefit of its accomplishment.
Regarding "hearing the Dharma and attaining peace": sentient beings are mired in the dust of worldly toil (*kleśa*), while those of the Two Vehicles are bound by emptiness and quiescence.
Those who hear this Dharma are thereby able to wash away their worldly toil and untie their fetters and attachments; they become liberated from all things.
To live one's life in outward leisure and ease is peace and security in the present world. To be reborn in a good realm is the retribution for hearing the Dharma.
To experience happiness through the Way is the fruit of practicing the Way. As for "through the Way," it means that the happiness experienced differs according to each respective path:
by practicing the ten wholesome actions, one receives the happiness of humans and devas; by practicing the Truths and Conditions, one receives the [happiness] of the Two Vehicles.
Joy. By practicing the six perfections, one experiences the joy of a bodhisattva, each according to their own path. Those who leave behind various obstacles:
those in the evil realms leave behind karmic obstacles to enter the human and celestial realms; those in the human and celestial realms leave behind phenomenal obstacles to enter the Two Vehicles;
those of the Two Vehicles leave behind ontological obstacles to enter the stage of a bodhisattva—each fulfilling their respective capacities. Therefore, it is said: "Among all dharmas..."
According to one's capacity and strength, one may gradually enter the Way.
Just as that great cloud rains upon all, the Tathāgata’s teaching has a single characteristic and a single flavor; [the beings] do not themselves perceive or know the merit they have attained.

This commentary elucidates the merit of his transformative teachings. It states that although the Tathāgata’s skillful means in preaching the Dharma are manifold, in reality they consist of but a single mark and a single flavor, just as a single cloud brings a single rain.
"Liberation, detachment, and cessation" refers to the essence of this single mark and single flavor.
The characteristic of liberation means it does not bind all phenomena; the characteristic of detachment means it does not conjoin with any sensory objects; and cessation...
When signs are extinguished, birth and death are forever ended, and one ultimately reaches the unsurpassed path of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As for sentient beings who hear and uphold [the teaching] yet do not realize the benefits they have obtained:

it is because the True Transformation is secretly revealed through a single sound and operates in profound stillness—just as the heavens and earth produce a hundred excellences, and rain and dew nourish all plants, which grow of their own accord.
Who, then, is truly capable of knowing this?
Why is that? [From here until] "and does not know their own superior, middling, or inferior nature.

This clarifies that by observing the faculties (*indriya*) and adapting the teaching so as not to conflict with their nature, beings are able to realize themselves. [This concerns] the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Since dispositions and desires differ, the resulting recollection, contemplation, cultivation, and attainment likewise differ.

Only the Tathāgata can know and transform them, yet those beings do not know it themselves. What matters are recollected? This refers to matters concerning humans and devas, up to and including matters concerning Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.
How is this recollection performed? It is either correct or erroneous, conditioned or unconditioned.
It is for this purpose. By what means does one practice mindfulness and so forth? This refers, for example, to whether one proceeds by way of the great or small, the sudden or gradual;

or by way of samādhi and prajñā, or vitarka and vicāra. By what means is attainment achieved? This refers, for example, to attaining the Dharma of the Śrāvaka through the Four Noble Truths, up to attaining the Dharma of the Bodhisattva through the Six Perfections.
Thus, the objects upon which mindfulness and reflection dwell differ from one another; this is what is meant.
The Tathāgata is able to perceive, exactly as they truly are, those who dwell in various stages.
This detailed explanation clarifies the Tathāgata’s thorough knowledge of the faculties [of sentient beings]. △ Fifth, the concluding praise of Kāśyapa.

"The Tathāgata knows that this is a dharma of one characteristic and one flavor" (up to) "he preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate, which is difficult to understand and difficult to know.

This reiterates the preceding passage on the "one characteristic, one flavor," etc., to clarify that the preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate is difficult to understand and difficult to know, thereby praising Kāśyapa for his ability to believe and accept it.
That which is characterized by the "one characteristic, one flavor," etc., is precisely that which is realized by the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding this Dharma, although the Tathāgata knows it, he observes that the dispositions and desires of sentient beings differ;

thus, he provisionally protects them and does not immediately explain it clearly. Therefore, it is extremely difficult to understand, yet Kāśyapa is able to believe and accept it—this is what is called "rare."

This restates the preceding text. While the previous statement spoke of reaching ultimate all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), this statement speaks of ultimate *nirvāṇa* as the mark of eternal quiescence.
The former was spoken in reliance on correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), while the latter is spoken in reliance on the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
their principle is one and the same. "Ultimately returning to emptiness" means that through self-liberation and detachment from cessation, one reaches ultimate, eternal quiescence.

When the marks [of phenomena] are thus understood, the mind of consciousness and its objects—mere shadows—are all swept away, returning to the wondrous emptiness of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), which is not a void of annihilation.
△ Sixth, the seven verses that restate this by means of gāthās; first, the verse restating and establishing the preceding meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Dharma King who destroys existence has appeared in the world; according to the desires of sentient beings, he teaches the Dharma in various ways."

This describes the meaning of Kāśyapa’s preceding praise of the Buddhas as having attained supreme mastery over the Dharma, knowing the various desires and inclinations of all sentient beings, and preaching the Dharma accordingly.
Sentient beings have lost the truth and sink into delusion, obstructed by ignorance and trapped within the various realms of birth and death.
The Great Awakened One appeared in the world to preach the True Dharma in order to shatter these veils.
By means of the non-existent, one eliminates obstructions and stagnations; therefore, he is titled the Dharma King who Shatters Existence. △ Second, the verse shows what was not yet fully addressed:
"The Tathāgata, out of reverence... (until)... causes them to attain right view."
The verse reveals the profound teaching of the compassion of equality. That he remained silent for a long time without speaking was to await the proper opportunity.
For those with wisdom will believe, while those without wisdom will doubt; thus they would forever lose the great benefit.
Therefore, he used gradual guidance, teaching according to their capacities so that they might attain right view. This constitutes the profound revelation of equal compassion. And as for Kāśyapa...
The leaves speak of what has not yet been reached. △ Third, the verses clarify the parables in four parts. First, the verse illustrating the original:
"Kāśyapa, you should know: it is like a great cloud arising in the world, covering everything."
This is like the appearance of a Buddha in the world. △ Second, the verse on the subtle revelation through the single voice:
"The cloud of wisdom contains moisture" (extending to) "the entire land is thoroughly saturated.
When the great cloud is about to rain, lightning flashes and thunder rolls. This is like the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, emitting light and preaching the Dharma. Wisdom...
"The clouds containing moisture that obscure the sunlight" refers to the wondrous great clouds of a compassionate mind that extinguish the flames of affliction.

"The clouds gather in dense masses and descend to reach the earth; they are close at hand and can be grasped" is a metaphor for how the compassionate mind reaches down to look upon all things with equality.
"Its rain falls universally and equally" is a metaphor for how the benefits of the Dharma are uniform, reaching all four directions alike.

The lower part of the analogy illustrates that [the rain] makes no distinction among the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). That the entire land is thoroughly saturated illustrates how the teaching pervades the great trichiliocosm.
△ Third, the verse praises true knowledge and its subtle transformation:
"Mountains, rivers, steep gorges... medicinal herbs and trees all flourish."
This is like the various capacities of sentient beings being different, yet their responses do not fail them. Previously, only grasses and trees were mentioned;

here, the addition of the "hundred grains" and so forth is because grasses and trees represent the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of the Three Vehicles—specifically those with the capacity to enter the Path who have not yet manifested within the marketplace of the world.
Therefore, the hundred grains and so forth are added to illustrate that all living beings, down to the most minute, receive the moisture of its benefit. [As for] the dry land...
This is like those who have not yet been moistened by the water of the Dharma; because they all receive benefit and nourishment, it is said that [the rain] "universally saturates" them.
"Medicinal trees" refers to medicinal herbs and trees. △ Fourth, the verse on the different ways in which the parables are formed.
The clouds produce [rain] (up to) which each grows lushly.
△ Fourth, the verse on the application of the Dharma has four parts. First, the application of the original parable:
The Buddha is likewise; appearing in the world, he is like a great cloud that universally covers all.
△ Second, the single sound of the Esoteric Teaching was revealed.
Having appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings, he analytically expounded the reality of all dharmas;
though there are many gates of skillful means, they do not depart from the true mark (*dharmatā*).
"The Great Sage, World-Honored One" (up to) "and the bliss of nirvāṇa.

This verse proclaims the traces of his manifest transformation and the deeds of delivering sentient beings. "Causing all to leave suffering behind" and below refers to the [four immeasurables] such as causing those not yet delivered to be delivered.
Because they attain deliverance up to the point of nirvāṇa, they leave suffering behind and abide in peace within the world.
There is no supramundane bliss that cannot be attained.
All the hosts of devas and humans [attain] the nectar-like pure Dharma.
This verse calls upon the devas and humans to listen to the Dharma.
That Dharma is of a single flavor (up to) acting as the causal condition.

This refers to the verses on the "single characteristic" and "single flavor," etc. To constantly act as a condition for the Mahāyāna means that it ultimately leads to the attainment of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Third, the unification of true knowledge and subtle transformation.
I observe all things (up to) without weariness or fatigue.
This is the great compassion of true knowledge, which is equal in its mysterious transformation. △ Fourth, the formation of differences through combination.
All sentient beings who hear my Dharma receive it according to their capacity and abide upon the various stages (*bhūmi*).
These stages are as explained below: beginning with the human and celestial realms and culminating in the tenth stage.
Those who dwell among humans and devas as wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or the various Brahmā kings are the minor medicinal herbs;

they represent the vehicles of humans and devas. A wheel-turning king rules over the four continents; Śakra, the King of Devas, rules over the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; and Brahmā, the King, rules over the heavens of the first dhyāna.
Knowing the untainted dharmas (up to this point) refers to the medicinal herbs;

this is the Śrāvaka vehicle. Attaining the small fruit of the untainted state and giving rise to the six supernormal powers and the three knowledges constitutes the common practice of both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
However, among them, those of sharp faculties attain the realization of a Pratyekabuddha.
Seeking the state of a World-Honored One, [they think], "I shall become a Buddha," and practice the meditative concentration of diligence;

these are the superior medicinal herbs, the Bodhisattvas of the *pitaka* teachings. Although they rely on the provisional vehicle (*upāyayāna*) to cultivate the Bodhisattva path and diligently practice with the goal of attaining Buddhahood, they have not yet departed from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); therefore, they are classified as superior herbs.
Furthermore, "all the sons of the Buddha" (up to) "this is called a small tree" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
These rely on the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) teachings to cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva; they constitute the initial stage of the Mahāyāna.
Because although their faculties (*indriya*) are great, their shade is not yet extensive, they are called "small trees.
Those who dwell securely in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)—up to those called "great trees"—are Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*).
These rely on the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva, transcending the Three Vehicles and dwelling securely therein.
With supernormal powers, he turns the wheel of non-retrogression and delivers billions of beings; thus his protection is vast.
The Buddha teaches with impartiality, yet those who receive it each differ according to their own capacities.
The conclusion establishes that while [the Buddha's] manifest transformations differ, his ultimate transformation is secretly identical to the Creator.

By means of this analogy, [it is shown that] although the preceding metaphors and explanations are extensive, they clarify only the appearance of a single drop within the ocean of the Buddha’s true wisdom.
[End of section. This verse clarifies the intention that the Tathāgata’s incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits cannot be fully described.
△ Fifth, explaining the progressive advancement according to the capacities of beings:
"I rain down the rain of Dharma... gradually increasing in lushness and excellence."
This explains the benefit of progress. Below, the capacity for progress is explained.
"The Dharma of all Buddhas" (up to) "all attain the fruit of the Way" is the general heading;
what follows is the specific explanation.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas each attain increase.
Regarding those who advance by means of the dharmas of the two vehicles, those in their final existence are about to realize the fruit of pratyekabuddhahood.
They will no longer undergo rebirth among humans.
If various bodhisattvas [proceed] until they attain increase—
those who advance by relying on the Vaipulya teachings— this is so.
Furthermore, there are those who dwell in dhyāna (up to) attain growth.
These are those who advance by relying on the Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
In this way, Kāśyapa (up to) each attains the realization of reality.
In summary, the differences arise from the various capacities of those who encounter the teaching. Those of China call them "those whose roots of goodness have blossomed";
through the Buddha’s subtle transformation, each attains the realization of the fruit. △ Sixth, clarifying that the paths of all Buddhas are identical.
Kāśyapa, you should know that [this applies] up to all Buddhas as well.
They secretly manifest their mysterious transformation; the Way of every Buddha is the same. △ Seventh, concluding the previous section and opening the subsequent one:
"Now, for your sakes... all shall attain Buddhahood."

Summarizing the preceding discourse, it establishes the ultimate reality and discards the provisional. The passage concerning "opening the future and bestowing predictions" explains that the most ultimate reality is precisely the establishment of the real;

that "none are in extinction" is the discarding of the provisional; and that "those who practice this path shall all attain Buddhahood" is the textual account of opening the future and bestowing predictions.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Six: The Prophecy (Vyākaraṇa-parivarta). Section Four:
The Prophecy for Those of Middle and Lower Capacities. Part One: A Brief Exposition of the Structural Meaning.
Mahākāśyapa and the others, having realized the meaning of the parables, have attained the true path of the Buddha and shall ascend to the rank of Buddhahood; therefore, he speaks to them.

The chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecy (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) concerns the fruit to be attained in the future. This single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the time when the capacities of all beings have become genuine and solid, and what was to be accomplished has been fulfilled;
therefore, in the teaching of the main body of the doctrine, there is no further business to be done. It directly unifies the three vehicles into a single consistency.
He opened the way for the four types of views and proclivities to enter awakening, bestowing a prediction of enlightenment upon each one and sealing their attainment of Buddhahood;
this was merely to demonstrate that his original vow had been fulfilled through the completion of his meritorious practice.

However, in the past, Vimalakīrti once questioned why Maitreya was granted the prediction of a single lifetime, arguing that within the stage of the "True Position" (samyaktva-niyāma), there is fundamentally no such thing as receiving a prediction or attaining bodhi—yet [Maitreya] had already entered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The "Correct Position" (samyaktva-avasthā): how could it be hindered by lingering traces? Furthermore, because there is a self, there is the bestowal of a prediction (vyākaraṇa). Does one who has entered the Correct Position still possess a self?
Although there is no bestowal of a prediction within the Correct Position itself, this does not preclude the bestowal of a prediction.

Is the Ocean of Nature in the *Avataṃsaka* not the Correct Position? Yet, from the beginning of the Ten Abodes to the end of Wondrous Enlightenment, the bestowal of predictions is repeatedly heard, as for example: [text continues].
What is called the pure mind and what is called the sublime realm—how could they ever be non-existent?
Vimalakīrti said: "In preaching the Dharma, one speaks neither of existence nor of non-existence. It is by way of causes and conditions that all phenomena arise.
There is no self, no agent, and no recipient; yet the karma of good and evil does not perish. One who has realized the truth is indeed without a self. Nevertheless, [the efficacy of] goodness...
How could the karma of evil have no record of its own? How could it be something that might be forgotten?

Whether it be the poverty or wealth, nobility or lowliness, long life or shortness, suffering or joy experienced by those in this world—created in the past and received in the present, summoned before and answered after—it is like casting a wide net that lets nothing escape;
even as one sinks through vast kalpas, nothing is lost. Who, then, records this? That which is now...
Regarding the "bestowal of predictions" (vyākaraṇa): this is specifically intended to assist in clarifying the principle that [the Dharma] does not perish, thereby inspiring the practitioner.
△ Second, the actual commentary on the text has three parts. First, Kāśyapa receives his prediction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken these verses... [up to] "the kalpa named Great Adornment.

All the texts concerning the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa) consist of two parts: that which precedes the Ten Epithets constitutes the prediction of the cause, and that which follows constitutes the prediction of the fruit.
The varying numbers of disciples who come to behold the Buddha each follow their own vows and conditions; this is due to the efficacy of their service to the Buddha.

They are not the same; each follows according to their respective capacities and powers. The differences in the names by which they are designated as Buddhas follow according to their respective causal practices.

Mahākāśyapa, during his stage of practice, served the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he lit lamps to continue the illumination and applied purple-gold to the Buddha’s images.
Furthermore, because he brought forth clarity regarding the wondrous nature of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he was thus named.
The light, the land named Radiant Virtue (Guangde), and the eon named Adorned (Zhuangyan) all correspond to his causal practices.
The Buddha’s lifespan will be twelve small kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma will likewise endure for twenty small kalpas.
The body of the pure dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing.
Yet, that which appears in future ages, abides for twelve kalpas, and then passes away, is merely a manifestation following the power of great compassionate vows.

That the teachings of the True Dharma and Semblance Dharma each last twenty kalpas before their extinction is merely a matter of flourishing or declining in accordance with the karmic resonance of sentient beings. The dharmatā of the Buddha-body is, in truth, [immutable].
There is neither addition nor subtraction within this interval.
The realm of the land is adorned and free from all impurities and evils (extending until) various precious flowers are scattered everywhere in purity.

All that is experienced as the environment resulting from one's condition is due to the state of the mind-ground. Broken tiles, rubble, thorns, and brambles are the result of a defiled mind; excrement and filth—[are likewise so].
This is the retribution for a pure or defiled mind. Ravines, pits, mounds, and hills are the retribution for a deceitful mind.
Because the Buddhas have no defilement or deceit, their buddha-fields are adorned and free from all impurities and evils; this is because they cultivate only pure and wondrous practices.

Thus their lands are level and upright, pervaded by a hundred jewels. As it is said in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*: "According to the purity of one's own mind, so is the purity of the buddha-field. Following that...
"When the mind is pure, all merits are pure; this is the proof thereof.
In that land, there are immeasurable thousands of billions of bodhisattvas... (down to) even though there are Māras and their followers, they all protect the Buddha-dharma."
Question: Śākyamuni Buddha still required arduous subjugation even after attaining enlightenment; why was there no demonic activity for Kāśyapa alone? Answer:
Śākyamuni manifested his transformation in the five turbidities, where he acted as a laboring companion to the various demons. If there were no demonic activities, it would not be called an evil age.
Kāśyapa attained Buddhahood in a virtuous land; therefore, although demons existed, they all protected the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse, addressing the bhikṣus:
[from] "The matter was thus" [to the end].
The verses should clarify the mind as expressed in the prose; "tamed and gentle" refers to the ultimate state of compassion. He has attained great spiritual power.

Generally speaking, "responsive transformation" (nirmāṇa) refers to that which is unfathomable. It reaches [all beings]. One who possesses great supernatural powers (mahābhijñā) responds without acting and pervades everywhere without deliberation;

thus, they differ from the lesser sages. The "body of no-outflows in the final existence" refers to the essence of the fruit of the śrāvaka, while the "son of the Dharma King" refers to the śrāvaka of great resolve.
△ Second and third: The two sages request a prediction.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana (up to) then spoke these verses with a single voice.
Regarding the Dharma-exposition stating that the twelve hundred arhats shall all likewise become buddhas, the bestowal of their predictions was thus completed.

In this context, the specific conferral of the prediction upon Kāśyapa as the foremost disciple means that the predictions for the three sages need not be further elaborated; such is the case for Maudgalyāyana as well.
My mind was not at ease, like one who encounters a royal feast yet dares not eat immediately; therefore, I have ventured to request with trepidation.
O Great Hero, Fierce World-Honored One... [until] removing the heat and attaining cool serenity.
The first four lines praise and express gratitude for the gift of the Dharma through analogy; the subsequent lines request that [the teaching] be recorded and seek further benefit.
It is like coming from a land of famine—only after arriving there does one dare to eat.
This is an illustration; the following is the self-explanation:
"We are also like this" (up to) "only then shall we be truly at peace and happy.
We constantly reflect upon the faults of the Hīnayāna, which is like coming from a land of famine. This refers to our [aspiration] to become Buddhas.
It is as if one has suddenly encountered the meal of a great king.
O Great Hero, O World-Honored One, who ever desires to bring peace to the world, we pray that you grant us a prediction; like one who is hungry, we require instruction on what to eat.
This concludes the formal invitation. △ Third, the three sages receive their prophecies; this section also has three parts. First, the prophecy for Subhūti.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the minds of the great disciples... [omitted] ...the land shall be named Ratnasaṃbhava.
When form and mind first dissolve, the myriad dharmas are all empty; when principle and phenomena return to their source, all is reality.

In the past, Subhūti understood emptiness as being without name or mark—this was when form and mind first dissolved. Now, having realized the fruit of truth, he conversely designates names and marks—this is when principle and phenomena have returned to their source.
Furthermore, at the time of his birth, the household goods suddenly became empty; now, in this kalpa, they are called "existent."
"Jewel" (*ratna*) is also a term for the land named Ratnasambhava. "Nayuta" refers to the numerical unit *hai*.
That land is level and even (extending until) it liberates immeasurable bodhisattvas and assemblies of śrāvakas.
The ten titles cited clarify the primary retribution (the Buddha’s own body), while the adornments of the eon and the land clarify the secondary retribution (the environment).
That the lotus trees, terraces, and pavilions are all composed of jewels corresponds to the name of that eon and land.
As for the statement that the Buddha constantly dwells in space to preach the Dharma, it demonstrates that one awakens through emptiness and realizes the truth by means of emptiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"O assembly of bhikṣus... for twenty intermediate kalpas, Subhūti has resided at the head of the monastic community gathered on the sublime Vulture Peak Mountain; at the great assembly of the Prajñāpāramitā, he has realized emptiness."

First: although their virtue, conduct, and spiritual practice may seem comparable to that of a "subordinate sage" (ārya), they must still serve countless Buddhas to realize the fruit of their records.
While those who follow the path of the Buddhas gradually fulfill the Great Way, those of the Hīnayāna merely contemplate signlessness (animitta) without cultivating great deeds;
thus, even after passing through many kalpas, they do not achieve perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one must resolve upon the great mind of Bodhicitta and be fully equipped [with its practices].
This is the Great Path of the Bodhisattvas; thereafter, one attains Buddhahood. The people joined their palms to listen to and receive the Buddha’s words;
they all spoke with sincere faith, delighted in goodness, and were free from vulgar customs. △ Second, the prophecy for Cāṇūra.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the assembly of bhikṣus (up to) and spoke in verse:
"The assembly of bhikṣus (up to) adorns his land."

The Jāmbūnada gold is of incomparable purple brilliance; the *candana* fruit is likewise golden in substance. Because Pūrṇa was foremost in the exposition of the Abhidharma (*abhidharma-arthaviniścaya*), his rational nature is pure and translucent.
Furthermore, this is the fruit of the merit he accumulated by diligently sweeping the grounds of the Buddha in past lives, thereby perfecting its majestic purity.
As for "severing all existence" (*sarvabhava-prahāṇa*): when principle reaches its ultimate limit, the emotions are forgotten, and not even a speck of dust can be established. Thus it is said.
That realization of the Way is pure and penetrating; it does not mean a negation that abandons existence for non-existence. △ Third, Maudgalyāyana receives his prediction.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the great assembly... (until) "the Semblance Dharma shall also abide for forty minor kalpas."
The fragrance of *tāmālapatra* sandalwood is pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive; Maudgalyāyana, who is foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), is like it.
In the northwest, there is a Buddha named Tāmālapatra-candana-gandha-ṛddhi; thus, it is clear that "fragrance" is used as a metaphor for supernatural power.
One *yojana* is forty *li*. When Maudgalyāyana made offerings to the Buddha, he erected a stūpa one thousand *yojanas* high.
The term "ten days" refers to that which is established through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

All these causal records of practice are intended to urge on the *śrāvakas* and expand their great resolve, causing them to relinquish mere empty tranquility and extensively cultivate the Great Practice in order to achieve the Buddha-way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"My disciple here... you all listen well. Regarding the phrase "a tall golden *kīla*":
*kīla* (in the full terminology, *caitya-dhara*) refers to the pillar atop a stūpa, shaped like an inverted bowl, which serves as the pinnacle of the stūpa.
It is called a *stūpa-yaṣṭi* because it serves as its external marker. It is made of gold; since the stūpa is one thousand *yojanas* high, the length of the marker may be known from this.
Maudgalyāyana’s recorded verses, ending with the phrase "it shall likewise be so during the Semblance Dharma," have concluded.
From the passage beginning "My disciples, endowed with majestic power," he grants the predictions for the five hundred [arhats] and opens the third cycle.
The Opening of the Exposition of the Dharma.
*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Three, Part One;
*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Three, Part Two.
Commentary by the Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wénlíng on the "Parable of the Phantom City," Chapter Seven of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Part Three:
The One Round of Teaching through Causes and Conditions. Section Two: For Those of Inferior Faculties. First: A Brief Exposition of the Structural Analysis and Meaning.

The conjured city is fundamentally non-existent yet established as a provisional means to rescue those whose cultivation is obstructed and whose aspirations have ceased, leading them forward until they reach the place of treasure.
This is a metaphor for how the minor fruits are not real but are provisionally established to rescue those who delight in the small and seek realization therein.
It is to lead them and cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. What is called "teaching by means of causes and conditions" refers to everything from the preceding parables up to the medicinal herbs;

all these illustrate that while the Dharma is one, the capacities of sentient beings differ. Fearing that those of inferior faculties might think it is ultimately unattainable for them, [the Buddha] teaches accordingly.

Consequently, they give rise to weariness and regression. Thereupon, it is clarified that because past causes have already brought about transformation and instruction, and the present conditions are now ripe such that the supreme fruit is near, they are enabled to avoid falling back and instead abandon the "Transformation City" (hwa-seong) to hasten toward the "Jewel Place" (po-so). Part Two:
Explanation of the Text According to the Outline, in two sections. First: The Actual Exposition of the Causes and Conditions, in six parts. One: Designating the Fundamental Beginning.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus... [up to] "the kalpa named Great Signs.
As for Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, he is the Buddha who is the fruit of the true wisdom of the One Vehicle. Regarding the essence of his wisdom: it encompasses the ten voids and is thus "Great" (mahā);

it penetrates and illuminates throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and is thus "Pervasive Wisdom" (abhijñājñāna); it is peerless among all things and is thus "Victorious" (abhibhū). Speaking in terms of its traces...

From this perspective, he is the patriarchal master of Śākyamuni during his stage of causal practice (*hetu-bhūmi*); by logical inference, he is the awakened essence (*bodhi-tattva*) that is the fundamental source of all sentient beings.
Although the awakened essence of sentient beings is originally such as this, because they are deluded within their own form and mind (*rūpa-citta*), it appears small rather than great;
because they are confined and obstructed within the shell of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is hindered rather than penetrating; and thus it remains latent, submerged in delusion.

Because consciousness is vulgar, it is inferior and cannot prevail. If one can thoroughly understand the delusions and stagnations of form and mind and shatter the shell of ignorance, then supreme wisdom will manifest before them, no different from that of a Buddha.

As for the statement regarding "immeasurable and inconceivable kalpas," this clarifies that the essence of this wisdom has been present since beginningless time; it is not something that can be reached by the calculations of emotional dust or numerical measures.
"O monks, it is as if one were to take all the earth element within a trichiliocosm—
setting aside the earth that is already manifest— and use this as seed to produce further earth."
"Suppose there were a person who ground it into ink... [as before] ...would it not, World-Honored One?
This refers to an extremely vast amount of earth.
Suppose, monks... [as before] ...one were to grind it all into dust, and for each particle of dust, one kalpa."
These kalpas are exceedingly numerous;
since that Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, it has been hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Yet, supreme wisdom is neither ancient nor new, and from the beginning it has never entered parinirvāṇa; nevertheless, that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa has been thus long ago.
This is merely spoken out of sentiment for those of inferior faculties. As for people like us, how many kalpas have passed since we lost our supreme wisdom and have been wandering in delusion?
Truly, it cannot be calculated by dust or ink.
The explanation of the Dharma mentions the causes for those to be transformed, citing only the time since attaining Buddhahood without stating the number of kalpas; as for the parable, however—
To cite the deeds of teaching performed by twenty trillion Buddhas is, in this context, to cite the causes and conditions spanning aeons as numerous as motes of dust;
thus, the distinction between those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties becomes clear.
By means of the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, I perceive that which occurred in the distant past as if it were today.

Because sentient beings perceive through their own knowledge and views, they are deluded and transmigrate, engaging in false conceptualizations; thus, for them, the Buddhas who surpass such wisdom are separated by kalpas as vast as dust and ink.
Because the Tathāgata perceives through his own knowledge and views, past and present are one and the same time; thus, he regards that which is remote and ancient as if it were this very day.
This, moreover, is the great penetration of Śākyamuni.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I recall past lives... [until] penetrating immeasurable kalpas."
This verse praises the fundamental beginning of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and demonstrates Śākyamuni’s clarity and penetration of past wisdom.

To know that the other Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa is as if it were today; likewise, for the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, seeing his parinirvāṇa as if it were now, they also know the events of that assembly’s parinirvāṇa as if they were seeing them today. The Buddha’s wisdom is pure, subtle, and penetrating.
"Reaching immeasurable kalpas" is a verse praising Śākyamuni’s great penetration.
"Commanding the bhikṣus to know" indicates that he is about to recount the causes and conditions of past lives, so as to lead them to believe that the Tathāgata’s clear vision is without error.
△ Second, the narration of past causes, in twelve parts. First, the Great Penetration attains enlightenment.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus (up to): "Yet the Buddhadharma still does not appear before them.
The Dharmakāya and the life of wisdom have no beginning; thus, even five hundred *koṭis* of *nayutas* of kalpas would be but a lifespan responding to conditions, not to be considered long.
That which is called the Buddhadharma is the true wisdom of the One Vehicle, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

Those of superior faculties attain sudden enlightenment and immediately realize the Buddha-way. Those of inferior faculties, whose obstructions are heavy, must necessarily rely on gradual cultivation.
Even after ten minor kalpas of the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, [the teaching] did not yet manifest before them; it was merely manifested in response to those of inferior faculties.

This is because those of inferior faculties have lost their supreme wisdom due to the delusive obstructions of the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*). Since this has been for an exceedingly long time, they must necessarily accumulate merit through practice.

Because he successively eliminates and remedies [afflictions], it is said that from one intermediate kalpa up to ten intermediate kalpas, once the obstacles of delusion are completely severed, wisdom then manifests before him.
This is why his great penetration accords with the capacities of beings in such a manner. Thus the Prince praised him, saying:

"For the sake of delivering sentient beings, after immeasurable billions of years, you have finally attained Buddhahood. This clearly demonstrates his manifestation in accordance with the capacities of beings.
At that time, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (up to) "shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

This describes Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū about to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The devas prepared seats and invited the Buddha. Some say that although he originally sat at the site of enlightenment, the Buddha-dharma did not manifest;
thus, by shifting his seat to this place, he immediately attained bodhi. This signifies that one must eliminate traces and forget conditions before [realization].
He accords with the Way. However, as it says below: "As soon as he sat upon this seat, ten small kalpas were fulfilled. This suggests that it was not merely by shifting his seat that he attained it.
From the moment he sat upon this seat until his parinirvāṇa, it was likewise so.
"Suitable sitting" refers to the initial sitting. When he first sat, flowers rained down and music was played; it was likewise so until his parinirvāṇa.
This speaks to the supreme degree of veneration by the devas.
The various bhikṣus (up to) attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This signifies that the ten afflictions (*daśānuśaya*) were exhausted, supreme wisdom was perfectly manifested, and they achieved the state of Most Perfect Enlightenment. △ Second, the Prince followed the Buddha.
Before that Buddha left the household life, he had sixteen sons; the eldest was named Zhiji (Jñānakūṭa).
The manifestations of all Buddhas are fundamentally intended to symbolize the Dharma. Before Dīpaṃkara left the household life, he had eight sons;

before Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū left the household life, he had sixteen sons. These all symbolize the eight consciousnesses within the bonds of saṃsāra. The former [eight] correspond to those of superior faculties, being upright and...
Because it is heterodox, there are only eight [consciousnesses]. This, when contrasted with those of inferior faculties for whom the heterodox and orthodox are intermingled, results in sixteen.
One named Jñānakūṭa (智積) is so called because his wisdom has an accumulation; thus he is consciousness remaining in bondage.
If one functions without such accumulation, this constitutes the Great Pervasive Supreme Wisdom. A son of Dīpaṃkara named Saṃcetanīya (有意) likewise possesses an accumulation.
Regarding this meaning:
each of the sons possessed various rare and extraordinary articles for play and enjoyment...

(until) having completed their circumambulation of the Buddha, the son of Lamp-Light stopped speaking, as he governed the four continents; this symbolizes that those of the highest capacity have only the four great elements as their burden.

Thus it is said. That the sons of Jñānavijaya each possessed various playthings and objects of pleasure signifies that those of inferior faculties have various desires and accumulations to which their deep minds are attached.
That they abandoned their treasures to go to the Buddha indicates that because they possessed such accumulations, they had not yet attained great penetration;
only by being able to abandon desire and attachment can one realize penetrating wisdom. The mothers raised by the princes were not the same.

Therefore, it is said that "the various mothers followed him weeping," because love is difficult to abandon suddenly. The Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) was the father of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and the grandfather of Jñānākara.
△ Third, the Prince’s Praise of the Buddha, in three parts: first, praising the fulfillment of his vows and the attainment of the Way.
With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One, reciting in verse:
“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue... Excellent, auspicious, and unsurpassed!
It has been long since You attained Buddhahood, awaiting the fulfillment of Your vow to deliver sentient beings. Excellent, auspicious, and unsurpassed! Thus they praised His auspiciousness.
The Way is honored. △ Second, praising the perfection of the merits of concentration and wisdom:
"The World-Honored One is most rare" (up to) "abiding in the untainted Dharma.
Being serene and undisturbed is the perfection of concentration; reaching the ultimate state of being untainted is the perfection of wisdom. △ Third, rejoicing at having encountered [the Buddha].
Encounter.
Now that we have seen the World-Honored One (up to) never again hearing the name of the Buddha, those who have attained this wholesome benefit will remove the blindness of suffering;
they recognize the path to the exhaustion of suffering and know how to seek liberation. "Blindness" refers to—
To say that there is no eye of wisdom within is to claim, in effect, that there is no sun of wisdom without.

That the path to the exhaustion of suffering is what is called "teaching the various paths for exhausting suffering and pointing toward nirvana" is indeed the benefit for those at the initial stage of the mind.
"Now the Buddha has attained the supreme [state]... I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
This marks the conclusion of the celebration. △ Fourth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha in verse... they spoke these verses once more.
The Wheel of Dharma takes up and conveys [beings] without obstruction.
The Hero of the World is without equal... (until) "he shall turn the unsurpassed wheel.
The first four lines praise his virtues and request the teaching. From "deliver us" until "so it is for all sentient beings," [the remaining verses follow].
This refers to the aspiration for the benefits of the Dharma. From the World-Honored One, they learn that sentient beings will eventually turn the unsurpassed wheel;

thus, they pray that he will preach according to their capacities. "What is contemplated and what is practiced" refers to the capacity for turning toward the Path. "The power of wisdom and the power of merit" refer to the substance for receiving the Path.
"Karmic actions from past lives" refer to the causes for attaining the Path. Each of these possesses degrees of smallness or greatness, and shallowness or depth.
The Buddha knows and perceives all things; therefore, he acts in accordance with the capacities of his audience. △ Fifth, the auspicious signs move the devas.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: (up to) "How is it that sentient beings suddenly arise within this?"
Sentient beings are firmly bound by ignorance; they experience the obstruction of the earth element such that it does not pass through, thereby veiling their wondrous luminosity.
For this reason, whenever Buddhas attain the Way, they cause the earth to tremble and emit light, demonstrating the overturning and shattering of ignorance to manifest the light of wisdom.
In the midst of that land, in the place of profound darkness, is what is called the dark space between the two Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
The sentient beings dwelling therein were formerly in such deep obscurity that they could not see one another; it was only through light that they saw each other, and thus doubt suddenly arose.
Indeed, human beings are born from the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and their various characteristics, yet they are shrouded by the ignorance of delusion (*avidyā*).

Truly, it cannot be illuminated by the majestic radiance of the sun and moon. Only when supreme wisdom opens and clarifies does one realize that the characteristics of sentient beings are likewise like this:
suddenly appearing as illusory existences from within the realm of indistinct vagueness.
Furthermore, the palaces of all the devas within that realm [surpass] the radiance of the various devas.
Although the devas possess their own constant light, it does not equal the Buddha’s radiance. △ Six: The Various Devas Request the Dharma (Five sections). One:
Five Hundred Brahma Kings from the East (Four subsections). First: Moved by the Buddha’s Radiance.
The Buddha’s great radiance moved those in the ten directions; each followed the light to the Buddha to present offerings and request the Dharma. Furthermore, there were four categories [of beings].
At that time, from within five hundred million *koṭis* of lands in the eastern direction... (up to) he spoke in verse:
Our various palaces (up to) illuminate the ten directions.
When those gods of great majesty and virtue are about to be born, auspicious light first appears; they are called the "Glorious Virtue" (Mahābhāga) gods.
△ Second, following the light to visit the Buddha.

Immediately, the various Brahma Kings [up to] offered their palaces, praying that [the Buddha] would graciously accept and dwell therein.
They scattered flowers upon the Buddha to honor the Teacher, and simultaneously made offerings to the trees to revere the Way.
The flowers were like Mount Sumeru, and the trees were ten *yojanas* high; these were all transformations manifested through the power of the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*. It was like the Dragon King.
"Though rain falls in torrential torrents throughout the ten directions, how could that water be so vast? It is merely transformed by the dragon.
Then, the Brahma Kings, before the Buddha, with single-minded devotion and in unison, spoke in verse:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and extraordinary" (up to) "I only pray that you will compassionately accept us.
This praises his accumulation [of merit], for he possesses immeasurable virtues and is able to rescue and protect all.
"All sentient beings of the ten directions universally receive his bounty. This praises his benefit [to others]. "From where we have come," etc., expresses their long-standing devotion.
"We offer this as a tribute through the merits of our past lives. △ Fourth, the Request for the Buddha to Turn the Dharma Wheel.

O Hero of the World, Honored One among Two-legged Beings, we pray that you will expound the Dharma; by the power of your great compassion, deliver all suffering sentient beings.
The Path to Nirvana is the wondrous path that brings immediate liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
Knowing that the time had not yet arrived, he accepted the invitation and sat in silence. △ Second, the five hundred Brahmā kings from the southeast:
