The *kalaviṅka* is called the "fine-sounding bird"; its voice is clear and harmonious, evoking joy, and is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s Dharma-voice.

This lower heaven (*adhaḥ-svarga*) says that one hundred and eighty kalpas have passed in vain without a Buddha; the Southern Heaven (*dakṣiṇa-svarga*) says that one has obtained a vision [of a Buddha] after one hundred and thirty kalpas;
the upper heaven (*ūrdhva-svarga*) says that in the past, immeasurable kalpas passed in vain without a Buddha. That they differ in this way is because of faith (*śraddhā*).
One knows that the Buddha’s body is omnipresent and manifests at all times;

it is only because sentient beings perceive according to their own conditions that there appear the notions of duration, brevity, birth, and extinction. As the eyes of sentient beings, he dispels the confusion of the evil realms.
As the father of sentient beings, he serves as their refuge and destination. △ Fourth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Brahma Kings, having praised the Buddha with verses, spoke these verses with one mind and in unison:
"The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma... [until] those who are patient and virtuous increase."
"To deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction so that they may attain great joy" means: they suffer because they have lost their true nature and are submerged in delusion;

they rejoice because they are freed from clinging and released from bondage. "Attaining the Way or being born in heaven" means: those above may deeply penetrate to attain the Way, while those below may obtain blessings and be born in heaven.
"Enduring and doing good" means exerting effort to practice virtue.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.

Our various palaces... [until] because of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

"We pray that the Honored One among gods and humans... shall now proclaim the profound and far-reaching sound."
The drum, the conch, and the rain are all metaphors for the Great Dharma, which can issue commands to awaken the multitudes and bring benefit and moisture to all things.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.

△ 2. Seeking Light and Approaching the Buddha.
At that time, five million *koṭis* of Brahma kings, together with their palaces, [came] and requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
△ Third, the prostration and offering to the Buddha.
At that time, the Brahma Kings bowed their heads to the ground in homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and spoke in verse:
“Excellent is the sight of all Buddhas... (omitted)... may we all together attain the Way of the Buddha.”

"How excellent it is to behold the Buddhas! This deva has passed through immeasurable kalpas before obtaining even a single vision [of one]. Thus, he exclaims "excellent" to celebrate his own good fortune.
Previously, the triple world was called a "burning house" (āgneya-śaraṇa), named for the pressing nature of its manifold sufferings.

Here, the triple world is called a "prison," named for the entanglement and stagnation caused by karmic burdens. To speak of saving the world and exerting oneself to praise liberation from this prison—

This refers to the compassionate vow. The phrase "Universal Wisdom Widely Delivers" praises the power of wisdom. Those who dwell in the darkness of the ten directions do so because they lack the radiance of Great Wisdom;
due to this absence of the light of wisdom, the three evil realms increase while the celestial hosts gradually diminish.
As for those who do not hear the Dharma from the Buddha: the Buddha-dharma can mend one's nature and clarify the spirit; externally it nourishes physical strength, and internally it nourishes wisdom.
Wisdom is the causal condition for wholesome karma; it can bring about pleasant matters and give rise to the perception of pleasure. Because they have not heard [the Dharma], the opposite occurs.
As for the "perception of pleasure," it refers to the perception of pleasure that arises from wearying of suffering. The final verse serves as the extensive dedication of merit.
△ Fourth, the request to turn the wheel of Dharma.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings, having praised the Buddha with verses, spoke these verses:
"World-Honored One, you turn the Wheel of Dharma... [you] have practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas."

The preceding refers to the "Gate of Ambrosia" (amṛta-dvāra), while this refers to the "Drum of Ambrosia" (amṛta-dundubhi). Both are so named because they are capable of removing suffering and affliction;
however, "gate" signifies entry through awakening, whereas "drum" signifies alerting and inspiring.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Seven: The Parable of the Phantom City (continued). △ Section Seven:
Accepting the Invitation and Opening the Gradual Teaching.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [until] immediately turned the wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions.

The three turnings are: the turning that reveals the characteristics, the turning that exhorts to practice, and the turning that realizes through witness. These cause one to enter the three stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

"Revealing the characteristics" means revealing the specific modes of the Four Noble Truths so that one may know the direction to follow; this corresponds to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

"Exhorting to practice" means revealing the benefits and efficacy of the Four Noble Truths so that one may know how to cultivate them; this corresponds to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
"Realization" means demonstrating: "I have realized it; you too should realize it. This refers to the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding the "three turnings," these generally correspond to the three faculties (*indriya*): for those of dull faculty, three are required; for those of middling faculty, two suffice; for those of superior faculty, only one is needed.
As for those of the highest superior faculty, the Way is present upon the mere sight of it, leaving no room for words. Thus, there is what is called the "Twelvefold Teaching of the Dharma."

Treatise: There is what is called the Wheel of Dharma of Twelve Aspects (*dvādaśākāra-dharmacakra*). The teaching (*deśanā*) acts as the agent that turns, while the practice (*pratipatti*) is that which is turned.
Based on the three turnings—demonstration, exhortation, and realization—of the Four Noble Truths, this constitutes the turning of the twelvefold teaching.

Based on the three awakenings—through seeing, cultivation, and learning—of the Four Noble Truths, this constitutes the Wheel of Dharma of Twelve Aspects. The traditional view holds that within a single turning, one causes those who hear the Dharma [to attain these results].
There arises the true, noble eye of wisdom and the illumination of knowledge. These three turnings, each consisting of four aspects, constitute the twelve modes of activity (*dvādaśākāra*).
They are not separate from the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Neither śramaṇas nor brahmins, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās, nor anyone else in the world, can turn them back.
This means that because these individuals have not yet attained correct realization, even though they engage in transformation, they remain stuck in mere verbal designations, namely:
"this is suffering," "this is the origin of suffering," "this is the cessation of suffering," and "this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering."

The characteristics of what is turned over are precisely the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. That all are called "suffering" is because the Four Truths are established on account of suffering, for the purpose of providing the path to extinguish it.
Birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth—these eight manifest afflictions press upon one with urgency.

It is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*). The afflictions, fetters, and karmic actions summon the eight sufferings of the future. It is called "origination" (*samudaya*). This applies to all three periods of time;
that is to say, past origination brings about present suffering, and present origination brings about future suffering.

When the fetters and karmic actions are exhausted, the eight sufferings of birth and death are forever ended. It is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). To counteract the fetters and karmic actions, one cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). It is called...

The Path: see the *Jingzang Jingyan wen* (Text on the Pure Treasury and Pure Eye) regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the extensive exposition of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), up to: "With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease."

The detailed exposition of the Four Noble Truths is the teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination. From "ignorance conditions volitional formations" up to "birth conditions old age and death," etc., it demonstrates the characteristic of arising;
this is the detailed exposition of the two truths of suffering and its origin.

From "the cessation of ignorance" up to "the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress," it demonstrates the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment; this is the detailed exposition of the two truths of cessation and the path. Thus are the Four Noble Truths.
For those of inferior faculties, I shall briefly set forth the coarse characteristics, which are fundamentally based on the traces [of phenomena]: the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.

For those of middling faculties, there is the subtle contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, which is fundamentally based on the mind. This refers to the fundamental luminosity of the nature-intelligence (*prakṛti-jñāna*), which is wondrously profound and perfectly clear.

Due to the sudden flickering arising of delusive objects, it momentarily becomes obscured and darkened; this is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When a single thought-moment first moves within the essence of ignorance, it is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). It is obscured...
When obscured by movement, one loses that essential clarity; because the attachment to stillness gives rise to cognition, the transformation of wisdom (*jñāna*) is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Among the twelve links of dependent origination, these three constitute the root, while the remaining nine are the branches and leaves; they mutually condition one another to form the conditions of the three periods of time.
Wisdom is fundamentally without knowing, yet it knows by virtue of consciousness. When its form becomes a deluded mind, it is termed "name" (*nāman*); this refers to the six [sense bases].

It is the master of the thief. By nature it is originally unborn, yet it arises due to consciousness. Its form is a phantom substance, which is called "form" (rūpa) and serves as the basis for the four aggregates (skandhas).
Thus, "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) refers to the state of the initial conception in the womb, the phase of the coagulated fluid.

From the stage of *kalala* (congealed coagulum), the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are fully formed; this is called the "six entrances" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Once the faculties have developed and one has emerged from the womb, the meeting of the faculties with their respective objects is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

The experiencing of those preceding objects is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Because there is that which is felt, the mind of feeling arises, and through feeling, one clings to it—this is "clinging" (*upādāna*).
Because of grasping (*upādāna*), the afflictions and karma become bound together; because good and evil take on form, it is called "existence" (*bhava*).

Because these various bonds of existence serve as the cause for birth within the three realms, it is called "birth" (*jāti*). Once there is birth, aging, death, and suffering follow in its wake—this is the characteristic of the arising of this [cycle].
If one wishes to extinguish it, what is essential? One should know that it is ignorance (*avidyā*).

It does not possess a real substantial body. Originally, the single source of the mind is vast, wondrous, and profoundly still. Because one establishes cognition upon what is known and seen, deluded objects momentarily arise, and thus ignorance exists.
If one knows that seeing is itself non-seeing, then the nature of wisdom is truly pure, returning once more to its wondrous stillness, penetratingly clear and perfectly lucid;
this is called the extinction of ignorance. Consequently, everything from one's own conduct downward is entirely extinguished. This is because...

When the root no longer exists, the branches have nothing to which they may attach; this is the characteristic of cultivation and abandonment (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*). Now, the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination share the same names but possess many meanings.
There is what is called the "Small Vehicle" (*Hīnayāna*) version of the four truths of arising and ceasing: therein, the *saṃvṛti-bheda* (segmented) birth-and-death is termed Suffering (*duḥkha*);

afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are termed Origin (*samudaya*); analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is termed Cessation (*nirodha*); and the category of wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is termed [the Path].
Regarding the Path (*mārga*): there is what is called the "Great Vehicle’s Unconditioned Four Truths. Here, the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) is designated as Suffering (*duḥkha*);

the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is designated as Origination (*samudaya*); non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) is designated as Cessation (*nirodha*); and the category of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is designated as the Path.

Alternatively, they are called the "Eight Truths," which is to say that these are combined with the aforementioned [four]. Furthermore, there are the "Immeasurable Four Truths," which are based upon the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
It is taught that the manifestation of the origin of all sufferings clarifies the primary meaning (*paramārtha*). Seeking cessation and the path externally, one finds nothing at all to be attained;

this is called the Four Noble Truths. The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are likewise so. Therefore, although the dharmas of the Truths and Dependent Origination belong to the Two Vehicles, they actually penetrate the Mahāyāna.
Their essential purpose is to sever the root of birth and death and extinguish the cause of ignorance, thereby causing one to return [to the source].
It is simply the wondrous nature of the fundamental luminosity. Those who practice the Way and study the teachings should deeply clarify this point.
From the Buddha amidst the great assembly of devas and humans (up to) being endowed with the eight liberations.
This refers to those of sharp faculties who heard the Dharma at the first assembly and attained the benefit of the *āyatanas*.

"Not receiving any dharmas" means awakening to the truth that conditions are empty and realizing there is nothing to which one may cling. Since the mind is fundamentally liberated, the presence of reception (*vedanā*) constitutes a burden;

since the nature is fundamentally luminous and settled, the presence of attachment constitutes obscuration. Therefore, by not receiving any dharmas, one subsequently [purifies] the mind of all outflows (*āsrava*).
One attains liberation, and further achieves meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the three clarities (*vidyā*), and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Thus, the sage and the ordinary person are of one essence, and delusion and awakening share a common source. If a person can truly awaken to the cause of their afflictions and entanglements, comprehend the origin of their turbid confusion, and realize that they ultimately do not grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), then meditative concentration, liberation, the six supernormal powers, and the three clarities shall all be attained.

During the second, third, and fourth preachings of the Dharma (up to an incalculable number of times), those who hear the Dharma in succession attain the faculties of the lower and middle grades. Those of sharp faculties awaken to a thousand truths upon hearing it once.
Those of middle and lower capacities possess much learning but little awakening; thus, it is only upon reaching the third and fourth periods that they finally obtain the canopy.
From this point onward, it was no longer taught in a single session. Furthermore, there were those of lesser faculties who obtained the canopy, their number being beyond calculation. △ Eighth:
Requesting the Great through the Small.

This correctly describes the request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. However, while all previous requests were for the turning of the unsurpassed wheel [of Dharma], Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū only preached the teachings on the Truths and Dependent Origination. Furthermore, regarding those who await this request:

the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas proceeds from the gradual to the sudden, relying upon provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality. This is because if one were led without a gradual approach, they would be startled and lack faith; it is not merely...
The teaching does not allow for skipping stages, as it is intended that learning should not leap over levels.
At that time, the sixteen princes [until] the Buddha himself realized and knew.
Having heard the Dharma and obtained canopies, the sixteen princes then left the household life and further sought the Mahāyāna; they have all already attained perfection.
This means that because they have already accomplished their great resolve, they request that the Great Dharma be preached.

When we say "our own vows are inferior," it is a self-proclamation of our great resolve in hoping for the preaching of the Great Dharma. The Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision is precisely what is called the One Great Matter.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King... [the King] immediately granted his permission.
△ Ninth, accepting the invitation to preach the sudden [teaching].
At that time, that Buddha accepted the Śrāmaṇera’s invitation... [the Buddha] was protected by the mindfulness of the Buddhas.

It was only after twenty thousand kalpas that he finally remained silent regarding this essential teaching in order to await the proper opportunity. Thus, prior to those twenty thousand kalpas, he had already preached the teachings of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā.
As the verse says: "He taught the six pāramitās and the matters of various supernatural powers.
Although Śākyamuni manifested a lifespan of eighty years, he preached the Prajñāpāramitā and other teachings for forty of them. This refers to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
His present lifespan is five million billion nayutas of kalpas; thus, it is appropriate that he should preach this sutra for twenty thousand kalpas.
Having spoken this sutra, [all] together upheld, recited, and mastered it thoroughly.
Rejoicing in the Great Dharma, they reverently uphold and proclaim its illumination. △ Tenth, the faculties of those who hear are not equal.

When this sutra was being preached—for eighty-four thousand kalpas—the bodhisattvas would necessarily believe, while the śrāvakas or sentient beings might not believe. This is what is meant by: "When the superior person hears the Way, they apply themselves diligently."
And they put it into practice. When the man of middle capacity hears the Way, he is as if it exists and as if it does not. When the man of inferior capacity hears the Way, he merely laughs at it.
That which has never ceased or been abandoned is what is called "blazingly proclaiming" and "uninterrupted preaching. △ Eleven:
The Śrāmaṇera Expounds the Sublime.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras [up to] generated the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This was a detailed exposition for the sake of the assembly who were in doubt. The sixteen princes represent the eight consciousnesses while still bound by afflictions (*saṃkleśa*);

the sixteen bodhisattvas represent the eight wisdoms that have emerged from such bonds. Furthermore, the number sixteen is used to demonstrate the subduing of the eight heterodoxies through the eightfold noble path.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in each of eighty thousand kalpas, he delivers many multitudes": this signifies that once the Way of Great Penetration is attained, there is nothing among the eighty thousand dharma-gates that is not understood.
It is not only the Eightfold Right Path that constitutes wondrous wisdom; even the eightfold wrong path is wondrous wisdom.
It is not only through the Eightfold Right Path that one can deliver others; even through the eightfold wrong path, one can deliver them. As it is said:
The nature of the Sage is such that there is nothing it does not penetrate; whether in accordance with or contrary to conditions, all are skillful means.

It is precisely because it is thus that each is able to expound the wondrous for as long as an eon, and each is able to deliver sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Were it otherwise, it would not suffice to be called the Way of Great Pervasive Penetration.
△ Twelfth: The Seal of Certification of Great Pervasive Penetration.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [until] made offerings to him.
He approved what was said and praised his virtuous conduct, causing the multitude to draw near to him in devotion.
Why is this? [Until] the Tathāgata’s wisdom of *samyaksambodhi*.
The three vehicles attain the wondrous; thus they all return to the One Vehicle. △ Third, showing the present conditions, in five parts: First, questioning the past to connect it with the present.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus (up to) "it is not exhausted even now."

The present gathering of those previously transformed is due to current conditions. Those among the assembly who have always been with their teacher are so because the conditions for their transformation were profound;
thus they have encountered hundreds of millions of Buddhas, yet the conditions [for their transformation] were not exhausted, and so now they meet once again.
2. A detailed account of their names and traces.
"O Bhikṣus, I now speak to you... (up to) the second named Sumeruśikhara.
This records the names and traces of the sixteen princes who attained Buddhahood. When heaven and earth established their positions, the Way operated within them.
The Sages took these as their model to open up things and accomplish tasks, thereby encompassing the Way of the world.
Thus, the Buddhas of the eight directions each rely on one direction to manifest one virtue; this is how they open up things and accomplish tasks.
Examining the beginning and tracing the end, there is no aspect of the world's Way that is not encompassed. In the East, Zhen (Thunder) signifies movement, and joy is also movement.
Furthermore, Akṣobhya means "Immovable," and the summit of Mount Sumeru is the ultimate state of immovability. As the Sūtra says:
"Unmoved by praise or blame, like Mount Sumeru. This Buddha appears in response to the movements of sentient beings, yet his essence remains unmoved.

Moreover, while residing in a land of movement, he demonstrates that movement itself is stillness. Since these two Buddhas both manifest their transformations and their virtues mutually support one another, they are given two names despite being one.

This may be explained as follows. Someone might say: "The Eight Trigrams (*bagua*) are a book of the Central Xia; to cite them to correlate with the teachings of Zhuchi (Buddhism)—is this not the intention of the Buddha?
Li Zhangzhe used them to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and Lü Guānwén used them to explain this chapter.

Such critics disparage them; why then do you follow in their footsteps? I reply: India and China constitute but one world. As for the extent of its borders and frontiers—*fang*... [text fragment]... [the principle applies universally].
While their positions are identical, the hexagrams represent the natural principles of Heaven and Earth; how could they alone not be the same?
Fuxi depicted them to show them to humanity, and our Buddha modeled them to establish the Dharma; each silently attained the same essence.
Although this scripture lacks the explicit text of the eight trigrams, it clearly contains the imagery of the eight directions. By borrowing phenomena to clarify principles, how could it not be so?

This is acceptable. Yet, to be bound by narrow views and to engage in disparagement is not the way of a person of realization. Long ago, when five hundred arhats each interpreted the Buddha’s words, they asked which one accorded with the Buddha’s intent.
The Buddha said, "None of them accord with my intent. The assembly asked, "If they do not accord with the Buddha’s intent, will they not incur offense?
The Buddha said, "Although they do not accord with my intent, each follows correct principle and is fit to serve as holy teaching. There is [a passage to this effect].
Blessings are without fault; I shall maintain only this to counter the errors of those who might doubt.
To the southeast are two Buddhas: the first is named Lion’s Sound, and the second is named Lion’s Mark.
In the southeast, the trigram Xun represents gentleness and compliance. The "lion's voice" refers to that which is spoken without fear;
the "lion's appearance" refers to that which is manifested without fear. This Buddha responds to sentient beings with compassionate gentleness and preaches the Dharma with fearlessness.
In the south are two Buddhas: the first is named Ākāśasthita (Abiding in Space), and the second is named Nityanirvṛta (Eternally Extinct).
In the south, "li" (separation) signifies vacuity and luminosity. As for Ākāśasthita, his essence reaches into the void to respond to all realities.

As for Nityanirvṛta, he realizes that the very substance of all dharmas is inherently vacant and quiescent; this is the mark of *nirvāṇa*, which is eternally extinguished and does not undergo further extinction. This is...
This refers to the state of constant extinction (*nitya-nirvāṇa*).
Regarding the two Buddhas of the southwest: the first is named *Tejas* (Imperial Mark) and the second is named *Brahma-tejas* (Brahma Mark).
In the southwest, the trigram *Kun* represents the means of sustaining life. *Tejas* signifies the spirit emerging to respond to phenomena; it is the imperial, Brahma-like purity.
This Buddha responds to things through his spiritual power; all things derive their existence from him, yet his virtue remains eternally pure and is never defiled by those things.
To the west are two Buddhas: the first is named Amitābha, and the second is named Sarvalokadhātudurgatipariśodhana (The Purifier of All Sufferings in All Worlds).
In the west, the trigram Dui represents destruction and fracture. Amitābha is called "Immeasurable Life. The sufferings and afflictions of the world are precisely the impermanence of birth and death.
This Buddha, at the very moment of destruction and fracture, manifests immeasurable life; thus, there is ultimately no birth or death.
By doing so, he delivers the world from the sufferings and afflictions of birth and death.
The two Buddhas of the northwest are first named Tamālapatracandanagandha-ṛddhi and second named Merudhvaja.

In the northwest, the element of dryness represents strength and vigor; the fragrance of *tamāla* sandalwood is pure, far-reaching, and subtly pervasive, which serves as a metaphor for spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
Penetration. The appearance of Mount Sumeru likewise possesses no sense of motion. This Buddha’s supernatural power responds to things like the unceasing Way of Heaven:
silent and unmoving, yet it penetrates through being stirred.
In the north are two Buddhas: the first is named Cloud Sovereign (Meghasvabhāva), and the second is named Cloud Sovereign King (Meghasvarāja).
In the north, the trigram Kǎn represents danger and entrapment. "Cloud Sovereign" signifies benefiting sentient beings without deliberate thought;

"Cloud Sovereign King" further represents the ultimate state of mastery. These Buddhas cover all with unconditioned compassion (apratihata-maitrī) to benefit those in perilous and difficult circumstances.
Though born, one is without mind and without attachment, as free as a cloud.
To the northeast is the Buddha named Destroyer of All Fear of the World.
In the northeast, the direction of Gen, lies the place where all things begin and end; the principle of beginning and ending, as it pertains to things, is...
Formation and destruction—manifesting as birth and death for human beings—are what the world fears.

Yet this Buddha, amidst the terrors of birth and death, awakens all beings through the Way of the one true, concentrated, and eternal, enabling them to realize that it is without beginning and without end, and thus enter the state of neither dying nor being born; thereby, the fears of the world are utterly extinguished.
The sixteenth is our Śākyamuni Buddha, [up to] *sambodhi*. Regarding "Śākyamuni":

*Śākya* means "Capable One" (*nengren*), and *muni* means "Silent One" (*jimo*). This signifies that his virtue is benevolent in saving all classes of beings, while his Way is silent and unconditioned (*wuwei*).
Because he manifested his transformation within the *Sahā* world, he is titled "Capable One. This [direction] succeeds the northeast and maintains it.

As for the "Manifestation" (biao): although the Great Awakened One possesses the virtue of encompassing both the beginning and the end, his Way is perfectly responsive and does not stagnate within any fixed direction or corner.
Being without beginning and without end, he serves as the synthesis of all virtues.

Indeed, emerging from the unmoving to respond to the myriad movements, being able to be both supple and firm—this is called fearlessness. Emptying himself to respond to things, he manifests longevity and directs his spiritual power.
Even down to saving those in peril and extinguishing their fears, there is nothing that is not the Śākyamuni’s skillful conduct according to circumstances.

Therefore, while the virtues of the Buddhas of the eight directions are recounted in detail, they are all summarized by Śākyamuni. This is precisely his supreme virtue, which encompasses heaven and earth and brings all things to completion through its subtle workings, being without fixed location or substantial form.
Were it not for the realization of the unsurpassed Right Path, how could he be thus? Hence it is said:
Śākyamuni attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in the Sahā world-system. △ Third, the accomplishment of those to be converted:
[the account of] the bhikṣus and others when they were śrāmaṇeras (up to) their gradual entry into the Buddha-way.
This clarifies past causes and present conditions, so that one may know how their meritorious practice has become profound and is now brought to fulfillment.
That they were first converted as śrāmaṇeras clarifies the past cause; that they are being converted at this time clarifies the present condition.
That they should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of these teachings is the very fulfillment thereof.
Why is this? Because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
As for why those who have already received instruction over vast eons still enter [the path] only gradually, it is because the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and understand.
Nevertheless, there is no sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; yet, that it is so difficult to understand is due to the dust [of afflictions].
This is because one is habituated to one's own hindrances. Judging from those of us today, it is fortunate that we have heard the True Dharma;
this cannot be without causes from past lives. Who knows that we may not be the lingering dust of Jñānavijaya, or disciples yet to come?

Yet, as our karmic obstacles remain dense and the fruits of the Path are still distant, even though we have been sheltered by the teaching for vast eons, we are only now gradually entering it. If one can be diligent...
Advancing, one may still have hope; but if one were to regress and fall, how could one know the duration of future time?

Could it not exceed the number of preceding *kalpas* by even this much? Thus, that which is called "difficult to understand" is not that the Buddha’s wisdom is difficult to fathom, but rather that the capacity of the individual is difficult [to awaken].
Those immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time—up to and including the śrāvaka disciples—are these very people.
The preceding section clarified the causes for receiving transformation; this section points to the individuals being transformed. △ Fourth, the extensive salvation of those remaining.
"From 'After my parinirvāṇa' (up to) 'except for the skillful means by which the Tathāgatas preach the Dharma.

The previous passage spoke of 'future śrāvakas,' referring to those who have already received transformation; this passage speaks of 'furthermore having disciples,' referring to those who have not yet received transformation.
Through successive causes and conditions, they shall ultimately encounter a Buddha and attain liberation by relying on the One Vehicle."
Regarding those who become Buddhas in other lands: they manifest their parinirvāṇa here while responding to conditions there. As for having different names:
the *Avataṃsaka* states that the names and traces of the Tathāgata correspond to the various minds of sentient beings and are not the same;
this refers to the ten thousand [Buddhas] in each of the four continents, and so on, throughout the ten directions. △ Fifth, the conclusion and reconciliation of the ultimate reality.
"O bhikṣus... [they] shall attain extinction (nirvāṇa) solely through the One Buddha Vehicle.

The preceding section clarified the initial provisional [teachings], while this assembly concludes with the ultimate reality. "The time for nirvāṇa has arrived" means that the conditions for conversion are nearing their end.

"The assembly is pure" means that their faculties and capacities have already matured. As for the purity of the assembly, they have already severed delusions and eliminated [afflictions] within the teachings of the *pitaka*.
This is the "knot. One whose faith is firm has already gained mutual trust regarding the nature of the mind within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
To thoroughly comprehend the dharma of emptiness is called having awakened to *prajñā*; to enter deeply into meditative concentration is called wondrously reaching the profound source.

When this is so, all ailments have been eliminated and the medical prescriptions are also discarded; therefore, the two provisional [teachings] are set aside and the one reality is specifically clarified. "Attaining extinction" means attaining...
This is the fruit of the True and Eternal Way. △ Fourth, the illustration clarifying the provisional and the real, in six parts. First, establishing the analogy:
"Bhikṣus, you should know... (up to) if such a person hears it, they will immediately believe and accept it."

For those who delight in the minor [vehicle], he provisionally teaches the minor fruits; they then accept this with faith, like being stranded at a conjured city. △ Second, the actual citation of the parable:
"Suppose there were a perilous and difficult evil road, five hundred yojanas in length, desolate and devoid of people, a place of terror."

It is like the various births and deaths, afflictions, evil realms, and perilous difficulties that are vast and far-reaching. Regarding the "five hundred yojanas," the ancient commentaries provide many explanations;

here, we take it to mean that those of the two vehicles, having severed the fetters and delusions of the three realms and departed from the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*), realize the *nirvāṇa* with remainder.
This corresponds to reaching the "transformed city" after passing three hundred yojanas; yet they still remain stagnant within the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*).

If one turns the mind toward the Great Vehicle and advances to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), exhausting all residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), this is like being four hundred *yojana* away from the place of treasure.

Furthermore, advancing to the eighth stage and above, one exhausts ignorance (*avidyā*), leaves behind the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*), and realizes *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
this is like reaching the place of treasure after passing five hundred *yojana* through a vast wilderness where no people dwell.
This analogy illustrates that birth and death are long and far-reaching; lacking true knowledge and vision, one gives rise to groundless fear.
Suppose there is a great multitude of people who wish to traverse this path to reach a place of precious jewels.
It is like the three vehicles seeking Buddhahood. △ Third, knowing the proper course and suitability:
"There was a guide, wise, intelligent, and far-seeing... (up to) "...desiring to pass beyond these perils. The guide is the one who points out the way;
he is an analogy for the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. He opens up what is obstructed and stops what should be stopped. He opens...

For example, severing delusions is like clearing a blockage, while giving rise to hindrances is like creating an obstruction. Furthermore, that which is wholesome is open, whereas that which is unwholesome is blocked; only thus can one proceed without difficulty.
△ Fourth, the minds of the multitude become weary and retreat.
The people he has brought along grow weary and retreat on the way (up to: "I now wish to turn back."
It is like those of the Two Vehicles who seek the Way and find it difficult to advance but easy to retreat. △ Fifth, the establishment of expedient means for salvation:
The Guide possesses many skillful means and thinks thus... (up to)... "they may also be able to go."
This is like the two vehicles, which, having severed the fetters and delusions of the three realms, subsequently rest in their minor fruits before advancing toward the ground of wisdom.
Whatever they do according to their inclination is simply in accordance with their capacity; this is the meaning of gradually attaining entry into the Way.
At that time, the exhausted multitude attained a sense of swift peace and security,
due to their hearts’ longing for rest and their aspirations.
Thereupon, the people entered the conjured city, conceiving the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought that they were secure.
Delighting in the small while forgetting the great. △ Sixth, setting aside the provisional to establish the real:
At that time, the Guide, knowing this multitude of people... [until] "...is merely for the sake of rest.
Because the transformation is not truly real, it ceases in an instant; only the precious destination is real. Because the provisional is not truly real...
In the end, they were abandoned; only the One Vehicle is the reality. △ Fifth, the combined manifestation of the provisional and the real, in five parts.
First, the combined citation of the parable: "O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is likewise so. Now, for your sakes, I act as the Great Guide."
△ Second, one should collectively understand what is appropriate and expedient.
One should know that the various births and deaths, afflictions, and evil realms are perilous, difficult, and long-lasting, and thus must be abandoned and crossed over.
△ Third, the assembly collectively becomes lax and regresses.
If sentient beings were to hear only of the Single Buddha Vehicle (yāna), [they would] only then be able to achieve success.
If they were to hear only of the Single Vehicle without the aid of skillful means (upāya), they would grow weary of the Great [Vehicle] and have no desire to see the Buddha;

they would be daunted by its complexity and anxious that the path is too long. Therefore, skillful means are necessary. Previously it was said that the evil realms are long and distant; here it is said of the Buddha—
That the Way is long and distant is because, while above one observes sentient beings with right view, here one observes the Buddha-way with inverted views.

From the very beginning, the Buddha-way is not remote from people; fundamentally, there is nothing to be cultivated or realized. It is only because of the difficulty of returning to the source after drifting away in the cycle of birth and death that its length and distance are perceived.
It is because of the difficulty of remedying the accumulated obstructions of delusion and karma that its arduousness is perceived.
Suffering is long-lasting toil that arises from inverted delusions; what connection does it have to the Way?

If there were no birth-and-death and no deluded karma, then the essence itself would be quiescent and pure—what more would there be to treat? The vision of long duration and the labor of diligent effort would then have nothing at all upon which to operate.
Those who are ignorant do not realize this, and thus they cast blame upon the Buddha’s Way, eventually giving rise to [false views].
Laziness and regression. This is why the Great Awakened One described their inverted views in order to guide and encourage them. △ Four: Harmonizing Expedient Means to Rescue.
The Buddha knew that these minds were timid, weak, inferior, and lowly (up to the point where he) spoke of the two types of nirvāṇa.
The Middle Way refers to the intermediate stage between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The "two nirvāṇas" refer to the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles;
this corresponds to what is stated below regarding the second stage. △ Fifth, the synthesis of the abolition of the provisional and the establishment of the real.

If sentient beings abide in the second stage (up to) "I manifest as an ear," this refers to those who abide in the second stage—meaning they are stalled at the provisional fruits of the Two Vehicles and do not know how to advance; therefore, I speak to them of the Buddha-wisdom.
This causes one to observe and deliberate so as to advance toward and attain the actual fruit. △ Sixth, the restatement by verse, in five parts.
First, the verses on the former causes, in eight sections. First, the verse on the Great Universal Enlightenment and Attainment of the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddha of Great Pervasive Wisdom and Victory... their hearts were all filled with leaping joy.
2. Verse on the Princes Following the Buddha.
The sixteen sons of that Buddha, each surrounded by a retinue of thousands of millions of billions, all proceeded together to the place where the Buddha was.
△ Third: Verses on the princes’ praise of the Buddha and their request for the Dharma.
Prostrating with head and face at the Buddha’s feet... [until] "shaking all things.

"The Holy Lion" praises the holy powers and fearlessnesses. From "The World-Honored One is difficult to encounter" onwards, he eulogizes the original intention of his transcendence of the world and requests the Dharma.
△ Fourth, the verse on the auspicious signs moving the various devas to request the Dharma.
In the various worlds of the eastern direction... [up to] ...turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
△ Fifth, the verses on accepting the invitation and opening the gradual teaching:
O World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom... [up to] ...you all should know this.
"From ignorance to old age and death"—this enumerates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). All arise from the condition of birth;
were there no birth, there would be no such manifold afflictions and calamities.
When this Dharma was proclaimed, six hundred trillion *koṭis* attained the end of all suffering and all became arhats.
This verse praises those of sharp faculties who heard the Dharma and obtained benefit during the first assembly. The *Fengsu tong* states: ten myriad is called a *yi*;
ten *yi* is called a *zhao*; ten *zhao* is called a *jing*; ten *jing* is called a *zi*; ten *zi* is called a *hai*.
The *hai* is a comprehensive large number, which is precisely what is meant by *nayuta*.

During the second period of teaching the Dharma (up to the point where one cannot reach its limit), the verses describe how those of middling and inferior faculties successively obtain benefit. △ Sixth: Verses on Requesting the Great Based on the Small.
At that time, the sixteen princes [attained] the supreme purity of the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).
The wisdom-eye of the Hīnayāna does not yet escape the shadows of objective conditions; thus, none can match the World-Honored One’s foremost, pure wisdom-eye.
Therefore, they vowed to attain it. [Section Seven: Verses Accepting the Invitation and Preaching the Sudden Teaching.]
The Buddha, knowing the mind of the youth—up to the verse [describing him] as being like the sands of the Ganges—knew the youth’s mind.
He immediately spoke of what was previously mentioned: that which the Buddha personally realizes through his profound resolve.

He then spoke of the six *pāramitās* and so forth, which refers to the events previously mentioned regarding the passing of twenty thousand *kalpas*. The six *pāramitās* are precisely the *prajñā* [of the previous passage].
If one teaches the various supernatural powers (abhijñā), this refers to the Vaipulya teachings; these merely distinguish the real dharma as the beginning of the Mahāyāna.

Only after this does one teach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for those [teachings] consisting of verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the *Saddharma* adapts to the capacities of beings through various extensive and abbreviated forms;
thus, Śākyamuni taught it within a single period, whereas Dīpaṃkara taught it for sixty [eons].
Regarding the duration of the preaching: it was preached for eight thousand great kalpas. This present sutra consists of only twenty-eight chapters.
Never-Disparaging heard twenty quadrillion verses from Vimalacandra; while Priyadarśana [heard them] from Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī.

Thus, one hears eight million billion *akṣobhya* verses; this is because the teachings are more extensive or concise according to the length of one's conditions and the breadth or narrowness of one's faculties.
In reality, the Dharma that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is without end or limit.
Therefore, while the *Avataṃsaka* has texts in three divisions, a single word of its Dharma-gate could not be fully recorded even if one used the ink of the oceans.
Thus, even verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges would not be considered many. △ Eight: Verses on the Śrāmaṇera’s Expounding of the Sublime.
After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra (up to the point where the assembly was as vast as the sands of the Ganges).
△ Second, two verses now provide the conditions for the present. First, one verse interrogates the past to connect it with the present:
"After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who heard the Dharma have been born together with their teacher in every Buddha-field wherever they may be."
Due to the conditions of the Lotus Sutra, they have encountered one another life after life. △ Second, the verses recounting their names and traces:
These sixteen śrāmaṇeras fully practiced the Buddha-way; now, currently existing throughout the ten directions, each has attained perfect enlightenment.
△ Three verses on the accomplishment of those to be converted.
At that time, for those who hear the Dharma... [up to] "...lead you toward the Buddha-wisdom.
This clarifies that through distant conditions and profound merit, they are brought to fulfillment. △ Four verses on the conclusion and the ultimate reality.
For these fundamental reasons, I now preach the Lotus Sūtra to lead you into the Buddha-way; be careful not to harbor fear or alarm.
△ Third, the verses on the parable of the provisional and the real, in five parts: first, one verse illustrating the original [parable].
For example, it is like a perilous and evil road extending for five hundred *yojanas*.

The venomous beasts represent birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the water and grass represent the roots of the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhi*). △ Second, a verse on knowing the proper methods and suitability.
At that time, there was a guide who possessed strong memory and wisdom; with a clear and resolute mind, he rescued the multitude from their perilous difficulties.
△ Third, a verse on the weariness and retreat of the assembly's minds.
The multitude were all exhausted and said to the Guide: "We are now utterly weary; we wish to turn back from here.
△ Fourth, a verse on establishing expedient means to provide relief.
The Guide forms this thought... (up to)... "each may follow what they delight in.
The previous passage spoke of manifesting a single city, which served as a general analogy for the Path and its Fruit (*mārga-phala*).

This subsequent mention of the outer walls, houses, men, women, and so forth, provides a detailed analogy for the virtues and functions within the Fruit. A kingdom or district possesses cities; a fortified city with double walls constitutes the outer wall (*khaṭvā*).

A city takes its outer walls as its defense; likewise, one should take virtue as one's support. A residence is a metaphor for the virtue of reliance, adorned with the ultimate emptiness and stillness.
Gardens and groves are metaphors for the virtue of protection, surrounded by the trees of untainted dharmas.
Bathing pools are metaphors for the virtue of purity, with the waters of the eight liberations flowing through them as channels. As for the towers and pavilions...
This is like the virtue of transcendent penetration. Taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) as its main gates, it is filled with men and women;
these are what are called the man of sincere good heart and the woman of compassionate heart.

However, while this analogy refers to the realized virtues of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), there are aspects that resemble the virtues of the Mahāyāna; these are merely provisional advances made by means of "semblance-measure" (*sadr̥śa-pramāṇa*). Therefore, in summary—
Speaking in terms of the conjured city: when the conjured city is extinguished, all such things are likewise extinguished.
This is an analogy for the virtues of the Two Vehicles, which have never possessed actual realization and ultimately end in destruction.

Scholars of the world who seek to know the Way through inferential knowledge and perceive the nature through semblance-measurement—those whose conditions lack actual realization—are just like this. △ Fifth: Verses on the Abolition of Expedient Means.
Establishing the Reality:
Since all people have entered the city, they shall together proceed to the place of treasure.
△ Fourth, the verse that combines and reveals the provisional and the real (four parts). First, the verse that combines the analogy with the original [teaching].
I am likewise thus: the guide for all.
II. Verse on Knowing the Directions Together:
Seeing those who seek the Way faltering and abandoning their efforts midway, unable to cross over birth and death and the perilous paths of affliction.
△ Third verse: Harmonizing with provisional means to provide relief.
Thus, by the power of skillful means, for the sake of calming [them], he speaks of nirvana, saying: "Your suffering has been extinguished; that which was to be done is all accomplished."
This statement that "it has already been accomplished" is a provisional advance; yet when one abides in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), it is said in truth that it is not yet accomplished.
△ Fourth, the verse on the synthesis of abolishing the provisional and establishing the real.
Having known that they had reached nirvāṇa, they all attained arhatship. Thereupon, he assembled the great multitude and preached the true Dharma for them.
As prescribed:
"The skillful means of all Buddhas... [up to] ...this is truly cessation."
This causes them to observe and deliberate that what has been attained is not real, urging them to strive toward the actual fruit.
△ Fifth, the concluding verse:
"The Teacher of all Buddhas taught nirvana in order to bring rest; once they have known this to be rest, he leads them into the Buddha-wisdom."
This concludes the summary of the meaning of the chapter on the "City of Manifestation.
*Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Three, Part Three;
*Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Four, Part One.
Commentary by the Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wēn’lǐng.
Chapter Eight: The Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples. Part Two:
The Realization and Attainment of Prophecy by Those of Inferior Faculties. Section One: The Realization and Attainment of Prophecy by the Assembly of Those Beyond Training (aśaikṣa).
First, a brief outline of the topical divisions is presented.
The teachings of the three assemblies were each expounded according to the capacities of those present, and their respective realizations are here recorded.

In the preceding "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, one cycle of teaching was delivered through causal conditions to accommodate those of inferior faculties; at this point, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and the five hundred arhats and others attained realization therein.
[Subhūti] attained realization. The Buddha then confirmed this for him and bestowed a prediction (vyākaraṇa). For these five reasons, it is called the "Chapter on the Hundred Predictions.

Now, although Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was predicted first, followed by the assembly of five hundred and two thousand, the title specifically takes the "Five Hundred" as its name because Pūrṇa was a great disciple who, while inwardly concealing his true nature, outwardly manifested as the leader of the multitude;
thus, although he was predicted first, he was not the primary subject [of the chapter].

Furthermore, since the "Chapter on the Thousand and Two Disciples" appears at the end, it should not be designated as a formal chapter. Among the ten great disciples, there were none who did not possess superior faculties;

their realization and attainment of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) were fundamentally without priority or sequence. It was simply that each specialized in a particular virtue, manifesting a totality according to their respective capacities.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is foremost in expounding the Dharma; because these five hundred arhats constantly preach the unsurpassed path, they are called "Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabha).
Since they are the proper vessels for this teaching of the Dharma, Pūrṇa is appointed to preside over them, just as Ānanda and Rāhula do for others.
He was also a great disciple who presided over the assembly of students; each had their own reason for this. △ Second, the correct interpretation according to the text, in five parts.
First, Pūrṇa’s realization:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [up to] gazing at the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never for a moment leaving it.

I have heard of the teaching of wisdom and skillful means according to what is appropriate; this comprehensively encompasses the teachings of the three assemblies. Furthermore, I have heard of the Great Record;
this comprehensively encompasses the accounts of Śāriputra and others receiving their prophecies. Again, I have heard of the Causes and Conditions;

this specifically encompasses the matter of the Prince of Mahābhijñājñāna. Again, I have heard of the Supernatural Powers; this specifically encompasses the matters of the Master’s divine transformations. These are rarely heard.
Thus, he attained what had never been experienced before. Because his delusions were removed, his mind was purified and he leaped for joy.
Thereupon, he left his seat to pay homage, and subsequently offered praise and made a vow, thinking: "[The Buddha] is able to know our profound inner resolve and original vows."
The preceding section was arranged by the compiler of the sūtra; this, however, is the actual speech of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
From the words "extraordinary and rare" up to "clinging everywhere," he generally praises the teaching of the Dharma during the three turnings of the wheel.

"We cannot proclaim the Buddha’s merits with our words" is a general praise of the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa); even the virtues of the Guide’s spiritual transformations cannot be fully proclaimed. Only...
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has now fulfilled his original vow by pledging to protect and uphold [the Dharma].
His "profoundly resolved original vow" refers to his diligent protection and assistance in proclaiming the Buddha-dharma, extending even to such acts of assistance in the past and future;
it does not refer to seeking a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Second, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus (up to the point where it says): "No one is able to exhaust the eloquence of his discourse.
This was to confirm and bring to fulfillment the profound depths of his original vow. He asked the assembly, "Do you see?

because the assembly merely knew the outward traces of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, yet did not know his profound practice; therefore, he opened the discourse to demonstrate it to them. He is foremost in preaching the Dharma.
"Describing their correct practice" refers to their various meritorious virtues. "Describing their manifold deeds" refers to their diverse activities.
"Describing their fundamental vows" refers to their diligent protection and maintenance [of the Dharma]. "Describing their eloquence in discourse" refers to their skillful oratory.
"Do not think... [and so on] up to "...constantly perform the Buddha-work to transform and teach sentient beings.

This first part provides a general summary, which is then elaborated upon extensively. The mention of "the places of ninety billion Buddhas" specifically elaborates on the distant causes for protecting and proclaiming [the Dharma].

Regarding those who "clearly understand and thoroughly penetrate the empty Dharma of the Buddhas," this is not like the followers of the Two Vehicles who are stalled in the emptiness of annihilation (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, those who attain the fourfold unimpeded purity of preaching the Dharma speak according to reality and do not become mired in names and signs.
The supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva are not to be compared with those of the Two Vehicles. "In accordance with their lifespan" means speaking of the duration of one's entire life.
"Causing them to establish themselves in Bodhi" means causing them to take firm stand upon the Right Path. This is for the sake of purifying the Buddha-field by transforming sentient beings.
This means that one’s own practice is perfected by relying on the practice of benefiting others. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"A bodhisattva takes up a buddha-field according to the sentient beings they transform. What is called "purifying a buddha-field" means purifying one's own mind so as to bring about the purity of the buddha-field.
That one must necessarily teach and transform sentient beings in order to purify a buddha-field is because, in essence, afflictions (*kleśa*)...
Yet he is able to purify [them]; it is not like the two vehicles, which seek purity by wearying themselves of worldly toil.

Viewed from this perspective, this wood is merely a manifestation of a great master of expedient means (mahopāya-kauśalya) appearing to propagate the Dharma. Therefore, the verse praises him through the theme of "inner secrecy and outer manifestation."
The various bhikṣus (up to) gradually fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.
The preceding section presented the remote causes; this section cites the three periods of time to clarify the profound practice of preaching the Dharma and proclaiming transformation.

Furthermore, his prior virtuous conduct was such that he attained the adornments of the Buddha-land of the Tathāgata Padmaprabha, and shall eventually attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because their extensive learning and secret practices constantly supported one another, Rāhula’s fruits of the *kalpa* of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma were equal to those of Ānanda;
furthermore, in the future, he will likewise be the elder son of Ānanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When I was a crown prince... [omitted] ...in order to seek the unsurpassed path.
He bestowed a prediction upon Rāhula that he would continue the Buddha-way so that it might flow on unceasingly. Thus, while concealing the traces of his great power, he manifested [this teaching].
Manifesting as a son of the Buddha, his merits are incalculable; only a Buddha can know them. This is called "secret practice.
△ Sixth, two thousand receive their predictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw two thousand individuals, both those still training and those beyond training, [up to] the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

Because these too had been transformed by him in the past, he now bestowed upon them their prediction [of enlightenment]. Their minds were supple, meaning their faculties and capacities had already matured.
Question: Although his vision did not explicitly reveal past causes, Ānanda—being profoundly learned and widely erudite—already knew them implicitly.

Since the names of the two thousand fruits were all identical because their causes were identical, he understood that both those in training and those beyond training immediately realize the true mark (dharmatā).
This is called the true mark.
Its lifespan is one kalpa; its land’s adornments, its śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and its True Dharma and Semblance Dharma are all entirely equal.
It is said that these two thousand [bodhisattvas] will simultaneously attain Buddhahood, and their physical environments, dharmas, and transformations will all be identical.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
These two thousand śrāvakas (up to) gradually enter into nirvāṇa.
Regarding those whose fame spreads far and wide as they gradually enter nirvāṇa: when their emergence and the fulfillment of their merit are complete, they return to the One without a trace;
such is the nature of every Buddha. △ Seventh: The Disciples’ Praise and Thanks.
At that time, two thousand learners and non-learners, having heard the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
“O World-Honored One, Lamp of Wisdom, Hearing the sound of this prediction, Our hearts are filled with joy, As if drenched by nectar.”
Praise of the Lamp of Wisdom. Hearing the Record, Rejoicing and Offering Thanks.
