Chapter Ten: The Dharma-Master. Part Two:
Bestowing Extensive Records to Perfectly Encompass the Previous Records. First: Dividing the Sections and Briefly Narrating.
One who is able to uphold the True Dharma and is thus fit to serve as a teacher for others is called a "Dharma Master.

This "Broad Record" (Guǎjì) is provided to complete and encompass the preceding record; it is titled the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" because it extensively records those who uphold the sutra and extols them.
The sutra cites the eight classes and fourfold assembly present before him, as well as those who hear the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

[The Buddha] rejoices and bestows predictions upon all; this is called the "Extensive Prediction. Although previously, in response to the three periods of the Dharma, he bestowed predictions for the three types of faculties, the scope of those recipients was not yet exhaustive.
Therefore, this [present teaching], which is universally inclusive, constitutes the essential core of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Since it is the essential core, it rightfully belongs to the orthodox tradition (*zhengzong*). That the old scholastic divisions treat this as merely the "Circulation" (*liutong*) section is merely according to their own particular views.

△ Second, the explanation of the text according to its topical outline (kośa-vibhāga), in two parts. First, the extensive record of the exaltation, in five sections. First, the bestowal of the extensive record, in two parts.
First, the present extensive record:
At that time, the World-Honored One, because of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja... [until] shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
[The Buddha] bestowed the *Vipula-vidyā* (Extensive Record), which was originally taught by Bhaiṣajyarāja to the Mahāsattva.

This is because the dharma-benefits of the *Vipula-vidyā* are vast and profound, and its excellence is such that none but those with deep karmic affinity from past lives or great Bodhisattvas are able to realize and know it. Bhaiṣajyarāja—

This is none other than the Bodhisattva Xijian (Sukhādarśana), who for a long time upheld this sutra by burning his body and setting his arms ablaze; he may truly be said to have deeply realized his karmic affinity from past lives.

The "eighty thousand great beings" refers to the eighty thousand bodhisattvas at the beginning of the sutra, as well as those among the eight classes of beings and the fourfold assembly present before him who were all granted predictions of enlightenment.
As it is said: "If there are any who hear this Dharma, there shall not be one who does not become a Buddha. Part Two.
The subsequent sections provide a detailed record.
The Buddha told Bhaisajyarāja (up to the point where he says), "I also bestow upon him the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Regarding those who will appear after his parinirvāṇa, although their karmic conditions have not yet manifested, he also provides these prophetic declarations; thus, this chapter contains a detailed record.
There is nothing not perfected; there is nothing not encompassed. △ Second, extolling that person:
"If there should be another person... [down to] ...he has taken birth in this human world out of compassion for sentient beings."
From "receiving and upholding" through "joining palms with reverence," there are six types of Dharma-preachers: first, receiving and upholding;

second, reading; third, reciting; fourth, explaining; fifth, transcribing; and sixth, making offerings. Because these are able to overcome the six kinds of difficulties, they must necessarily arise from the merit of past offerings to the Buddha and great vows.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if anyone asks [this question]... they will surely attain Buddhahood in a future age.
This causes Bhaiṣajyarāja to proclaim and clarify the supreme cause.
Why is this? If good sons and good daughters... extensively expound this sutra while born in an evil age.
The preceding explanation clarifies that because the conditions are superior and the person is honored, one shall become a Buddha.
Merely being able to embody the merit of the six types of Dharma-preachers within a single phrase is sufficient to warrant honoring and revering them as one who shall attain Bodhi;

how much more so when one is able to receive and uphold an entire sutra? In such a case, the conditions are even more superior and the person even more honored; their attainment of Buddhahood is certain.
Regarding those who have personally relinquished pure retribution: these are individuals who have attained the fruits of the Pure Land and manifest birth in an evil world.
If such good men or good women [should hear this,] they should extensively explain it for others.
One who carries a mandate is entrusted with a solemn charge; one who reverently upholds this scripture should be regarded as carrying the command of the Tathāgata himself.
Since they perform the great task of extolling the teachings as entrusted by the Tathāgata, they ought to be held in the highest esteem.
△ Third, do not disparage or revile [the teaching].
O Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there should be an evil person who, with an unwholesome mind... their transgression is exceedingly grave.

The World-Honored One of Ten Thousand Virtues and Great Compassion cannot be reviled. Yet, even if one reviles him, the transgression remains relatively light because he lacks the power [to retaliate].
Because it causes harm. Those who disparage those who uphold this sutra commit an even more grievous offense, for they sever the lineage of the Buddhas.
△ Fourth, exhorting others to have faith and turn toward it:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, whoever reads and recites the Lotus Sutra... [up to] ...should offer them as a treasury of celestial jewels."
To adorn oneself with the adornments of a Buddha means to be endowed with the manifold virtues of a Buddha.
To be one who is borne upon the shoulders of the Tathāgata means to be held in high esteem by the Buddha.
If even the Buddha honors them, then it is certainly appropriate for people to likewise revere and respect them according to their respective circumstances.
"Why is this so? [This continues] until "for the sake of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This interrogative and explanatory passage clarifies the meaning of those who ought to be honored. △ Fifth, the fivefold verse summary. First, the verse praises the teacher who transmits the person and the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"If one wishes to abide in the Buddha-way... and also make offerings to those who uphold it," [it means] "natural wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), which is precisely primordial awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and true wisdom. To abide in the Buddha-way and achieve this wisdom, one must necessarily rely upon—
The Dharma Master has elucidated this. Therefore, one should diligently make offerings to those who uphold the Lotus Sutra.

"All-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the fruit-wisdom of all Buddhas. Those who wish to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and swiftly attain this wisdom must rely upon this sutra for cultivation and realization;
therefore, one should uphold this sutra and also make offerings to its upholders. △ Second, verses extolling the person [who upholds it].
If there are those who can receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, know that they are envoys sent by the Buddha, out of compassion for all sentient beings.
Having praised the great vows accomplished in the presence of the Buddhas, they have been born into this human world out of pity for sentient beings.
Regarding those who are able to receive, uphold, and make offerings to the teacher of the Dharma,
the verse states that such persons relinquish their own pure karmic retributions and so forth, and are sovereign over where they wish to be born; wherever they desire to be born,
they possess mastery according to their vows.
"In the evil world after my parinirvāṇa... [until] I hope they may hear it for even a moment.
This command is to be honored, so that they may seek the wondrous Dharma.
If there are those in a future age who can receive and uphold this sutra, I shall dispatch them among human beings to perform the work of a Tathāgata."
It is not that the Tathāgata has sent them away; rather, none would be able [to do so]. △ Third, the verse admonishing against disparaging or slandering:
"If, throughout an eon... (up to) its sin would exceed even that."
As categorized:
"If someone seeks the Buddha-way" (up to) "their merit would surpass that.
This reveals and praises the merit [of such seeking]. △ Fourth, the verse exhorting faith and orientation.
"Throughout eighty billion kalpas... until I have now attained great benefit.

This passage concerning the offering of verses, flowers, incense, music, and the supreme gifts among humans expresses the resolve to persevere without weariness for eighty billion kalpas, hoping for even a moment's hearing.
By hearing [the teaching] for even a moment, one immediately attains Bodhi; therefore [it is said].
For the sake of great benefit. △ Fifth, the conclusion and proclamation that reveals its superiority:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I now tell you: among all the sūtras I have preached, the Lotus Sūtra is the foremost."

Therefore, one should properly place faith and take refuge in it. △ Second, manifesting its excellence and exhorting its upholding, in eleven parts. First, its profundity and subtlety make it difficult to understand.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed Bhaisajyarāja... (up to)... this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the most difficult to believe and the most difficult to understand.

It has already been explained that [this teaching] is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth; it is now explained that it is identical to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and it shall be explained that it is identical to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

However, it is specifically the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* whose expressed meaning is entirely the "wondrous Dharma" (*miaofa*) and whose revealed content is entirely the "true aspect" (*shixiang*). Because this is not within the knowledge or vision of ordinary sentient beings, it is difficult to believe;
because it is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas, it is difficult to understand. 2. Do not bestow [the teaching] upon those who are not the proper vessel.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this sutra is the secret and essential treasury of all Buddhas. (Omitting intermediate text) How much more so after their parinirvāṇa!

To grant this secret and essential Dharma recklessly would cause those with overweening pride to withdraw from their seats; to proclaim it openly would be like a destitute son fearing his father, leading to resentment, slander, hatred, and jealousy.
If such is the case even while the Tathāgata is present, how much more so in the evil age after his passing? Is it not so?
Selecting the Opportunity. △ Third, being able to uphold it is supreme.
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know" (up to) "the Tathāgata will then rub his head with his hand.
This sutra is difficult to hear; those who believe and accept it are also rare. Therefore, anyone who copies, upholds, reads, or explains it is not acting as if they were the Buddha himself.
They come to provide protection; yet, by their own faith, vows, and roots of goodness, they would be unable to do so.
To be covered by the Tathāgata’s robe means to have attained the power of the Buddha’s patience (*kṣānti*). To dwell together with the Tathāgata means to settle one's mind in harmony with the Buddha.
To have the Tathāgata stroke one’s head means to receive the Buddha’s consolation. Because of this, they are able to uphold and expound [this teaching] in the evil world of the future.
This is the Dharma. △ Fourth, the place where it resides should be revered.
From "Wherever the Medicine King [is]" (to "In this place there is already the entire body of the Tathāgata"):
the threefold exposition and all other auxiliary manifestations are none other than the entire body of the Tathāgata.
This stupa should be honored with all flowers and incense (up to) for the sake of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This is because its cause is correct and its conditions are superior. △ Fifth, it serves as a vital ford on the Path.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, there are many—both householders and those who have left the home life—who are able to practice the bodhisattva path well;
yet, to practice the bodhisattva path without having heard this sutra is like wishing to quench one's thirst while not knowing that water is required.

If there are sentient beings who seek the Buddha-way (up to) *samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is like a person digging a well who has already drawn near to the source of the spring. △ Sixth, providing an analogy for the essential ford.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is like a person who, parched with thirst, requires water [until] his mind becomes certain that water must be near.
Digging for water on high ground is like practicing the Bodhisattva path without finding its essential method; seeing only dry earth is like being at the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).
Continuing one's efforts without ceasing is like progressing gradually from the stage of Dry Wisdom; seeing moist soil is a metaphor for successively hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

If one gradually reaches the "mud" analogy, it means that although one has first heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one still lags behind in cultivation and merely draws near to the water of the Buddha’s wisdom.
As for suddenly reaching its true source, the wondrous clarity manifests perfectly without the need for effort;
compared to what was previously practiced, all of that appears as turbid dregs. The reason the sutra does not speak of this here is what is called "leading on."
Yet he does not prompt them, allowing them to advance of their own accord; for in the state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), there is no room for verbal instruction.
△ Seventh, the combined manifestation of the analogy:
"The Bodhisattvas are also like this" (up to) "now the Buddha transforms and brings them to maturity, revealing and teaching [them]."
The fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi both belong to this sutra; thus, if one has neither heard nor understood it, how can one attain the Way?
Opening the gate of skillful means is like digging a well; revealing the true reality is like seeing the water.
The Dharma Flower Sutra-treasury is the Tathāgata-garbha of sentient beings. Within sentient beings, it is latent amidst the afflictions of worldly toil; within Bodhisattvas, it is latent...
Regarding the myriad practices, as for the place of jewels, it lies more than five hundred *yojanas* away; it may be called deep, firm, obscure, and remote.
Because no ordinary person can reach it, only a Bodhisattva can reveal and demonstrate it. △ Eighth, the clarification of those who are not suitable vessels.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are bodhisattvas [from here up to] "you should know that these are those of overweening pride":
those with great faculties who have newly resolved their minds, and those with small faculties who possess overweening pride—neither of them are suitable vessels. △ Ninth:
The teaching is given when the physical form is present.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, if there are good men or good women (up to) "how they should speak":
first the heading, then the explanation.
These good men or good women (up to) "extensively preach this Lotus Sūtra."
Now, as for the way of preaching the Dharma and transforming others through teaching: one must first have a place of one's own before one can bring peace to others;
one must first have something for oneself to wear before one can cause others to submit; one must first have a basis for oneself before one can lead others to realization.

The Tathāgata takes compassion as his chamber, gentleness and forbearance as his robe, and the emptiness of dharmas as his seat. Having entered the chamber of compassion, he himself possesses [these qualities].

This is the place where one dwells. To don the robe of gentle forbearance is for oneself to have that which is worn. To sit upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas is for oneself to have that upon which one relies.
Only when one is thus endowed with the essence of a Buddha may one extensively expound this sutra.
If one has not yet realized this essence, one lacks self-mastery and correctness; how then can one act as a teacher for others? Therefore it is said: "Abide securely within this, and only then..."
One should expound this Dharma extensively without indolence. Now, those who occupy the precious flower-seat and engage in the practice of the sages and commoners ought to deeply discern this:
that the emptiness of all dharmas is not a nihilistic emptiness, but rather refers to the state of being vast, open, and thoroughly realized regarding all dharmas.
△ Ten: The Buddha’s Transformation, Protection, and Assistance.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, in other lands (until) I shall return and explain it for them so that they may attain fulfillment.
This is the great matter of the Buddha’s power of transformation and its praise. "Other lands" refers to worlds in other directions;
appearing in different countries means manifesting through the skillful means of concealment and revelation to transform sentient beings. △ Eleven: Reiteration by Verse (six parts).
The first verse reveals its excellence and exhorts one to uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra. This sutra is difficult to hear; those who can believe and accept it are likewise rare."
Those who wish to advance easily along the right path without indolence should rely on this as their essential ferry-crossing. △ Second, the verse illustrating the essential ferry-crossing:
"Just as a person who is thirsty and needs water [until] they know for certain they are near water."
△ Three verses combined reveal [the meaning]:
"Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know" (up to) "is close to the Buddha’s wisdom.
This definitively clarifies that the śrāvakas enter directly into the Buddha-wisdom. △ Four verses specifically explain the embodiment.
If a person speaks this sutra (up to the point of) "because of mindfulness of the Buddha, one should endure," they should endure all evils by taking the Buddha as their object of mindfulness;
this is what is meant by "donning the robe of the Tathāgata. △ Fifth, verses on the Buddha’s transformation, protection, and assistance.
"From my thousands of millions of lands... [up to] 'I can cause the great assembly to rejoice.
All of these concern the dispatching of emanations from other lands to provide protection and assistance.

If a person possesses these virtues—namely, the virtues of compassion, gentleness, and patience—and is able to see my body while reading the sutras in a place of emptiness, I shall cause them to practice gentleness upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas."
Through the virtue of patience, one causes the mind to be empty and the environment to be tranquil; thus, within this state, the entire body becomes clearly visible.
This is called the "Body of Pure Radiance. If one does not possess this virtue, yet merely recites this sutra while wishing to perceive me through physical form, such practice is a deviant path.
△ Sixth, the conclusion and exhortation to follow a teacher.
If one draws near to a Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path. By following and training under such a teacher, one shall behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
the entire bodies of all these Buddhas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, reside herein.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eleven: The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa. Part Three:
All Buddhas of the Three Assemblies Perfectly Realize the Previous Dharma. Section One: Indicating the Outline and Explaining the Meaning.

From the opening of the assembly until this point, the three cycles of the Dharma have been complete, and the fourfold assembly has received their full predictions. The Dharmakāya is already perfected, and the original vows are fulfilled.

It is already sufficient. Therefore, the past Many Treasures Stūpa of the Leaping Vow manifested its entire body, and all the Buddhas who have manifested their divided bodies throughout the ten directions to preach the Dharma gathered in perfect assembly for complete realization.

The reason for this is that the path of cultivation and realization taught by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—past and present—is fully and perfectly contained herein. II. Explanation of the Text According to the Outline.
Twenty-three. First, the appearance of the jeweled stupa.
At that time, before the Buddha, there appeared a stupa made of the seven treasures, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.

This extraordinary and magnificent jeweled stupa is the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruition-retribution) of his fruitive and practical cultivation; its various ornaments manifest the functional efficacy of those virtues.
The various adornments represent the manifestation of the myriad virtues; the five thousand railings represent the power of dhāraṇī;
the thousands of myriads of chambers correspond to immeasurable compassion; and the countless banners and streamers correspond to the subduing of heterodoxy and the manifesting of the orthodox.
The hanging precious necklaces represent the descent of manifold virtues to transform beings below. The billions of precious bells represent the wide resonance of the Dharma-sound.
Fragrance emanating from the four sides symbolizes that spiritual powers reach everywhere and respond to all as desired.
The canopies of the seven treasures reaching up to the celestial palaces symbolize the supreme majesty of manifold virtues. △ Second, the offerings of the various devas to the stupa.

The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down māndārava flowers (up to) paying homage with reverence and praise, for they knew that the Tathāgata’s entire body was present there. △ Third, the seal of praise for Śākyamuni.
At that time, a great sound issued from within the jeweled stūpa... [up to] "all are truly real.
This "equal and great wisdom" (平等大慧) is precisely the true wisdom of the One Vehicle (一乘實智). △ Fourth, the fourfold assembly’s joy and wonder.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, having seen the Great Jewel Stūpa [and so forth], stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
Because they heard the praise of the true teaching of Mahāmati, they attained the joy of the Dharma. △ Fifth, the occasion for the question on eloquence.
At that time, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas (up to) who also uttered these sounds therein.
△ Sixth, Śākyamuni’s explicit proclamation:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna (up to) praising him, saying, "Excellent!"

Prabhūtaratna’s parinirvāṇa left his entire body undispersed, as if he were still in meditative absorption; yet, by the power of his vows, he was able to manifest and certify the sutra wherever it was taught.

This demonstrates the sovereign power of the Dharmakāya, which is neither subject to extinction nor birth, enabling those who hear the wondrous Dharma to realize that there is no extinction or birth and to attain sudden awakening to the true nature of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Therefore, he manifested such a certification of the teaching.
After that Buddha attained enlightenment... (up to) "one should erect a great stūpa.
This describes the origin of the stūpa.
That Buddha, by means of his supernormal powers and the power of his vows... (up to) praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Not only here. Mahāpratibhāna (up to) praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
This concludes the indication of the present occasion. △ Seven: The Vow to See Many Treasures.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna [said]: "We wish to behold this Buddha-body.

At that time, [the beings] from the Sahā world... (until) their hearts were filled with great joy, and they all paid homage from afar.
△ 16. Both sides received benefit.
Immeasurable sentient beings heard the Dharma and attained realization; (up to: the six directions of the Stainless World shook.
This was the benefit received by that assembly and the auspicious response from that land. As for "the record of the Way," it serves as a seal of authentication for their attainment of the Way.
In the Sahā world, three thousand sentient beings (up to the point of) receiving their predictions.
This assembly, having received this benefit, also attains the prediction of the Way. △ Seventeen: Concluding the Manifestation and Exhorting Faith.
The Bodhisattva Jñānākara and Śāriputra, along with the entire assembly, accepted this in silence.
Having heard the account of the dragon girl, both Jñānākara and Śāriputra were initially struck with astonishment and doubt, yet in the end they all accepted it in silence.
Indeed, the benefits and efficacy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are so manifest and swift that who would not believe them?
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on Entrustment (Dhāraṇī-parivarta). Part Two:
The Vows of the Holy Multitude to Maintain [the Teaching]. First, a brief outline and introduction.

Because of the preceding entrustment and because of the exhortation revealed above, the assembly vows to maintain and proclaim [this teaching] in order to broaden the transformation of beings through the Way. Therefore...

This is titled "The Chapter on Upholding. Regarding the beginning of the text: first, Bhaiṣajyarāja and others vow to uphold [the Dharma] in this world; next, the assembly of śrāvakas vows to uphold it in other worlds;

finally, the great bodhisattvas vow to uphold it throughout the ten directions. This world, Sahā, is difficult to transform and cannot be sustained by anything other than the vast vow of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Because other worlds are lands of goodness, the śrāvakas are capable of upholding it there. As for the ten directions, they are vast.
Therefore, it was necessary to have eight hundred trillion great bodhisattvas. △ Second, the exegesis of the text according to the topical outline, in three parts.
First, the vow to uphold this teaching in this land:
At that time, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja... [until] ...should receive, uphold, read, recite, and expound this sutra.
This is because the end of the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" reveals the difficulty of being exhorted to uphold [the teaching];
thus, figures such as Bhaiṣajyarāja exerted the power of great vows, undaunted by that difficulty, and prayed that the Buddha need have no concerns.
In the evil world hereafter, the roots of goodness of sentient beings will diminish further (until they reach the point where they offer various kinds of worship without sparing their own lives).

This passage leads into the meaning of the metaphor comparing [the difficulty of teaching] to the conflagration at the end of an eon that consumes Mount Sumeru; it is through this that the vow is made.

Although the wicked violence of the final age may be like the conflagration at the end of an eon, and the arrogance of those with haughty minds may be as high as Mount Sumeru, making them difficult to transform and teach—
One vows not to avoid anything; hence it is said that one should give rise to great forbearance and not begrudge body or life.
△ Second, the vow for others consists of two parts: first, the assembly of śrāvaka monks.
At that time, among the assembly, five hundred arhats [from "because their minds were not sincere" onwards]—
this summarizes the intent of the objection using the analogy of the Great Earth being lifted by the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), while the śrāvakas themselves measured their own strength.
"I vow to transform other regions into virtuous lands. △ Second, the assembly of śrāvaka nuns.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī (up to) all became Dharma-preachers.
Mahāprajāpatī is translated here as "Great Path of Loving-kindness" (Dà Àidào). Desiring to vow to uphold the sutra, she had not yet received her kinsman's instruction;
thus, she stood with uplifted gaze in reverent contemplation. Gautamī is translated here as "Leader of the Nuns. It was from Mahāprajāpatī that women first began to leave the household life.
Therefore, he was titled "Lord of Nuns.
In this manner, you shall gradually fulfill the path of a bodhisattva and attain buddhahood;
your fruit-name shall be "Joyful Vision" (Priyadarśana), because as a Dharma Master you gladden people with the joy of the Dharma.
At that time, Rāhula’s mother Yaśodharā [attained] a Buddha-life span of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Yaśodharā manifested her traces as a sign of great compassion and the joy of the Dharma, which accord with great wisdom;

wisdom and compassion were practiced in tandem, after which she became fully endowed with myriads of virtues and adorned by the radiance of the thousand marks. Therefore, the name of the resulting fruit is "Endowed with Ten Million Radiant Marks."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī [up to] spoke these verses:
"O World-Honored One, Guide, who brings peace and security to devas and humans; having heard this prediction, our minds are fully at ease."
This concludes the record of the thanks. [The assembly] vowed below to uphold [the teaching].

After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses (up to) the extensive proclamation of this sutra, they likewise felt intimidated by the Sahā world due to their limited capacity. △ Thirty directions vow to uphold [the teaching], part three. One: A glance.
Entrustment.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from this world and other worlds;
neither partial nor exhaustive was his view. Thus, with a blue-lotus-like turn of his gaze, his intention encompassed the ten directions. (8)
The "ten trillion" refers to the assembly gathered from the ten directions. △ Second, the benefit of wisdom and silent compliance:
These bodhisattvas are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) [down to] those in other directions who see and protect them from afar.

Since even this single Sahā world is already fearful, corrupt, and evil, the ten directions are truly difficult to traverse; therefore, they attribute their success to the Buddha’s power and further seek his protection.
△ Third, the simultaneous recitation of verses in four parts: first, the courageous making of vows.
Immediately, all the bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison and spoke these verses:
"We pray that you do not worry; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of this terrifying and evil age, we shall widely proclaim [the Dharma]."

This verse is also spoken with the intent of encouraging the upholding [of the precepts] by employing the previously mentioned manifest difficulties. Therefore, its words all describe the various hardships of the final age.
△ Second, the extensive exposition of the power of patience has four parts. First, the vow to endure ignorance.
When there are ignorant people who revile us with harsh words and even attack us with knives and staves, we shall endure it all;
for it is due to the darkness of ignorance and delusion that the heterodox and the orthodox contend against one another. △ Second, the vow to endure heterodox arrogance.
In this degenerate age, there are bhikṣus whose minds are crooked with false wisdom; claiming to have attained what they have not attained, their hearts are filled with pride.
These are the thorns of the great forest, the weeds and tares of the great field.
There may be those who, from being forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) up to being arhats with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*),
merely rely on the Dharma to borrow its prestige, using deceptive speech and hypocritical conduct to pilfer fame and seek gain, thereby unwarrantedly receiving veneration.
*Āraṇya* is translated here as "a place of tranquility."
Such people harbor evil intentions and discriminate against this sutra;
out of foolish envy for the worthy and deceitful slander of the true, they merely reflect the sentiments of the final age.
"Always amidst the great assembly... they shall all endure it.
These are all words of overflowing malice; that is to say, they delight in exposing our faults. To slander is to claim that we ourselves composed this sutra.
Thus, the piercing words "You are all Buddhas" are all words of contempt. △ Third, the vow to endure fear and evil.
In the midst of this turbid and evil age, [they shall] protect and uphold what the Buddha has entrusted.
As described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, evil spirits may enter their bodies; evil Māras can fly about and possess people, exposing their private affairs.
To revile is to restrain one through the application of the law, which is akin to using a tether; to abuse is to let loose one's words without restraint, which differs from formal punishment.
△ Fourth, the vow to endure expulsion:
"The World-Honored One himself should know... all should endure this matter."
The teachings given according to what is appropriate are difficult to understand in their underlying intent; thus, the turbid currents of ignorance obscure them.

People may speak with foul mouths to slander them, frown in resentment, or even expel them without toleration. Yet, because one recalls the previous command to uphold [the teaching], one should endure all of this.
△ Third, its dissemination through the sense bases.
"In all villages and cities (up to: we pray that the Buddha may dwell in peace and security.
The World-Honored One’s messenger said, "It is by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power that I am able to preach well without fear;
I pray that the Buddha will remain secure and not harbor any anxiety. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the vow with utmost sincerity.
In the presence of the World-Honored One and all the Buddhas who have come from the ten directions, I have made this solemn vow. The Buddhas themselves know my heart;
"all those who have come from the ten directions" refers to both Prabhūtaratna and his manifested bodies.
