The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Fourteen: The Practice of Peaceful Conduct. △ Part Three:
The Wondrous Practice of Upholding the Sutra. Two sections. First, the heading and exposition of the principles of the classification.
Myriad practices rely upon the three karmas and are rooted in wisdom and compassion. Wisdom is used to dwell within oneself; compassion is used to respond to external things. All [of these]...
If one desires not to lose its correctness, then being correct brings peace and joy; being incorrect leads to peril and sorrow.

Therefore, this section specifically relies upon Mañjuśrī’s correct wisdom to demonstrate the four dharmas of great compassion: correct body, correct speech, and correct mind. This is titled the "Chapter on Peaceful and Joyful Conduct.
Following the previous "Chapter on Upholding," the bodhisattvas, out of reverence and compliance with the Buddha’s intent, vow to protect and maintain this [teaching] in the evil age.
The sutra pledges to endure all hardships, yet the Great Sage considered that being able to endure hardships is not equal to ensuring that there are no hardships at all;
therefore, he taught the four practices of peaceful and happy conduct (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*). Once these four practices are correct, the single nature becomes tranquil and still;

when still, one merges with the Way (*dharma*), and when active, one unites with the spirit (*shen*). Thus, one remains whole and is not crushed by external things; even when facing peril and hardship, one remains unaware of them.
Regarding such perils and hardships: by nature, one is not swayed by external things. Even when confronted with desire and aversion, one does not perceive them as desire and aversion.

If one personally practices this conduct, then even while traversing an evil age and upholding the scriptures, entering amidst the clamor and splendor to respond to the world, there will be nowhere one goes that is not peaceful and joyful. This is what is meant by ensuring that there are no difficulties.
△ Second, the explanation of the text according to its topical outline, in two parts. First, Mañjuśrī’s praise and request, in two parts. First, the praise preceding [the request]:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta... (up to) ...to protect, uphold, read, and recite this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This concludes the section on praising the practice of upholding [the sutra]. △ Second, the request for the future:
"World-Honored One, how can bodhisattva-mahāsattvas preach this sutra in the evil world of the future?"
"May I ask, what kind of conduct must one practice to be able to preach this sutra without encountering any difficulties?
This is the initiation of the Dharma of Peaceful and Joyful Conduct (*sukhavihāra*). Mañjuśrī’s request demonstrates that one initiates correct practice by relying on right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
II. The Buddha’s Demonstration of the Four Dharmas. This has two parts: first, the general presentation of the dharmas of conduct.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī (up to the point where he says):
"One should abide in four dharmas," which are the four modes of peaceful conduct (*caturvidha-sukha-vihāra*). First, right bodily conduct; second, right verbal conduct; third, right mental conduct;
fourth, the conduct of great compassion. To follow the three karmas with great compassion means that once the three karmas are correct, right wisdom is truly pure.
Having attained one's own benefit, one must give rise to great compassion and extensively practice the benefit of others.

When wisdom and compassion support one another, one will then be able to expound this sutra in an evil age without encountering various difficulties. II. Second, the detailed analysis and explanation of the four sections. First, the primary cultivation of bodily conduct.
This has three parts. First, the general indication of the two locations.
First, abiding in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice (*caryā*) and sphere of intimacy (*upaniṣad*), one is able to expound this sutra for the sake of sentient beings.

"Practice" refers to one's conduct and resolve; "intimacy" refers to habitual association. Second, not deviating from the Way—this is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice and sphere of intimacy.
This is the essential point of bodily conduct. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the two spheres has two parts. First:
The explanation of the two aspects of the sphere of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*) has two parts:

first, the practice of phenomena (*dharma-caryā*); second, within each of these two spheres, there is both the practice of phenomena and the practice of principle (*tattva*). Without phenomena, one cannot engage with the conventional; without principle, one cannot accord with the ultimate.

When one is proficient in both principle and phenomenon, and the ultimate and the conventional do not obstruct one another, only then can one benefit sentient beings and propagate the Dharma, finding peace and happiness in every situation.
Mañjuśrī... [up to] ...and his mind is not startled.
One whose sphere of practice necessarily abides in patience, when employing the six perfections according to the occasion to confront hardships, there is nothing superior to this.
Patience. For when one acts impulsively in pursuit of affairs, regret and blame arise; therefore, one must employ patience to govern oneself.
Only by being able to endure can one be supple amidst hardness so that things cannot crush one; be compliant amidst adversity so that things cannot harm one;
exercise discernment in affairs so that what is enacted is not violent; and observe the subtle so that what is encountered does not cause alarm.
By this, one successfully accomplishes the practice of peaceful dwelling (*sukha-caryā*). △ Next is the practice of principle (*li-xing*).
Furthermore, there is "no practice" regarding phenomena (*dharma*);
"phenomena" here refers to all practices of the Dharma. Although one practices these dharmas, one does not dwell in their marks (*nimitta*); this is called "no practice."
For where there is a standard, there is a capacity; when capacity and its object stand in opposition, and self and other become adversaries, then suffering arises and peace is lost.
Yet, when one contemplates all phenomena as they truly are (up to: this is called the sphere of practice of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva).
One contemplates all dharmas by means of the dharma one practices oneself. In accordance with the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), there is nothing to be contemplated;
nor is there any practice, nor anything to be practiced. When there is no discrimination, emotional consciousness is entirely forgotten, and both "is" and "is not" are simultaneously extinguished.
The conduct and disposition of the bodhisattva are thus alone. △ Second, the explanation of the "near abodes" has two parts. First, the inquiry:
What is meant by the "near abodes" of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
△ Second, the explanation of the text, in two parts. First, the practice of deeds, which takes precept and concentration as its essence; this also has two parts. First, the eight precepts.
First, avoiding proximity to those with power and influence:
"A Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not associate with kings, princes, ministers, or high officials."
Although external protection may be honorable, I fear that relying on such power will obstruct the Way.

If one’s resolve is set upon this [path], yet the body dwells in mountain forests while the heart hangs upon the imperial palace gates, can one ever find even momentary peace? △ Second, the precept against associating with non-Buddhists.
One does not associate with various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), including brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*) up to the *lokāyata* and those who oppose the *lokāyata*.
"Brahmin" refers here to renunciants who are non-Buddhists; "Nirgrantha" refers to householders who are non-Buddhists. *Lokāyata* is translated here as "evil sophistry";
"opposing the *lokāyata*" is translated as "evil questioning. One does not associate with non-Buddhists in order to cease divergent views. One does not...
To compose secular writings is to sever heterodox paths; to distance oneself from malicious debate is to avoid devious sophistry.
△ Third, one should refrain from violent games. This means not associating with any forms of violent entertainment, such as boxing, wrestling, or various other displays of martial acrobatics.

The *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "If one engages in various forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the mind becomes distracted. If even conceptual proliferation causes distraction, how much more so when one is closely involved in it?
'Mutual grappling' refers to seizing and pinning; 'mutual wrestling' refers to clashing horns. Nārāyaṇa is a deity of great valor and immense strength."
Now, "pointing to" refers to the performance of acrobatic feats and transformations for entertainment; that is, various magical illusions. △ Fourth, the precept against associating with the wicked:
furthermore, one should not associate with *caṇḍālas* (up to: ...), and when preaching the Dharma to them, one should do so without any expectation of reward.

This means to distance oneself from evil conditions. *Caṇḍāla* is translated here as "one who bears a stern insignia," meaning one who marks themselves with severity, such as by tattooing their bodies or wearing foul clothing.
In the *Vinaya Piṭaka*, there are references to both virtuous discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) and unvirtuous discipline (*duḥśīla-saṃvara*).

Such individuals generally refer to those of power and influence downward; even if one does not personally associate with them, if they come for the sake of the Dharma, one should speak to them purely.
△ The five precepts are close to the Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, one should not associate with śrāvaka bhikṣus who seek [only their own liberation] (up to: those who have no aspirations).
Because the Hīnayāna has not yet integrated its teachings and frequently gives rise to disputes, which obstructs the practice of peaceful conduct, one does not associate with them. Moreover...
He does not inquire after their welfare; this is not out of pride, but rather out of caution against intimacy. △ Sixth, the precept against associating with women:
Mañjuśrī... [up to] ...does not converse with young girls, virgins, widows, and so forth.
When preaching the Dharma, one should forget all emotional attachments and conceptualizations. When engaging in conversation, one should avoid situations that give rise to suspicion or scandal.
Young girls and virgins are not suitable counterparts for a host and guest; rather, they are the source of censure and ruin. △ Seventh precept: Avoid those who are sexually impotent.
Furthermore, one should not associate with or treat as close friends the five types of impotent persons.

Since they are not vessels for the Dharma and because associating with them leads to defilement, one should not be intimate with them. The details regarding these five types of lewd individuals need not be analyzed here.
△ Eighth: Purifying the Body and Mind.
One should not enter another's house alone. If there is a cause or condition that necessitates entering alone, one should simply maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha.
One does not enter alone for the sake of purifying the body; one mindfully recites the Buddha’s name for the sake of rectifying the mind.
If one preaches the Dharma for women— even more so for other matters—
if one’s deportment is not restrained, it will give rise to suspicion and defilement.
One should not take pleasure in keeping young disciples or śrāmaṇeras of narrow views, nor should one take pleasure in sharing the same teacher with them.
It easily leads to agitation and distress, obstructing peaceful and blissful practice. △ Second, the section on concentration:
One should properly engage in seated meditation (up to) "this is called the first place of intimacy.
△ Second, the rational practice, which takes contemplative wisdom as its essence, has two parts. First, correct contemplation.
This is the second stage of close proximity (*upaniṣad*). The first stage of close proximity takes precept and meditative concentration as its essence;

the second stage of close proximity takes contemplative wisdom as its essence. Thus, by harmonizing the preceding precepts and concentration so that they perfectly accord with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one accomplishes the sublime practice (*sucarita*).

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [from] until [the state of] being non-perverted, immovable, non-retrogressive, and non-reversing—perceives that all dharmas are, in their very essence, truly pure.
Not receiving a single speck of dust is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Being unmoving, indestructible, and free from all illusions and delusions is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The Bodhisattva contemplates all dharmas as empty; according to their true mark, there is nothing to be grasped.
Because there is neither addition nor subtraction, one’s vision is non-perverted and the mind is without fluctuation.
"Vision is non-perverted" refers to what the verse calls not discriminating among dharmas as existent or non-existent, right or wrong, and so forth.

"The mind is without fluctuation" refers to what the verse calls gathering the mind so it is unmoving, like Mount Sumeru. This is because the nature of the mind is fundamentally quiescent, existing only in relation to its conditions.
It becomes agitated. Because one perceives through inversion, one regards phenomena as having birth and arising;
thus, the mind undergoes movement and fluctuation, like the moon appearing to move because the clouds are racing.

If one can observe according to reality, the mind will neither move nor regress, and one will realize that phenomena are neither born nor arise, like waves becoming still when the wind ceases. Thus, regarding the mind and phenomena:
First: When viewed with a perverted mind, delusive objects appear in chaotic confusion; when viewed through the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), the true mechanism is naturally quiescent.
Therefore, in practicing the Practice of Peace and Bliss, one values the contemplation according to reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*). △ Second, clarification by means of analogy.
As in space there is no nature of existence (up to) the second stage of intimacy.
Regarding "no nature of existence": it means that the natures of arising, ceasing, and the characteristics of names and signs are all non-existent.
Since names and signs are all non-existent, they cannot be reached by verbal expression; thus, the path of language is cut off. It is immeasurable and boundless, as speech is like space.
It is inexhaustible. Being unimpeded and unobstructed, its speech is like space, which cannot be differentiated.
Such is the true nature (*dharmatā*); how could it ever be reached by words? Thus, whatever can be spoken is merely a phenomenon of inversion that exists through conditions.
One should know that there is nothing that does not arise from conditions or is not born from inversion; ultimately, [it is beyond expression].
It may be so stated. By constantly observing in this manner, one is able to integrate previous activities and practices to form sublime conduct.
△ Third, the restatement by verse, in four parts: first, a general verse summarizing the activities and practices of the two locations.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If there is a bodhisattva... [up to] "...and the place of intimacy.
First the heading, then the explanation.
One should always remain far from kings (and so forth), and never associate with them.

This precept involves distancing oneself from those with power, non-Buddhists, and those engaged in violent games and the like. Regarding the Tripiṭaka studies: they are the teachings of the ignorant, the Lesser Vehicle.

Those who break the precepts claim to have no practice; those who are mere names claim to have no reality; those who speak with frivolous laughter have many deviant ways; and those attached to desire have much defilement.

They seek manifest parinirvāṇa while failing to cultivate the holy life and vainly hoping for the fruits of the Path; such individuals are not upright persons, and therefore one should not associate with them.
If one should encounter such people, one must preach the Dharma to them.
This verse praises pure preaching of the Dharma. Because one is able to remain without attachment, one is fearless.
One must not associate with widows, virgins, or [other such women].
This precept enjoins the avoidance of women and those who are neither male nor female, as they constitute a violation of the discipline.
Do not associate with those who engage in violent sumo wrestling, various forms of frivolous play, or any types of courtesans;
this concludes the preceding section.
Do not remain alone in a secluded place... [up to] ...single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name.
This is the ultimate rectification of the body. To remain secluded in remote places or within the midst of market towns is the method for begging for food;
by thus subduing arrogance, one inspires the benevolence and goodness of others.
This is what is called the "place of practice" and the "nearby place. By means of these two places, one is able to dwell in peace and joy while teaching the Dharma.

This is a double conjunction. △ Second, the separate verses on the two points: the locus of practice and the practice itself. First, the verse on the locus of practice; second, the verse on the practice itself.
In the prose (*gadya*), these are each presented in connection with the practice of the matter; in the verse (*śloka*), they are each versified separately from the practice of the matter.
Thus, the meaning of the text can be distinguished.
Furthermore, one does not practice [anything] up to the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.

The verse further states that regarding phenomena there is no place to which one goes, up to the point of non-discrimination, and so forth; one does not practice the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas.
This means that one does not engage with the teachings of the Three Vehicles. △ Second, the verse on the proximate state has two parts.
First, the verse on correct contemplation: "All dharmas... are like Mount Sumeru."
The verse contemplates that all phenomena are empty, their true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), non-perverted, immovable, and unchanging, and so forth.

When one directs the mind toward the true mark of ultimate emptiness, it immediately becomes delusion; furthermore, to discriminate between existence and non-existence, right and wrong, is entirely perverted.
△ Second, the verse clarifies this through analogy.
Contemplating all phenomena (up to) this is called the proximate station.
The verse [describes them] as being like space, having the nature of non-existence, up to being unimpeded and unobstructed, etc., eternally abiding in a single characteristic;
that is to say, there is no difference such as arising, ceasing, movement, or regression. △ Third, the concluding verse on the two stations.

If there is a bhikṣu (up to) who is without timidity, it is because he has profoundly penetrated the principle that he is thus without timidity; that is to say, with a mind free from fear, he is able to preach with ease and composure.
At times, the Bodhisattva [from "at times" to] "is without timidity.
The verse constantly contemplates such characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and thereby explains the reason for being without timidity.
△ Fourth, the concluding verse on the correct bodily practice.
Mañjuśrī... [up to] preaching the Lotus Sūtra.
The first teaching is precisely the practice of right body. △ Second, the practice of right speech, in two parts: first, the formal prose exposition of the correct teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the passage from "Moreover, Mañjuśrī" up to "should abide [in equanimity] when proclaiming with the mouth":
this means that one must abide in the mind when speaking with the mouth. When the mind and mouth are in accord, then the practice of speech is correct.
When reading the sutras (up to) not speaking of the good, evil, strengths, or weaknesses of others:
there are Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sutras, and there are people with great or small capacities.

Because it is difficult to understand [the teachings] according to the suitability of the vehicle for the capacity, one easily seeks out faults when reading the sutras; therefore, one is cautioned against this. Regarding "not being arrogant toward other teachers": do not rely on...
One should not treat great offenses lightly or small ones with arrogance and partiality. As for not discussing [the duration of] long or short [penances]:
internally it quiets karmic activity, and externally it quiets disputes; this is the essential principle of speech and practice.
Even regarding śrāvakas, one does not mention their names to speak of their faults (up to: so as to cause them to attain all-knowledge).
To speak of their faults causes them to lose the Small [Vehicle], while to praise their virtues causes them to regress from the Great [Vehicle].

One neither harbors resentment toward those who obstruct the Path nor feels disdain for their baseness; this is not merely that such words do not leave the mouth, but that they do not even arise in the mind. This may be called...

This is the well-cultivated mind of peace and happiness. Because this well-cultivated mind of peace and happiness is free from praise or blame, resentment or aversion, one is able to guide others in accordance with their capacities.
△ Second, the repeated explanation by means of verses, in two parts.
First, the verse on the characteristics of verbal conduct.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in [teaching]... explaining according to the questions asked.

Always delighting in preaching the Dharma, he no longer engages in worldly discourse; thus his speech and conduct are naturally upright. His body is pure and his robes are clean, yet he does not seek after finery."

This is for the sake of elegance and purity; it is intended to correspond with the purity of one's own mind and the purity of the Dharma taught. Therefore, it is said that one is pure both internally and externally.
To "abide peacefully and respond to questions" means to empty oneself to meet with things, like a bell waiting to be struck.
In the West, fragrant oils are used as pure adornments.
"If there are bhikṣus (up to) causing them all to rejoice.
This refers to the correct speech that guides and reaches others in accordance with their capacities. Laziness obstructs vigor; indolence obstructs diligence;

and anxiety and affliction obstruct peace and happiness. Because Bodhisattvas wish to rely on speech and practice to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, [they must eliminate these obstacles].
"Eliminating the mind of indolence and abandoning all sorrows and afflictions; constantly preaching day and night" means that the resolve to propagate the Dharma is uninterrupted.
"Robes, bedding, and so forth... providing for their comfort and well-being" refers to the offerings of requisites.
Because one's aspiration lies in the Dharma and not in material things, one does not seek offerings of the four requisites such as clothing;

rather, one contemplates only the offering of the peace and joy of preaching the Dharma. For the offerings of the four requisites provide merely minor benefits, whereas the offering of preaching the Dharma constitutes a great benefit.
"From 'after my parinirvāṇa' until 'because they abide securely in patience,' it is clear that speech and conduct should take patience as their primary principle.

For those who preach this sutra, there will be no internal afflictions such as anger, distress, or sorrow, nor external difficulties such as verbal abuse, threats, beatings, or banishment; this is because they are able to abide securely in patience. Thus, patience is indispensable."

They do not rely [on external conditions], and thus all difficulties naturally cease; this is what is meant by "necessarily causing them to be free from difficulty. II. Verse Summary Concluding the Manifestation of Benefits:
"The wise are thus" (up to) "cannot be fully described."
Thus, for one who practices well: by cultivating the village through the aforementioned conduct of right speech, one cultivates the mind;

this is what is called "cultivating oneself. To be able to abide in peace and happiness is what is called "peaceful abiding. One who cultivates themselves and abides in peace is a follower of the sages.
As a follower of the sages practicing the Way of the sages, their merit and the Way become vast, and their virtue accords with all things.
How could its breadth ever be fully exhausted? △ Third, the primary practice of intention has four parts. First, ceasing karmic activities:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī... [do not] even slight or revile those who study the Buddha-way, seeking out their faults.
From jealousy, flattery, and deception down to frivolous conceptualization regarding all phenomena, these are all subtle wrong practices of the mental ground;
therefore, they must be rectified. When the Dharma is about to perish, worldly ways fall into ruin and wicked violence prevails; people are then full of jealousy and flattery.
Consequently, those who study the Buddha's teachings may easily encounter contempt and abuse, leading them to seek out others' faults.

Therefore, those who uphold the precepts and recite the sutras should harbor no jealousy or flattery; rather, they should regulate their conduct according to the times, thereby bringing their karmic activities to rest.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī [down to] should not engage in frivolous discourse regarding the dharmas or contend with others.

Among the fourfold assembly, there are those who seek the three vehicles; one should provide them with advancement according to their capacities and must not suddenly distress them so that they lose the benefit of the wholesome.
From the moment one speaks to such a person, all matters that cause distress should be avoided. One should not engage in inverted discrimination regarding the existence of the dharmas.

There is none. What are called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and contentious strife are all activities of the mental faculty (*manas-karman*); therefore, one should bring them to rest. △ Second, the arousal of practice:
One should conceive the thought of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings... [up to] ...conceive the thought of a Great Teacher toward all Bodhisattvas.

To conceive of them with compassion is to pity their wandering in delusion and to contemplate rescuing them. To conceive of them as one's father is to rely upon their Dharma-transformation and to seek their protection.
To conceive of them as one's teacher is to admire their practice of the Way and to desire to emulate it.
One should always, with a profound mind, pay homage and prostrate to the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions;
for they practice the Way out of compassion for sentient beings and act to benefit others with a profound mind, one should therefore revere them with a profound mind.
He preaches the Dharma with equanimity toward all sentient beings (up to: nor does he speak excessively. His speech is impartial and without favoritism;
his words accord with the Dharma and conform to reason. Although others may hold him in deep affection, he carefully gauges their capacity to receive it;
he values neither losing the person nor losing the truth of the teaching. △ Third, the manifestation of benefit.
When Mañjuśrī had spoken this Dharma, none were able to disturb or confuse him;
this must be the efficacy of being free from obstacles.
One will obtain good companions to study and recite this sutra together, and a great assembly will also come to listen and receive it.
Because they practice this practice, they find joy and gain friends; they are broad-minded and gather a multitude.
Having heard it, they are able to retain it; having retained it, they are able to recite it—up to—and honor, respect, and praise it.

Because this causes the benefits of the Dharma to spread and expand from one to another, even though the Dharma might otherwise be on the verge of extinction, it shall not perish; therefore, one should bring this to fulfillment.
This is the third practice. △ Fourth, the threefold summary verse: first, the verse on ceasing karmic activity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, One should abandon envy, anger, and pride, As well as a deceitful, delusive, and false mind; One should constantly cultivate straightforward conduct."
This is the essential practice of this intention:
do not look down upon others, nor engage in frivolous discourse regarding the Dharma, and do not cause others to doubt or regret by saying, "You shall not attain Buddhahood."
The verse states that one does not vex the fourfold assembly; this means to treat them with contempt. △ Second, the verse on the arousal of practice:
"This son of the Buddha preaches the Dharma" (up to) "preaching the Dharma without hindrance."
Patience is the foundation of the four practices; therefore, it is mentioned repeatedly.

From the passage "Having cultivated compassion for all beings" onwards, the verse corresponds to the section on "generating the thought of great compassion toward all beings. △ Third, the verse reveals the benefits.
The third dharma is thus. The wise should guard it and practice with single-minded ease and joy; they will be revered by immeasurable multitudes.
Upright, gentle, patient, compassionate toward the lowly, and respectful toward superiors—who would not love and revere one who practices this path with such composure?
Sixth: The Practice of Great Compassion. First, the Initial Arising of the Practice.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī [extends his compassion] even to those who are not bodhisattvas, giving rise to great compassion for them.
In the practice of the Mahāyāna, one always begins with right conduct through wisdom and concludes with the perfection of wisdom through compassion.

Therefore, in the four modes of peaceful and happy practice (*caturvidha-śukla-vihāra*), one first relies upon right wisdom and right action, and subsequently gives rise to great compassion to benefit sentient beings. However, some may...
Regarding the arising of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) or great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): loving-kindness is able to bestow happiness, while compassion is able to pity and rescue.

Those among the fourfold assembly who have faith and understanding of the Buddha-dharma are called lay bodhisattvas and monastic bodhisattvas. Those who are icchantikas and lack faith are not called bodhisattvas.

Because they are able to have faith and understanding, one gives rise to great loving-kindness and bestows upon them the joy of the Dharma; because of the icchantikas, one gives rise to great [compassion].
He feels compassion and pities their being lost and confused. △ Second, pitying and rescuing:
One should form this thought (up to) "causing them to abide in this Dharma.
These all constitute pitying their being lost and confused. Teaching the Dharma according to what is appropriate is precisely the method of opening up the three to reveal the one.
"Not hearing, not knowing, and not perceiving" refers to being deluded and self-obstructed. "Not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding" refers to being ignorant and self-degraded.
Nevertheless, although they do not inquire or understand, the Bodhisattva’s great compassion vows to ultimately deliver them.
△ Third, the elimination of faults.
When Mañjuśrī (up to this point) preached this Dharma, there was no fault.
In the fourth practice, wisdom turns toward the Dharma and compassion is mobilized; because the preceding practices are fully prepared, there is no fault. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained.

Because they are constantly protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas—from bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs up to all the Buddhas—they are joyfully submitted to by the seven assemblies due to the greatness of their loving-kindness and compassion. Because their conduct and Dharma are supreme, the devas turn toward them in devotion.
When faced with difficult questions, they will inevitably prevail over their opponents. By receiving this protection, they do not lose right mindfulness, for they are guarded by all the Buddhas.
Therefore, the various devas cannot but provide protection. △ Fifth, praising the Dharma, in four parts. First, praising its rarity to encounter:
"Mañjuśrī... how much more so to obtain sight of it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it."
Such an encounter is difficult to meet. Therefore, to pity those who do not believe or understand is to grieve over their great loss.
△ Second, the parable of the difficulty of attainment, in two parts. First, the parable:
Mañjuśrī... (up to) ...arising various armies and going forth to wage war.

The meaning of this analogy clarifies why this sutra is so difficult to hear and difficult to see: it is because the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) is rampant, there are many adversaries, and it is difficult to believe;

furthermore, it is not spoken falsely. The universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is a metaphor for the nirmāṇakāya Buddha; the various kingdoms are metaphors for the objects of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The petty kings are a metaphor for the Māras, such as the five aggregates. Their failure to obey his commands is a metaphor for ignorance and afflictions that have not yet been subdued.

His failure to exercise his majesty and instead mobilizing troops for a punitive expedition is a metaphor for how the powers of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, along with the dharmas of fearlessness, alone cannot subdue all subtle delusions;
therefore, he establishes the methods of severance and treatment through the three vehicles. This is...
This refers to raising various kinds of troops.

When the king sees those among his army who have performed meritorious service in battle (up to the point where) the king’s various kinsmen are greatly astonished and amazed—this is a metaphor for the multitudes of the Three Vehicles being able to subdue the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*).
According to the depth or shallowness of their merit, they obtain the benefits of all dharmas. Only...

The One Vehicle Dharma has not yet been preached to them. The crest-jewel of a Wheel-Turning King is used to stabilize his precious throne; to bestow it recklessly would cause the king and his subjects to be struck with alarm and wonder.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Supreme Vehicle, involves Buddhas handing it down to one another; to speak of it recklessly would cause the hearts of the multitude to be filled with shock and doubt.
△ Second, the combination.
Mañjuśrī [proceeds] with the Tathāgata and the various generals of the noble ones (ārya) to wage war against them.
Just as a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), manifesting his majesty, causes disobedient minor kings to eventually raise various armies, so too does he act;
here, "the kingdom" refers to the true realm of the Dharma-dhātu, and "the generals of the noble ones" refers to the assembly of those of the Three Vehicles.
Those who have performed meritorious deeds are likewise joyful in heart (extending to) not preaching this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them.
This is like bestowing rewards according to merit but not giving the crest-jewel. The "untainted faculties and powers" (*anāsrava-indriya-bala*) refer to the five faculties and five powers.
The "wealth of all dharmas" refers generally to the methods of utility within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). The "city of nirvāṇa" refers to the Middle Way.
The provisional fruit of cessation. △ Third, the analogy for attaining [the fruit] now, in two parts. First, citing the analogy:
Mañjuśrī... [up to] ...does not give it to others falsely, yet now he gives it.
Regarding the "jewel difficult to believe": if it were bestowed upon one for whom it was not appropriate, they would be greatly astonished and amazed. △ Second, the application of the analogy:
"The Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "that which was previously unsaid is now being spoken."
*Māra* is here translated as "the Killer. This refers to one who can bring about suffering and difficulty, killing the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).

The *kleśamāra* (affliction-māra) is the cause of birth and death; the *skandhamāra* (aggregate-māra) and *mṛtyumāra* (death-māra) are the fruits of birth and death. Therefore, to extinguish and destroy them is precisely to transcend the triple world.
Having many enemies means that the various māras have not yet been subdued; being difficult to inspire with faith means that the capacities of sentient beings have not yet matured. △ Four.
This reveals two aspects of the most supreme. First, the text reiterates [the previous point]:
"Mañjuśrī... having long protected the bright jewel, he now bestows it upon him.
This first teaching is like a single jewel atop one's head; the final bestowal is like the great merit long awaited. △
Second, the conclusion:
"Mañjuśrī... it is only from this day forward that I shall expound it for you all.
It has been kept secret like a treasure within a topknot; it is most supreme, like [a jewel] upon a king’s crown. For more than forty years, amidst birth and death..."
For a long night he maintains this, awaiting the opportune moment; therefore it is said, "guarding through the long night. △ Sixth, the sixfold verse summary.
First, the verse on the basis of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
One must constantly practice patience and have compassion for all beings; only then can one expound the sutras praised by the Buddha.

In this evil age, preaching the sutras invites much resentment and is difficult to believe; therefore, one should take patience and compassion as the foundation. △ Second, the verse on the arousal of compassion.
In the future age of the final dharma (until: one should give rise to compassion).
△ Third, the verse on compassionate rescue:
These people have not heard (until: may they be established therein).
△ Section Three: Praising the Dharma in Four Verses. First, the analogy for its difficulty to obtain:
For example, when a powerful person (up to) bestows bright pearls upon all, everyone rejoices at the gift;
yet the crest-jewel alone is difficult to grant, being reserved for great merit. △ Second, the verse on the application to the Dharma.
The Tathāgata is also like this... [omitted] ...and gives him a bright pearl.
△ Third, the verse on the most supreme:
This sutra is the most honored... [omitted] ...is spoken for you.
△ Five verses concluding the response.
From "After my parinirvāṇa" up to "these four dharmas," this concludes the answer to the question of how one can preach this sutra. △ Six: Attaining the fruit through practice, in three parts.
First, it removes obstacles to the fruits of happiness;
because one can practice the four modes of conduct, reading and upholding this sutra makes it easy to attain superior fruits.
One who reads this sutra [is like] the shining of the sun.

That one is always free from sorrow and affliction, with a complexion that is fresh and bright, signifies the transformation of the karmic obstacle (*karmāvaraṇa*) and the extinction of misfortunes and distress in the present life.
That one is not born into poverty, low status, or ugliness signifies the transformation of the obstacle of action (*karmāvaraṇa*) and the extinction of evil karma leading to future births.

That sentient beings look toward one with joy and longing, and weapons or poison do not take effect, signifies the transformation of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the extinction of coarse retributions in future lives. This is the radiance of wisdom.
Like the sun’s illumination, it turns away the veil of ignorance and extinguishes the darkness of delusion regarding the three periods of time.
"Delightful and yearned-for service" means one constantly enjoys sublime bliss; "the mouth is closed" means there is no way for evil speech to issue forth.
"Like the lion king" means that obstacles and fears are forever departed, and one wanders with ease and sovereignty. △ Second, first seeing the sublime fruit, in two parts. First, the heading.

If, even in dreams, one sees only auspicious matters, it is because the person who upholds this sutra has perfected the merit of the four practices and shall surely attain the sublime fruit; thus, the outcome is already determined within the realm of the yet-unmanifested.
Therefore, he first saw this in a dream. Because his practice was pure and his obstacles were cleansed, there were no longer any distracting thoughts;
he saw only wondrous matters. (The following section cites these wondrous matters. △ Second, the explanation has four parts. First, seeing the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
He beholds all Tathāgatas (up to) expounding the various dharmas.
Because his practice is pure and his mind is undefiled by discursive thoughts, he does not depart from the practice of the Dharma regarding the objects of self and others;
thus, having seen the Buddhas preaching the Dharma, he himself likewise acts accordingly. △ Second, receiving the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment.
The Buddha [taught] for the fourfold assembly (up to) them listening to the Dharma with palms joined.
△ Third, cultivating and realizing the true mark.
Furthermore, seeing one’s own body (up to) seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions.
"The bodies of all Buddhas are golden, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings. Hearing the Dharma and explaining it for others—such are the auspicious dreams one constantly has.
This reiterates the matter of seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions, thereby concluding the preceding section and initiating the subsequent one. △ Fourth, the Perfect Attainment of the Buddha Way.

Furthermore, the dream of becoming a king [up to] "like a lamp extinguished when the smoke has ended" represents the sequence of practices from beginning to end for attaining Buddhahood through cultivation. All such visions are preliminary indications that one will attain the fruit through practice.
When these signs appear before one, one shall surely realize this fruit. However, the reason all of these are explained by means of dreams is to cause [the practitioner] to...
The practitioner contemplates that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; they arise solely from causes and conditions and from inversion.
Although one personally sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and even attains the path of perfect Buddhahood, all are like dream-events, ultimately unobtainable.
There is neither permanence nor arising and ceasing. Constantly contemplate these marks; thereafter, you shall attain true peaceful and blissful practice in all places.
△ Third, the conclusion that clarifies the preceding text.
If, in a future evil age, one should preach this foremost Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the merits mentioned above.
*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Five, Part One.
*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Scroll Five, Part Two.
Commentary by the Bhikṣu Jiehuan of Kaiyuan Lian Temple in Wunling.
Chapter Fifteen: The Emergence from the Earth. △ Part Four:
Manifesting Traces and Exhorting to Uphold. Section One: Briefly Stating the Section Titles.
This reveals the traces of those transformed by the power of the wisdom of the Sublime Dharma.

In the lower realm of Sahā, there are bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers who have cultivated the Buddha’s wisdom for incalculable eons; all of them were transformed by Śākyamuni Buddha.
Because they always delight in quiet places and practice with diligent vigor, they do not abide among humans or devas, but dwell in the air below the lower direction to manifest [this teaching].

They always delight in profound wisdom that is free from all obstructions. Now, in order to manifest these wondrous traces and provide a model for posterity, and furthermore to initiate the secret teaching on the lifespan, they emerge from the earth, and thus this chapter is named accordingly.
Part Two: Exegesis of the Text according to the Outline, in three sections.
First, the introduction of the occasion; second, the request from other lands to uphold [the teaching]. First, the request from other lands to uphold [the teaching]:
At that time, [beings] from other lands... (up to) shall extensively expound this in this land.
This assembly of the Dharma-gathering wishes to come here from other lands to uphold this sutra. △ Second, the Tathāgata does not permit it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to the point where he said):

"As for the Buddha’s halting those who would protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound this sutra, it was not out of refusal or opposition; rather, it was intended to manifest his traces and manifest the Dharma.

To 'manifest his traces' means to reveal the Buddha’s transformations and demonstrate the manner of his arrival. To 'manifest the Dharma' means that this [Dharma] is inherently perfect and complete, requiring nothing external."

△ Second, the actual manifestation of the traces has six parts. First, the manifestation of the majestic deportment of the arrival, which has two sub-sections. First, the majestic deportment of the arrival:
When the Buddha had spoken these words... [they] simultaneously surged forth.
With profound wisdom manifest before them, they are unimpeded throughout the great trichiliocosm;
the bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, and they abide in the space of this world-system,
dwelling in the space beneath this Sahā world-system, thereby demonstrating that their constant joy and profound wisdom are without obstruction.

It is an obstruction. These bodhisattvas, having heard the sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, have come up from below. This is because he [the Buddha] speaks with his true essence, while they hear with their minds. As Mañjuśrī said: "Hearing with the mind penetrates the ten directions. (2) 1. Translation of the provided text: "It is an obstruction. These bodhisattvas, having heard the sounds spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, have come up from below.

This is because he [the Buddha] speaks with his true essence, while they hear with their minds. As Mañjuśrī said: 'Hearing with the mind penetrates the ten directions. 2. Translation of the structural heading: "Two. (This indicates the second section.)
The third section, "Manifesting the Sublime," first presents a mutual relationship between the one and the many:
from each individual bodhisattva down to even a ten-millionth part of a hundred-billionth of a *nayuta*.
This refers to the process by which the number of grains of sand, originally vast, is reduced to a minimum.
How much more so for those with retinues of thousands, tens of millions, billions, or nayutas; (down to) those with three, two, or one disciple.
This indicates that the number of attendants decreases from many to few.
How much more so for those who dwell alone and delight in the practice of seclusion—(down to) those whose merit cannot be known even by calculation or analogy.
This refers to how the singular, starting from few, becomes many. A verse says: "The solitary one, without retinue, its number exceeds the above.
At first glance, the sixty thousand sands of the Ganges seem more numerous than the solitary ones; yet upon close examination, the number of solitary ones far exceeds that of the sands.
Thus, the single self is not few, and the multitude of sands is not many. This is the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
The essence is free from all quantity; the limitations of "many" or "few" are merely established by the deluded minds of ordinary people.
This is why these multitudes arrive in such a manner—to dispel emotional attachments and manifest the subtle mystery. △ Second, the mutual manifestation of extension and contraction.
After these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, it appeared to the great assembly as though only half a day had passed.
This is the dharma-gate of the sages’ supernatural wisdom and skillful means: they can extend a single day to become an eon, and they can condense an eon to become a single day.
For while the Way undergoes no change or transition, sentient beings perceive duration and brevity; it is just like a person in a dream.
When a single moment is experienced as a dream spanning many years, it is evident that the perception of duration has no fixed nature from the outset.
Therefore, when the Sage manifests appearances according to the capacities of beings, he may display either extension or brevity, yet fundamentally there is neither extension nor brevity.

When it is said that Bodhisattvas praise the Buddha for kalpas, this is merely displaying extension within brevity; furthermore, when he causes the great assembly to perceive it as being like half a day, this is displaying brevity within extension.

To shorten [the time]. The reason for this is that one intends to manifest and proclaim the power of the Buddhas' wisdom and sovereign spiritual penetrations, so that the sentiments of longing for extension or contraction may be forgotten, and the true reality (dharmatā) may be deeply realized. As the *Avataṃsaka* says:
In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.

Thus understanding the events of the three periods of time, one transcends all skillful means and accomplishes the ten powers. Indeed, being able to universally contemplate in a single thought-moment that there is no going, coming, or abiding—
Thus, one understands that both this extension and contraction are merely skillful means. △ Third, the mutual interpenetration of the unobstructed and the obstructed.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, through the spiritual power of the Buddha, [extended] up to the lands and the void of space.

That the fourfold assembly, whose physical eyes are obstructed and lack supernatural penetration, is nevertheless able to see immeasurable lands, is due to the power of the Buddha’s supernormal faculties.
Indeed, when the one and the many are presented interchangeably, when long and short durations of time appear interchangeably,
and when seeing and obstruction are employed interchangeably, it is to clarify that the measure of things is infinite, time has no fixed divisions, and impermanence serves as a wake-up call.
Ordinary sentiment causes one to abandon inverted minds and limited views, relying instead on unimpeded wisdom for perfect, harmonious, and subtle penetration.
By means of this, one advances toward and accords with the secret teaching on the lifespan, thereby attaining entry into the Buddha’s wisdom and achieving the Buddha-body.
Therefore, although the matters and dharmas in this chapter serve to manifest traces and encourage upholding, they also serve to introduce the teaching on the lifespan. △ Two.
The leaders of the assembly inquired after his well-being.
Among that multitude of bodhisattvas were four guides, who spoke these verses:
"Is the World-Honored One at ease? (Up to: Has he experienced any fatigue?"
The question concerns the matter of dwelling in the endurance of patience (*kṣānti*) while sharing the sufferings of the people. △ Third, the Honored One’s Narrative Address:
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... [until] entered the Buddha-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*).
The phrase "receiving transformation life after life" specifically clarifies those transformed by the Original Gate concerning the Lifespan.

The phrase "also having planted roots of goodness in the past" concurrently clarifies those transformed within the Assembly of the Supreme Wisdom; because their karmic conditions for transformation were profound, upon first seeing and first hearing [the teaching], they all immediately believed and accepted it.
△ Fourth, rejoicing upon hearing the wind [of the teaching].
At that time, the great bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent... (up to) we rejoice accordingly.
Then the World-Honored One praised them... (up to) for having given rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
△ Section Two: Questions from the Assembly at Five Times. First, the questions from this assembly, which has three parts. First, the indication of the doubt:
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... (up to) ...inquired after the Tathāgata’s well-being.

Maitreya’s path is identical to the wisdom of the Great Awakened One, such that there is nothing it does not illuminate. He manifests doubt as one who is yet to attain the position of Successor (Upapadya) merely to benefit those with karmic potential in the future.
Therefore, the subsequent verse says: "I pray that the Buddha will expound for the sake of the future, so that they may achieve understanding.
II. The Request for Instruction has two parts. First, the general inquiry.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) asked in verse:
"Immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis (up to) by what causes and conditions have they gathered?"
A general inquiry as to whence they come and how they arise. △ Second, a detailed inquiry in two parts. First, the inquiry as to whence they come:
"With their massive bodies and great supernormal powers... from where do they come?"
Because his deportment was so preeminent and his intellectual power so extraordinary, he moved the assembly and inspired their inquiries.
When they asked about his arrival and his majestic presence, each of those bodhisattvas was but one part in ten million.
This verse describes the number *śata-sahasra* (hundred-thousand), which decreases from many to few,
ranging from ten million (*koṭi*) and *nayuta*, down to three, two, and one.
This verse describes the number *ayuta* (ten thousand), which likewise decreases from many to few.
Those who were alone without retinues and who delighted in dwelling in solitude all came to where the Buddha was; their number increased even further than before.
This verse shows that those who were few in number as individuals became many.

Thus, when this great assembly [from] "practicing which Buddha-way" saw that there were many doubts, they realized these beings had not been transformed by only one Buddha in a single lifetime; therefore, they questioned him in detail.
Thus, from "these various bodhisattvas" up to "the names of their lands," the question concludes by asking whence they have come.
△ Second, the question asks whence they have gathered:
"I constantly travel through various lands... I pray that you will explain the causes and conditions thereof."
△ 3. Request for Resolution.
"Now, in this great assembly... [omitted] ...I only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude.
△ 2. Questions from the Other Assembly.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Sixteen: The Tathāgata’s Lifespan. △ Part Five:
Revealing the Origin and Encouraging Upholding. This has two sections. First, a brief explanation of the chapter title.

In the preceding chapter, the manifestation [of the Buddha] was revealed; yet those who are deluded remain stuck on the traces and fail to realize the origin. Consequently, they harbor doubts regarding the duration [of the Buddha's life] and perceive the arising and ceasing of phenomena. Desiring...

It is difficult to accord with the reality of the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). Therefore, this [text] reveals the fundamental [nature] to resolve doubts and obstructions, so that one may know that the Tathāgata is fundamentally without birth or extinction;
his manifestation at Gayā was specifically for the sake of those with the capacity [for awakening], and the life-span he received accords with the nature of reality and is immeasurable.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata. The text states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are;
there is no birth-and-death from which to emerge, nor is there remaining in the world or entering parinirvāṇa. Later it says:

"There are bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this teaching of the lifespan, are able to believe and accept it, vowing to live long lives in the future to deliver sentient beings until they sit at the site of enlightenment."

The explanation of lifespan is likewise so. This clarifies that the fundamental and the phenomenal are of one suchness, and that the eternal nature of worldly phenomena is the lifespan that accords with the Dharma-nature;
all people possess this. If one can maintain right faith and accept it accordingly, one will not prematurely cut short one's life through the activities of a mind subject to birth and extinction.

Thus, the characteristics of the three realms can be known as they truly are. Consequently, one is able to manifest the span of one's lifespan to remain ever-present, and display birth and extinction to transform beings through successive generations.
One’s power of wisdom and spiritual efficacy become equal to those of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said: "Revealing the Fundamental and Encouraging its Upholding."
△ Second, the correct explanation according to the text, in three parts. First, the introduction to the exposition, in two parts. First, addressing the assembly to inspire faith:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas... [omitted] ...you should all believe and understand the Tathāgata’s words of truth.
Because the fundamental nature of the lifespan is profound and difficult to believe, he spoke of it again and again. What is true in the mind is called "sincerity" (cheng);
what is appropriate in speech is called "truth" (di). △ Second, deep faith and earnest entreaty.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattvas, headed by Maitreya... (down to) "...we shall faithfully accept the Buddha’s words.
△ Second, the actual manifestation of the original [teaching] has three parts. First, the actual exposition of the lifespan has three parts. First, the actual exposition.

At that time, the World-Honored One—[up to] by the power of the Tathāgata’s secret supernormal powers—manifests extinction or non-extinction according to what is appropriate and what is not appropriate. Gods and humans cannot fathom this; it is called the power of secret spiritual efficacy.
Throughout all worlds, including devas and humans, for immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one perceives only its traces;
yet its fundamental reality is truly immeasurable. △ Second, clarification by means of an analogy.
For example, suppose there were five hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta-asaṃkhyeya* [worlds]—could anyone know their number?
This is all like the analogy of surpassing the dust and ink of wisdom.
From Maitreya Bodhisattva and others, up to hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayuta-asamkhyeya* kalpas, this clearly demonstrates that the lifespan of the Buddha is immeasurable.
The lifespans of all Buddhas are entirely immeasurable; the lifespans of sentient beings are likewise so.
Yet, because they are deluded regarding true wisdom, they falsely pursue birth and death. It is as if one has fallen into hell... [until]... 至 (zhì).
"Countless kalpas"—is this not indeed "Immeasurable Life"? If one does not fall into delusion, then one is no different from a Buddha.
△ Third, revealing constancy:
From that time until now... leading and benefiting sentient beings.
From that time onward—meaning from the attainment of Buddhahood throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust—it is said that he has always been present here and yet also in other places.
Thus, it is not only his physical form that is eternally abiding, but it is also revealed that the land itself is eternally abiding.

One should know that the Sahā world and its billions of lands are none other than pure lands; they are one and the same Dharma-realm, never subject to destruction. As for those instances where there appears to be destruction...

That their cessation is entirely due to individual karma and deluded vision. △ Second, resolving doubts to reveal the fundamental reality, in three parts. First, questioning the ancient interpretation to resolve doubts.
Second, first, questioning the entry into extinction as recorded in the *Śrāmaṇera-phala-sūtra*.
"O sons of good family... [up to] ...in this way, all these are distinguished through skillful means (*upāya*).

Since it is said that he has long attained Buddhahood and constantly remains to benefit sentient beings, yet in the interim he himself speaks of matters such as receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the Dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, which makes him appear as if his traces were recent; furthermore, he now declares that he shall enter *nirvāṇa*."
The doubt that he still exists is merely an expedient teaching given according to the capacities of beings. △ Second, the inquiry into his various manifestations according to circumstances:
"O sons of good family... [up to] ...able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy."

The various faculties such as faith refer to the faculty of faith, the faculty of wisdom, and so forth. Observing those with sharp faculties, he immediately manifests a long life to preach the Great Dharma;

There are differences in age, and there are various ways of preaching the Dharma; all of these serve to guide beings according to their capacities and inclinations, thereby awakening their virtuous minds.
△ Second, the interrogation of the present and the resolution of doubts, in two parts. First, the interrogation regarding the fundamental and the manifested.

"Good sons (up to) all that has been spoken is true and not false.

To speak of seeing is to see it in words; to demonstrate seeing is to see it in practice."
Why is this so? (Up to: "The Buddha-works performed have never for a moment been abandoned.

This explains the principle above: that while there is no lack of reality, various differences and similarities are spoken of. Within the myriad phenomena of the triple world, there is no room for the mind to speculate.
From the deluded perspective of sentient beings, they appear as various and chaotic; from the true perspective of the Tathāgata, all things are [one].
In true stillness, there is neither birth-and-death nor even extinction; one does not perceive through the marks of arising and ceasing.
One who does not perceive the triple world as the triple world does not perceive through the marks of coming and going.
Since one clearly perceives without obstruction, there should be no divergent teachings; it is simply because the desires, natures, practices, and thoughts of sentient beings are manifold.
Because they are identical, the traces of teaching and transformation shown are likewise diverse.
"The Buddha-works performed" refers to these various manifestations of difference. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification.
"In this way, since my attainment of Buddhahood has been for an exceedingly long time... [until] it abides eternally and is never extinguished.

This clarifies that the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas for benefiting sentient beings are all like this. △ Third, the metaphorical clarification of the intent of skillful means, in eight parts.
First, the basis for establishing the analogy.
For example, it is like a skilled physician who is wise and discerning—whether there be ten, twenty, or even a hundred such individuals.
The Buddha is like the physician; his teaching is like the medical formula; and the underlying principle is like the excellent medicine.

The various dispositions, desires, conducts, and conceptualizations are what are called "many diseases. The Buddha is able to employ numerous causes and analogies to dispense the appropriate medicine according to what is suitable for each.
He eliminates them; this is called the skillful treatment of a good physician. The children of the burning house are spoken of in relation to the Three Vehicles;

The Metaphor of Turning Away from Enlightenment and Joining with Dust.
Because of certain affairs, he traveled far to another country; when the medicine took effect, he became delirious and rolled upon the ground.

Drinking other people's poisonous drugs is a metaphor for following false teachings; rolling upon the ground is a metaphor for wandering through the various realms of existence.

As for this innate goodness (*liangxin*): even if those with shallow capacity have not yet lost it, they are nonetheless obstructed by evil habits and are unable to personally realize the essence of awakening;
hence it is said that they "see from afar. When one prays for longevity, it is the hope that one will not meet an untimely death through violent or perverse causes.

Administering medicine to eliminate suffering means causing one to sever delusions and realize the Truth. Following the methods of the Buddhas' governance, one seeks the medicinal remedies for severing and treating [afflictions] employed by the sages and worthies.

It fully manifests the true color of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), displays the five fragrances of precepts and meditative concentration (*śīla-samādhi*), and encompasses all five flavors of milk and curd;

Its color, flavor, and fragrance are exquisite, and thus it lacks the toxicity of dizziness or vertigo. The Sage takes the illness of others as his own illness and the sorrow of others as his own sorrow.

This consists of two parts. First, the verse on the immeasurable lifespan.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed is immeasurable—hundreds of thousands of millions, billions, and asaṃkhyeyas."

△ Second, the verse on the eternal abiding of the true and transformation bodies, constantly preaching the Dharma to transform and teach countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way; thus it has been for immeasurable kalpas.
△ Second, five verses clarify the provisional [teaching] that reveals the fundamental [reality]. First, a verse on the skillful means of proclaiming extinction:

This is a general statement of skillful means (*upāya*). Below follows a detailed exposition of the intent behind those means.
"I always abide here" (extending to) "manifesting both extinction and non-extinction":

although they are nearby, they do not see me; this is for the purpose of subduing arrogance and self-indulgence, and to cause them to give rise to longing and yearning, thereby inducing weariness with [samsaric] existence.

"Extinction. It should be understood that it is simply because [the Buddha] is not heard from there that he is said to have "extinguished.

"I see all sentient beings... (until) I then emerge to preach the Dharma for them.

Such is his supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he has constantly resided on Vulture Peak Mountain (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) and at various other dwelling places.
△ Third, the verse on existing while undergoing destruction:
When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa—[and even] see the Buddha and the great assembly being consumed by a great fire—their own land remains peaceful and secure.
What kind of land is this? It is the Land of True Reward (Sukhāvatī), also called the Land of Nature (Dharmatā-bhūmi).

This refers to the lands of retribution and transformation; because they manifest based on deluded karma, they possess formation and destruction.

Because they manifest based on the true retribution, they lack formation and destruction. The characteristics of such formation and destruction are what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* calls "deluded vision resulting from individual karma."

It is like the illusory vision of lamp-shadows seen by those with cataracts; though those without the cataracts likewise do not see them, sentient beings perceive the conflagration while I remain eternally at peace.
Seeking it from within myself, I find that what is called the "nature-land" is not separate from my own nature, and what is called "Vulture Peak" is not separate from my own spiritual essence.
Being neither form nor vessel, even the kalpa-fire cannot burn it.
Pervading from antiquity to the present, it has always existed and is never extinguished.

One who attains this wondrous principle will find that the lifespan, the pure land, and all such matters are fully present within oneself, and thus will no longer harbor doubts regarding the Buddha. △ Fourth, a verse on responding to conditions through transformation.

I am also the Father of the World... [down to] falling into the evil realms.
Suffering and affliction are the entanglements of false karma; perversion is the false view of birth and death.

Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful expedients. (This concludes the fifth section, summarizing the preceding meaning.)

Every time he formed this thought—“By what means may I cause sentient beings to enter unsurpassed wisdom and swiftly achieve the Buddha-body”—he constantly contemplated skillful means to guide the various capacities of beings.

all of this was because he desired them to achieve success swiftly.

Gaining Benefit from Hearing the Dharma (in two sections). First, a brief summary of the chapter title.

It is extolled according to the faculties [of the listeners]. Therefore, it is called "Discriminating Merit. The text consists of five parts. II. Following the topical outline, there are five sections with detailed explanations.
First, the introduction by the scribe (the *sūtrakāra*).
At that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha’s discourse on the number of kalpas of his lifespan, which brought them great benefit.
The great benefit they obtained is as described below. Part Two: The Tathāgata’s Differentiation has three sections; first, the merit of entering the Path.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] "one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Because one hears of the lifespan [of the Buddha], one realizes there is neither arising nor ceasing. Through the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, one can perfect the practice.
Yet, because there is no realization and no patience, it is called the "patience of dharmas" (*dharma-kṣānti*). "Patience" (*kṣānti*) is the name for the perfection of practice.
Furthermore, there are a thousandfold more bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who attain the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining.
Upon hearing it once, they awaken to a thousand [teachings] and attain great total retention (*dhāraṇī*). All other dhāraṇīs emerge from this; therefore, it is called a "door.
It is like how all things flow forth from the *dhāraṇī*-door of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vajramaṇḍala*).
Furthermore, there were bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in another world-system who had attained the unimpeded eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
Having realized the Way for themselves, they encountered the source of truth at every turn; thus, they were able to speak with joyful and unimpeded eloquence.

This is the general designation for the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*): first, dharma; second, meaning (*artha*); third, terminology (*nirukti*); and fourth, joyful speech (*pratibhāna*).
Furthermore, there is another world [system]... where one attains the immeasurable *vartanī-dhāraṇī* of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Regarding all phenomena, one returns to the root and source; through skillful means, one benefits sentient beings with mastery over both the contrary and the compliant.
This is called the *vartanī-dhāraṇī* of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
Furthermore, throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world system, [they] are able to turn the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Having entered the stage of certainty, they preach the true Dharma, far surpassing the two vehicles and never again falling back.

Furthermore, there are two thousand [bodhisattvas] from the central lands (up to) those who are able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma—namely, the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle in which words and signs are quiescent and one.

From the *Śrutadhāraṇī* up to this point, these are all the virtues of bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*). The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "A bodhisattva who has attained the *dhāraṇī*s is in the fifth stage."
△ Second, the merit of attaining the fruit.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm [who attain] *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This refers to the distance of attaining the fruit according to their respective faculties. Regarding "eight births" and so forth: because they have transcended into the noble stage (*ārya-bhūmi*), it is as follows...

This is the birth into the family of the Buddha; it is not a birth characterized by the emergence and submergence within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Regarding the initial mention of "eight births," this refers to the transcendence into the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).

There are eight [stages] leading to the attainment of the rank of *miao-jue* (wonderful enlightenment); therefore, it is said that "each of the remaining [stages] has eight births until one attains the Way of the Buddha.
Next, regarding the mention of "four births," this refers to the transcendence into the eighth stage. There are [stages] leading to the attainment of the rank of *miao-jue*.

Fourth: those who will attain birth three times or twice—referring to the ninth and tenth stages—and those who will attain birth once, shall directly enter the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
They remain only one interval away from reaching Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bodhi*). Therefore, it is said: "With one remaining birth, one shall become omniscient.
The lifespan of the Tathāgata is the indestructible true mark (*dharmatā*) of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). To awaken to this true mark is to possess complete and unobstructed penetration.

Therefore, upon hearing this teaching, the assembly each attained realization according to their respective faculties. △ Third, the merit of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*):
Furthermore, sentient beings numbering as many as the atoms in eight worlds [generated] the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Hearing the reality of the fruition and principle gives rise to the mind of the true cause. First, the Bodhisattvas who have entered the Path and attained the fruit are cited;

subsequently, the sentient beings who give rise to the mind through sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) are cited; this is the proper sequence of events. Yet, the old [commentaries] place this passage in the initial listing.

Furthermore, their extensive correlation with the stages of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) contradicts the internal logic of the text. Therefore, it is unnecessary to correlate them here.
Question: The Dharma of the lifespan is one and the same; the nature of beings across ancient and modern times is identical.

In the past, sentient beings attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) upon hearing it but once, and Bodhisattvas, through profound penetration, attained the Way of the Buddha. Yet, compared to the sands of the Ganges, how much has been lost today? Answer:
Those who hear [the Dharma] today, even when counted by the thousands of worlds (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), are truly like the sands. The fruit [of their practice] is likewise profound.
Had they attained [realization], they would have obtained patience and become Buddhas, no less than those of old; it was simply that they were unable to have deep faith and profound penetration.
△ Third, the manifestation aided by wondrous omens:
When the Buddha spoke these words regarding the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (up to the point where they) sang immeasurable verses in praise of all the Buddhas.
All these auspicious signs rained down from the sky, pervading the nine directions, thereby assisting in manifesting the benefits of the Dharma regarding the span of his life.
Just as space is boundless and inconceivable, so too is this. Thus Maitreya praised him, saying: "The World-Honored One has preached the inconceivable Dharma of the span of his life;
its manifold benefits are as boundless as empty space. As for the mention of the "nine directions": [it refers to the eight cardinal points and the zenith].
Except for the site of the non-Dharmic assembly below, the Bodhisattva holds the banner as high as the Brahma Heaven, declaring that it fills the void to offer worship and praise.

there is no such possibility, because they have already fulfilled the primary cause; they advance and do not retreat. △ Second, the five verses on the merit of faith in the summary verse:

A profound mind means firm resolve; purity means clear wisdom; uprightness means freedom from hypocrisy; extensive learning means broad knowledge;
