The intent of this teaching on the lifespan lies in severing views of arising and ceasing to reveal the essence of true permanence. If one can understand this clearly, then—
Because one gives rise to unsurpassed wisdom equal to that of the Tathāgata, its merit is immeasurable. △ Third, the benefit of extensive upholding:
How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra, or teaches others to hear it—up to the point where it can give rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Upon hearing of the Buddha’s lifespan, one severs the views of arising and ceasing and reveals the true, eternal essence; this merely enables the arousal of superior wisdom.

By extensively hearing this sutra, however, one becomes endowed with the four types of knowledge and vision, exhausting the path of the One Vehicle, and is thus able to give rise to the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Yet, among those in the world who hear and uphold [the teachings], few take them to heart. Who, then, is truly able to give rise to superior wisdom and produce the seeds of knowledge?
Such a person is like one who encounters a royal feast yet does not eat, or who finds a jewel within their garment yet falls asleep in intoxication. How lamentable!
△ Fourth, the characteristics of profound faith and understanding.
Ajita, [the Buddha] sat surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas and preached the Dharma.
When the views of arising and ceasing are exhausted, the mark of true permanence becomes manifest before one's very eyes.

Furthermore, seeing this Sahā world—[extending] until [the description of its features]—and with the entire assembly of bodhisattvas dwelling within it, one forgets the distinction between the defiled and the pure.
Thus, every step taken is within a realm of supreme excellence.
If there are those who can contemplate in this way, it should be known that this is the mark of profound faith and understanding.
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of body and land is fundamentally one and the same; birth and death, defilement and purity, all arise from conceptual views.

Therefore, when views are exhausted and conceptualizations forgotten, the marks of true permanence and the sublime realm manifest before one at every point. This is not possible without profound faith and understanding.
This secret teaching regarding the lifespan must not be disclosed prematurely. △ Fifth, the extensive manifestation of the sublime merit, in five parts.

First, as if personally wearing the Buddha upon one’s head: Furthermore, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa... (until) such a person shall be considered as wearing the Tathāgata upon their crown.

hence it is said that this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding. If one reads and maintains it with a focused mind, the merit exceeds even that;
hence it is said that such a person "bears the Tathāgata upon their crown. To say they "bear him upon their crown" means they have attained the entirety of this teaching.
And there is nothing superior to this. △ Second, making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha:

This is because among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. The preceding section revealed the merit of sympathetic joy; this next section reveals the merit of copying and upholding [the sutra].
"Ajita... by means of this, you offer it directly before me and the assembly of bhikṣus."
There are thirty-two halls to accommodate the Sangha from the four quarters, in accordance with the Eightfold Noble Path.

It was previously stated that practicing the five *pāramitās* does not equal even a single moment of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*). It was also said that there is no need to further give rise to [them].
Stupas and monasteries do not abolish practice; they merely set aside phenomena to manifest principle, so as to lead people toward profound realization without being hindered by outward traces.
If one has already attained profound realization of the principle, yet does not cultivate practice, it is like a boat without oars—how could it ever reach the other shore?
Therefore, when principle and practice support one another, only then is one’s virtue supreme. The empty talk of the world [is otherwise].
If names and principles are thus abandoned while practice and reality are pursued, and if one does not cultivate the various *pāramitās* nor adopt even a single virtue, how can one remain at peace?
To become a dull-witted blockhead or a *cāṇḍāla*—one should reflect upon this three times. △ Fourth, the conclusion that clarifies the preceding characteristics.

For those of sharp faculties and wisdom, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, there shall not be a single unpleasant feature.

Part Two: The Merit of Perfect Retention. First: Explaining the Intent and Dividing the Sections.
In the preceding chapter, one who rejoices and briefly upholds [the Dharma] attains but one of the five qualities of a Dharma teacher;
since they have not yet been able to listen and read with single-minded devotion or practice according to the teaching, their merit is not yet perfected.

Although they have acquired the faculties and wisdom in full, they have not yet reached the retribution of the six thousand [merits]; thus, their virtue is not yet perfected. In this chapter, the practitioner is fully endowed with these five qualities. Six...
Possessing a thousand virtues in perfection, he is worthy of being a model; therefore, this chapter is titled "The Dharma Master.

While the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta) manifested the perfect prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) by relying on the person who upholds the sutra, this "Chapter on the Dharma Master" manifests the perfect merit by relying on the person who upholds the sutra.
Though the names are identical, their meanings differ; thus, the word "merit" (*guṇa*) is added here to distinguish it. △ Second.
The explanation of the text according to its sections has two parts. First, the general introduction:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Constant Diligence... (up to)... causing all to be purified.
One who upholds the Lotus Sūtra opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are none other than true awakening (*tathatā*).

One realizes all real marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); thus, form, sound, odor, taste, and touch are none other than the true Dharma. When true awakening confronts the true Dharma, the myriad phenomena are thoroughly illuminated and the great trichiliocosm is viewed as one.
Therefore, when the merit of perfect upholding is accomplished, one immediately attains the purification of the six sense faculties.
Virtue. Unless one possesses a mind that is pure and undistracted, and advances on the Path without weariness, it is not easy to attain this.

Therefore, it was addressed to the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence. As for the number being twelve hundred and eight: the world of sentient beings is established upon the vessel-world (the physical environment).
Because the boundaries are woven from delusion, there are the four directions; because bodily forms undergo constant flux, there are the three periods of time.
Consider that the world and the realm interpenetrate one another; the three periods of time and the four directions revolve to form twelve.

Based on this number twelve, they flow and transform through three cycles to become one thousand two hundred. Through the perfection of their circular maintenance, each faculty fully realizes its function.

Thus, there are twelve hundred merits. However, within these, distinctions of superiority and inferiority are established: the eye perceives what is in front and at its sides but does not reach what is behind;
the breath entering and exiting through the nose lacks the meeting point in the middle; and the body can perceive contact when joined but is unaware of it when separated.
In each case, one-third is lacking; therefore, they possess only eight hundred merits. This is merely a provisional calculation based on worldly treatises.
This measurement merely serves to manifest the general outline of its wondrous function.

If one allows the constant eye to perceive forms and thereby open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and the constant ear to hear sounds and thereby attain their true nature, then the myriad sensory objects will no longer create barriers, and the ten directions will be vast and clear.
When the myriad phenomena cannot escape the perfect illumination of the great chiliocosm, then the achievement of the one thousand two hundred and eighty [calamities] is not worth discussing.
As the sutra says: "The eyes born of one's parents see the entirety of the three thousandfold world.

How could there then be a deficiency of three parts or the inferiority of eight hundred? Thus, we know that this essence is fundamentally beyond measure and number. △ Second, the specific explanation has six parts.
First, regarding the eye-faculty, there are two parts. First is the introductory statement:
"These sons and daughters of good family (up to) see all and know all.
That which is born of one's parents—that which every person inherently possesses—is the pure fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which is not obstructed by the various sensory objects.
When the various dusts do not create separation, correct wisdom manifests before one; thus, all forms and images within and without the great trichiliocosm are seen and known.
This is what is meant by: "When the eye responds, it is like a thousand suns such that the ten thousand phenomena cannot escape their shadows and essences.
Question: The principle is indeed so; but as for the matter, how is it? Answer: The six sense organs are fundamentally pure, perfect, and luminous. Their original nature...
The direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of merit is thus; it simply accords with what has been realized.
Now, a Lesser Arhat sees a small chiliocosm, a Great Arhat sees a great trichiliocosm, a Pratyekabuddha sees a hundred Buddha-worlds, and a Bodhisattva sees a hundred thousand Buddha-worlds.
The Tathāgata perceives even the lands within a minute speck of dust; it is not merely a matter of the fruit-body alone.

Aniruddha, without departing from his physical body born of his parents, was able to contemplate the great trichiliocosm as if it were within the palm of his hand, such that he could see nothing therein that was not visible.

This is because when the dust of delusion is eliminated and awareness is purified, one reaches the ultimate unity of the profound stillness. How could it be that the principle is thus while the phenomenon is otherwise?

Ah! The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If one can go against the current of karma and attain the circular penetration (*vartula-saṃbheda*), it will surpass those with non-circular faculties by many kalpas.
Thus, one must not follow the current of karma with non-circular faculties and thereby doubt the teaching of the Sūtra.

If one truly understands that the power of the eyes is such as this, then there is no need for detailed analogies regarding the five faculties below. △ Second, the reiteration of the four [faculties] has four parts.
At first, he was granted permission by imperial decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, in the midst of a great assembly, one preaches this Lotus Sutra with a mind free from fear, listen now to its merits."
△ Second, the verse on virtues:
This person attains eight hundred merits of the preeminent eye. Because it is adorned by these, their eyes are exceedingly pure.

With the eyes born of one's parents (up to) seeing everything, Mount Meru—here translated as "Radiance"—is one of the seven golden mountains. This pure fleshly eye is possessed by all who are born.
Whenever one is able to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and perceive all true realities, then there is nothing within the great trichiliocosm that is not seen.

This is clearly evident; it is the realm of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). To clarify this through its manifestations: everyone knows that their own perceptions and views are inherently free from obstruction when separated from external objects (*viṣaya*).
Consider, for instance, the height of the sun and moon and the vast distance of the great void—it is many thousands of miles beyond measure.

In an instant, he again pacified the lands beyond the four seas. This could not have been accomplished by ordinary people without relying on wisdom and virtue;
thus, the function of the six sense organs is indeed as vast, profound, and unimpeded as this. △ Fourth, the conclusion and manifestation.
Although he has not yet attained the divine eye, the power of his physical eye is such as this.
△ Second, the four [aspects] of the faculty of hearing: First, the description of his virtues:
"Furthermore, Constantly Diligent... attains twelve hundred auditory merits."
△ Second, the narration of the merit, in two parts.
First, the general summary: "By means of this pure ear... within which there are various internal and external sounds and voices.

Miscellaneous categories:
the sounds of elephants, the sounds of horses, (up to) the sounds of laughter and the sounds of speech.

Male voices and female voices (up to) joyful voices and unpleasant voices.

The sounds of devas, the sounds of nāgas, (up to) the sounds of mahoragas.

the sound of fire, the sound of water, and the sound of wind.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"Multitudes of dusts do not separate them; they are neither destroyed nor mixed. △ Second, describing the merit:

This verse covers six pairs of miscellaneous categories, up to the two assemblies, the four sages, and the seven sections. Hearing without attachment constitutes "giving."
Because it is like an echo and so forth, it is able to purify. "Jīvajīvaka" means "co-life. △ Third, the conclusion on excellence:
From "The three thousand great thousandfold world-systems... up to "...merits are already thus."

from the fragrance of the *sumanā* flower and the fragrance of the *jāti* flower (up to) those dwelling here in this world, they are able to distinguish them all.

it is small but fragrant. *Pāṭala* is translated as "scented flower. *Tamālapatra* is translated as "noble stainless fragrance. *Tagara* is sandalwood incense.

Furthermore, one separately discerns the scents of sentient beings (up to) being able to hear them all and distinguish them without error.

Those who uphold this sutra, though dwelling here [until] there is nothing they do not hear or know.

Although one hears this fragrance (up to) recollecting it without error.
"Unimpaired and unerring" means there is no impairment and no confusion. The Elder who Sells Incense in the *Avataṃsaka* is well able to distinguish [fragrances].

They know all the various fragrances possessed by devas, humans, nāgas, and ghosts—fragrances that cure all diseases and eliminate all evils—and they fully comprehend even the distinct fragrances of all the stages of the bodhisattvas.

does it not likewise symbolize that those who uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* are able to penetrate diverse habitual tendencies, harmonize and integrate all wonders, and realize the fragrance of the Dharma-body of myriad virtues? △ The third section contains four verses in praise.
First is the general verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The nose of this person is pure; within this world, whether it be fragrant or foul things, he perceives and knows them all in their various forms."

from *sumanā* and *jāti* (up to) "by smelling the fragrance, one knows their body.
Among the seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), the woman-treasure (*strī-ratna*) occupies one. △ Second, celestial fragrances.
Whether the devas are walking or sitting (up to) he knows the location of them all.

from the deep and perilous places of various mountains (up to) their origins and locations.

"The various flowers and so forth of the heavens... by smelling the fragrance, one can know them all.
That which reaches far in its observation is called "observation" (*guan*); it is like what is referred to as "towers and pavilions for observation. Thus it proceeds upward in succession.
This refers to those from the six heavens of the desire realm upward. The Brahma-world is the first dhyāna; Ābhāsvara is the second dhyāna; Śubhakṛtsna is the third dhyāna;
and Bhavāgra is the summit of the form realm. △ Third, the broad fragrance of the four noble ones.
The assembly of bhikṣus (up to) can all know [the beings] by smelling their fragrance.
"Bhikṣus" here refers to both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "In every direction" means throughout the ten directions. △ Fourth, the concluding verse.
Although they have not yet attained the bodhisattva’s untainted (anāsrava) dharmas that give rise to the nose, those who uphold this sutra first obtain this characteristic of the nose.
When a bodhisattva leaves behind the body of segmented existence (prādeśika-kāya), all six sense organs arise based on untainted dharmas;
therefore, the nose, the body, and the mind are all said to be untainted. △ Fourth, the tongue organ, in three parts: first, the general heading.
Furthermore, through constant diligence, [he] attains twelve hundred qualities of the tongue.
Part Two: A Specific Explanation has two sections. First, the discrimination of flavors:
whether good or foul, [all things] are as delicious as celestial ambrosia; there is nothing that is not sweet.

The beautiful and the ugly, the bitter and the astringent, all belong to delusory objects. When one attains the pure tongue through non-attachment to these, then bitterness, astringency, sweetness, and sourness all become the flavor of the Dharma.

If [one uses] the tongue faculty... (up to) causing all to be joyful and happy.

△ Second, the verses on the manifestation [of the Buddha].
From "The various devas, nāgas, yakṣas... (up to) "...or at times manifests his body.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The floating dust and illusory transformations are falsely called 'characteristics,' whereas the essence of wondrous, enlightened clarity is eternally self-luminous.
It encompasses and emits the ten directions, manifesting according to karma. Therefore, for one who attains this essence, there is nothing that does not appear.

The mind becomes vast and empty, attaining freedom from all hindrances. Each person comes to know for themselves that the mind pervades the ten directions and encompasses all phenomena.
Looking back at the body born of one's parents, it is like a single speck of dust in the great void or a single bubble on the vast ocean;
its arising and ceasing have no source, and it is clearly seen as unobstructed. This is the realization. [Section] Three: Verses in Triplets. First, the verse on the "Luminous."
Pure. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

Although one has not yet attained the wondrous body of the dharma-nature that is untainted, all things appear within it by virtue of its pure and eternal essence.
The untainted Dharma-body is free from the limitations of分段 (segmentation/fragmentation), yet its eternal essence is not separate from segmentation.
Because it is solely pure, it is able to manifest all things. I have often observed the *Vairocana Ten Dharma-Realm Diagram*, seeing its forms but not clarifying their meaning;
I have recited the "Chapter on the Merits of the Body and Organs" from the *Lotus Sūtra*, hearing its meaning but not comprehending its forms. Now, by means of these two...
When the Dharma is clearly elucidated, the profound meaning of the wondrous marks becomes manifest everywhere. △ Six: The Four Aspects of the Faculty of Mind.
First, the general heading:
Furthermore, Constantly Diligent... [omitted] ...obtains twelve hundred merits of the mind-faculty.
△ Second, the specific explanation has three parts. First, profound penetration:
"By means of this pure faculty of mind (yid kyi dbang po, manas-indriya)... up to "...penetrating immeasurable and boundless meanings.

having understood this meaning, one is able to expound upon a single phrase or a single verse (up to) such that all is in accord with the True Dharma.

This is the meaning of "measure" (*pramāṇa*). The profound discourse delivered during the ninety-day summer retreat is precisely derived from this.

When one realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) of reality, then all the teachings spoken are none other than that true nature; therefore, they do not contradict one another. Even when discussing mundane matters, they remain in accord with the True Dharma. △
Third is the knowledge of capacities (*jñāna-gati*).
[He] knows everything from the trichiliocosm (up to... entirely.
Because his mind is pure, he possesses the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-abhijñā*). His conduct is that which accords with the ordinary mind; his actions are...
"Feeling and transformation" refers to the mind of sensation. "Idle proliferation" refers to the mind of discrimination. △ Third, the conclusion and clarification:
Although one has not yet attained untainted wisdom (until) this is also what was taught in the sūtras of former Buddhas.
In order to bring about the purification of the faculty of mind, for the true mark (dharmatā) and the Buddha share the same essence. △ Fourth, the triple repetition in verse:
first, the verse restating the general heading.

Explaining in sequence according to the Dharma, from months and four-month periods up to a year.

From "The countless Buddhas of the ten directions" to "fearlessness among the assembly," these verses show that the application of the purified mind is in profound resonance with the true reality (*dharmatā*).

this serves to clarify the excellence of their faculties.

Since this sutra exclusively discusses the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it elucidates each of the merits of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
If one can cast off the dust of emotional attachments and perceive with pure faculties, [one will realize this].
In this pure realm, one then beholds the surrounding mountains and forests where birds and beasts cry out;

their snouts frothing and lips moistened, with diverse forms and disparate intentions—none of which are not the true mark (*dharmatā*), none of which is not the wondrous Dharma. This is realized perfectly within a single body and constantly manifested throughout the six sense bases.
Fundamentally lacking nothing and never obstructed, the scriptural texts provide skillful means to reveal it from every side.
The practitioner must thoroughly expand their realization and enter into it.

Chapter Twenty: On the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging. Part Three:
Diligent Practice and Broad Benefit. Section One: A Brief Introduction and Summary.

As for "Never-Disparaging," this was the record of Śākyamuni’s former life during the time of King Majestic Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), when he diligently upheld the Sublime Dharma and extensively practiced the guidance of benefiting others.

Because he universally proclaimed the meaning of Buddha-nature to the fourfold assembly, bowing to those who were good and remaining unangered even when encountering those who were hostile, everyone respected him;
thus he was named "Never-Disparaging. He did not merely focus on recitation, but maintained the *Nirākāra-sūtra* with firm resolve.
Enduring insults while maintaining the practice of non-self is what is called "thoroughly upholding.

To extensively expound this sutra for ten billion years, transforming ten billion beings to cause them to abide in the Right Path, causing those with arrogant pride to believe, submit, and follow, and causing those who have completed their retribution to again attain the fruits of the Way—this is what is called "extensive benefit. This is indeed the former...
Though the five kinds of merit from upholding this sutra are complete, they are not yet refined; though the six thousand virtues gained through the former benefit are superior, they are not yet vast.
This is because the shadows of the conditions of person and dharma still persist therein. One must surely strive to reach the subtlety of the signless and selfless.
Regarding its recitation, one knows neither what to specialize in nor what to forget. Regarding its...
The fourfold assembly did not know whom to revere nor whom to disregard. Thus, wondrous conduct was manifested everywhere, and the billion-fold multitude transformed themselves of their own accord.

As for the mind of reverence or disdain, and the traces of sin or merit—all that is termed the "human dharma" or the "shadow of conditions"—all were submerged in the realm of the Perfectly Right and Equally Enlightened.
Only then did it become truly refined and vast; this is indeed the ultimate path of upholding the sutra.
Thus, the exhortation to uphold [the teaching] concludes with this chapter. △ Second, the formal explanation according to the text, in five parts.
First, restating the preceding sections on upholding and violating:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta... (up to) ...the purification of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The sin of slandering [this teaching] is as explained at the end of the "Simile Chapter" (Upamā-parivarta) and in the "Chapter on the Dharma-preacher" (Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta).

The etiquette for hearing and upholding it is as explained in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-preacher" (Dharmabhāṇakaguṇa-parivarta). To manifest the excellence of diligent upholding, these matters are raised first;

this is done to alert the assembly so that they may know the retribution for upholding or slandering is unfailing, thereby inspiring deep faith in diligent upholding and its vast benefits. As for Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he is [Mahāsthāmaprāpta].
This is the section on Śrīkūṭa. △ Second, the six sections on the remote causes for diligent upholding. First, the Buddha who was his teacher:
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in ages long past... [until] the land was named Mahāsiddhi."
Having passed through the remote past and served ten billion buddhas, he maintained the practice of signlessness and selflessness to bring extensive benefit.
One who does not possess the power of the Dharma cannot fulfill such a task; therefore, he addressed it to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. As for King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara:
With a great voice that pervades the world, he fearlessly preaches the Dharma for all as a King of Dharma.
Therefore, once Not-Light (Adīnamānasa) had attained this Way, he was able to preach the Dharma among the assembly with a mind free from fear. The eon was named Free from Decline (Vipraṇāśa).
It is said that when worldly paths flourished together, there was a kingdom named Mahāsiddha. It was said that its righteous governance was without deficiency.
Therein, the Buddha Vairocana-rāja (until) preached the Dharma corresponding to the six pāramitās, culminating in the wisdom of a Buddha.
This passage describes that Vimalakīrti also taught the three vehicles. Regarding "taking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as the cause":

taking the unsurpassed path as the cause, he expounded the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), enabling beings to proceed by means of these toward the realization of *bodhi*, the ultimate wisdom of a Buddha.
Those who attained Great Power were all named King of Majestic Sound (Vaiśravaṇarāja), from [the first] until [the last], all sharing the same title.
This was also like the case of the two ten-thousand Buddhas of the Lamp-Light (Pradīpa) kalpa, all of whom shared the same name because their paths were identical.
The mention of so many Buddhas clarifies the vast and remote nature of Śākyamuni’s past causes. △ Second, the time of revealing his origin.
From "At the outset, when the Tathāgata King of Majestic Sound had already entered parinirvāṇa" up to "named Constantly Non-Disparaging.
△ Third, explaining the name and manifesting the practice, in four parts. First, the practice of equality.
By what causes and conditions is Mahāsthāmaprāpta named "Never Disparaging" (Zhăngbùqīng)? [This extends] until the point where it says he shall attain Buddhahood.

This is because he universally predicted the fourfold assembly by means of the meaning of *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). Although the conduct and capacities of the fourfold assembly were unequal, Never Disparaging treated them as equal through the Buddha-nature;
therefore, he prostrated to and deeply revered them all, believing that they were all practicing the Bodhisattva path.
"All shall become Buddhas. For the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is fundamentally and spontaneously perfected. All worldly karmic actions accord with the True Dharma;
anyone who can perceive all practices as the Bodhisattva Path and know that all people shall become Buddhas—how could there be any room for contempt or arrogance?
II. Practice Without Characteristics (Animitta-caryā).
Yet this bhikṣu does not specialize in the recitation of the sūtras (up to: "You shall all become Buddhas.
This is the upholding of the *animitta-sūtra* and the practice of the *animitta-caryā*. △ Third, the practice of non-self (*anātma-caryā*).
Among the fourfold assembly, there were those who gave rise to thoughts of anger and impurity [up to] "you shall all become Buddhas.
For many years he was reviled, yet he did not give rise to anger; this is true non-self. Sentient beings, deluded and confused, cannot believe for themselves;
therefore, they regard his bestowal of predictions as false. Because the Bodhisattva’s great compassion does not abandon them but seeks to save and deliver them, he fled.
Even at such a time, he continued to exhort them earnestly. △ Fourth, the dual summary of name and practice:
Because he constantly spoke these words, he was called "Ever-Not-Light" (Sadāparibhūta).
△ Fourth, hearing and retaining.
When this bhikṣu is about to pass away, he extensively preaches this Lotus Sūtra for others.
Although at first he did not exclusively engage in recitation, in the end he is able to hear and retain many verses. His life-span increases by hundreds of millions, and he extensively [preaches].
As for what people say: because of the absence of marks and the absence of self, both the object and its reflection vanish together;

thus, divine wisdom and true illumination prevail, and the life of insight is not cut short. Such is this profound resonance. Although the majestic sound has ceased, the sound of the Dharma does not cease;
therefore, the sutras previously spoken can be heard in their entirety. Yet, hearing them within emptiness is shown so that one may forget the subject and object, severing all duality.
Only after the images [of subject and object] have vanished can one fully possess this Dharma; thus, one attains twenty koṭis of nayutas of verses.
Because both the grasper and the grasped are forgotten and images are severed, one immediately attains the merit of the purification of the six sense faculties.
Previously, by citing the merits of the six faculties, the Dharma realized was clarified; now, by citing the example of "Not-Light" (Adīnapraśa), the person who realizes it is shown. △
The five kinds of skillful guidance.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, free from overweening pride, [proceeded] toward the three types of awakening (*trividha-bodhi*).

Having seen, heard, believed, and submitted, the fourfold assembly followed him. This is what is called the manifestation of wondrous conduct throughout the world, whereby billions of beings are spontaneously transformed.

The power of great supernormal faculties (*mahā-ṛddhi-bala*) refers precisely to the benefit of hearing [the Dharma] and prolonging one's lifespan. The power of eloquence (*pratibhāna-bala*) refers precisely to the extensive exposition for a hundred million years.
The power of great sublime tranquility (*suśānti-bala*) refers precisely to the merit of the true and eternal purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
△ Sixth, the accumulation of merit.
After his life comes to an end, through the fulfillment of his meritorious virtues, he shall attain Buddhahood.
This passage cites King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, Candrasūryapradīpa, and Meghasvavibhu to clarify that by accumulating merit without disparagement, one reaches the Way;
it proclaims the profound antiquity of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s lineage. It intends to show that by preaching this sutra, one attains [enlightenment] just as King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja did.
Great Fearlessness. To clarify this Way is like the sun, moon, and lamps succeeding one another without end;
to distribute these benefits is like clouds that freely moisten and cover all things without limit. All who practice with diligence and seek broad benefit should aspire to reach this state.
△ Third, revealing the present conditions has two parts. First, the "Not-Light" [Chapter].
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? ... [until] ... one will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This clarifies that through diligent upholding, one perfects the Way for oneself, so that today that Way becomes ever more radiant.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he specifically [instructs] the fourfold assembly... teaching them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This clarifies the virtue of extensively benefiting and bringing others to completion; though they encounter adverse conditions, their benefit is not lost.
△ Second, the Assembly.
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, what do you think? [The text from here until "is one who is non-retrogressive" contains omissions and lacks clarity in its phrasing and meaning.
It should be corrected according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which states:
"The five hundred bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, such as Siṃhacandra, together with the upāsikās, constitute the fourfold assembly. Thus says the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:]
There were five hundred laymen of pure faith and five hundred laywomen of pure faith. △ Fourth, the conclusion which reveals the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]:
"Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should know that [from here until... you should always receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this sutra."
This concludes the summary that reveals the extensive benefit and exhorts one to uphold [the teaching] with diligence. △ Fifth, the reiteration through verse in three parts.
First, the verse on the distant cause for diligent upholding.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
In the past there was a Buddha (up to) who quickly attained the Way of the Buddha.

"General" (*jiang*) refers to one who leads from behind, while "Guide" (*dao*) refers to one who leads from the front. This means that by means of his divine wisdom and subtle power, Wei-yin led and guided sentient beings from both before and behind, causing them to hasten toward the Way.
To be "attached to dharmas" means to be confined by narrow views and bound by restrictive teachings, thereby remaining deluded.

This refers to the meaning of Buddha-nature. Regarding the phrase "when their offenses were completed," it means that after the multitude of arrogant ones had finished their transgressions, they again encountered the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging;
at the point of death, they heard the sutra and were transformed and brought to fulfillment.
After Never-Disparaging passed away, he met countless Buddhas, namely Sun-Moon-Lamp-Cloud-Sovereign and others. △ Second, the verse displays the present conditions.
At that time, the one who was "Not Disparaging" (Adhikaraṇaśūnyaka) was none other than this person who listens to the Dharma.
△ Third, the concluding verses summarize and manifest the exhortation to uphold [the teaching]:
"In my previous lives... such a sūtra as this."
This concludes the manifestation of vast benefit. "Causing them to abide in nirvāṇa" means causing them to attain the fruit of the path of true permanence.
From "hundreds of billions of koṭis of kalpas" until "quickly attaining the Buddha-way."

This exhorts one to maintain [the teaching] with diligence. Since it has been heard only after billions of kalpas and will be preached only after billions of kalpas, one should conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter and maintain it with deep faith and diligence, thereby accomplishing the Buddha-way. The section on "Exhorting to Maintain the Wondrous" concludes here.
△ Part Three: The Section on Circulation (Liu-tong-fen) has two parts. First, the explanation of the meaning and the division of the sections.
From the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" through the "Chapter on Entrustment," the remaining six chapters embody the preceding teachings;
they manifest the sphere of practice to circulate this path, and are thus called the gateway of the eternally great function where practice accords with wisdom.

The manifested traces of Bhaiṣajyarāja, Gadgadasvara, and Avalokiteśvara’s Sublime Adornment all manifest the reality-marked sphere of practice to accord with the previously mentioned sphere of wisdom, ultimately culminating in the constant practice of Samantabhadra; therefore, they are named the "Eternal Great Function."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-one: The Supernatural Powers of the Tathāgata. Part Two:
Detailed Explanation According to the Outline, Section Eight. First, the Initiation of the Propagation; Second, the Narration of the Meaning. First, the Narration of the Meaning.
The main body of the scripture having concluded, the intention is now to transmit its benefits to ten thousand generations.

For this reason, the Bodhisattvas extend their request, and the Tathāgata immediately manifests his supernatural powers to praise the virtue of the sutra, thereby inspiring the minds of the multitude so that it may be widely disseminated.
Thus, this section is titled "The Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Powers," serving as the prologue for its circulation. △ Second, the explanation of the text has four parts.
First, the Bodhisattvas extend their request.
At that time, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in a thousand worlds (up to) make offerings to him.

This refers to the assembly manifested by the Buddha in the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth," who appear before him to exhort him to uphold [the teaching]. Herein, they extend their request for the dissemination [of the Dharma].

This is the general explanation. To explain extensively, "receiving and upholding" refers to self-benefit, while [the preceding] refers to benefiting others. II. Praising with Supernatural Power. This has two parts.
First, manifesting superiority through supernatural power. This has six sections. First, manifesting the tongue and emitting light.
At that time, the World-Honored One [from the passage concerning Mañjuśrī and others] completely illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
That his broad and long tongue extended upward as far as the Brahma-world manifested the supernormal power of eloquent exposition.
That he emitted immeasurable light illuminating the ten directions manifested the supernormal power of wisdom-illumination. He first manifested these in order to praise the virtues of this sutra.

Regarding the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*): beginning from the protrusion of the tongue and the emission of light, up to the shaking of the various heavens and the pervading of the Buddha-fields, it concludes by stating that even if one were to describe the merit of this sutra for billions of kalpas using such supernormal powers, one could not exhaust it;
this most clearly demonstrates the supreme excellence of this sutra. The supernormal power of the Tathāgata is, in fact, the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The wondrous functioning of non-action is described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "The illusory arts of a magician can manifest all manner of things.
An asura transforms his body until it is equal in size to Mount Sumeru; a dragon king, in a mere instant, rains down refreshing moisture throughout the world.
If such are the supernatural powers of those who still possess greed, anger, and delusion, how much more so the sovereign power of one who is fully endowed with the wisdom of the Dharma-realm!"
Thus, although the tongue reaches the Brahma-world and its light pervades the ten directions, it is merely a single minute function within the wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
As for the "long-resident bodhisattvas" who dwell here in the lower regions of this Sahā world—the Brahma-world being the first dhyāna heaven.
Beneath the trees of various jewels, upon lion thrones (up to) he then withdrew his tongue-mark.
These emanated Buddhas of Śākyamuni likewise assisted in its manifestation through the same path. △ Second, the manifestation of sound that causes trembling.
At one time, they coughed and snapped their fingers together, causing the earth to quake in six ways.
From tongues only a few inches long, they manifested [light] reaching as far as the Brahma world; in the space of a single assembly, they manifested a duration of hundreds of thousands of years.
Again, with a single cough and a snap of the fingers, their voices pervaded the ten directions and shook the great earth, all manifesting their supreme spiritual powers.
Excellent. △ Third, by means of his supernormal powers:
the sentient beings therein—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth—were all filled with great joy, having attained what they had never experienced before.
Sentient beings from other realms throughout the ten directions possess obstructed minds, yet they are able to see these Buddha-activities of the Sahā world.
This is due to the Buddha’s supernatural power, which temporarily employs their own supernormal powers; this is intended to manifest his supreme excellence. △ Fourth, the various devas take refuge.
Immediately, the various devas in the void raised their voices and proclaimed (until): "All together they scattered [flowers] from afar across the Sahā world.
These were all due to supernatural power or its influence. △ Fifth, the unification of the different and the penetration of the obstructed.
The various objects scattered [as offerings] came from the ten directions and filled what is like a single buddha-field;
this, moreover, was a manifestation through supernormal power. △ Sixth, the conclusion that reveals the merit of the sutra.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, including Upariṣṭha and the others, saying: "Even if one were to speak for an eon, one could not exhaustively describe the merit of this sutra.
Upariṣṭha was the leader of the assembly who emerged from the depths. Such was the breadth of his tongue and the distance of his bodily radiance. With a single cough—
With a single snap of the fingers, he can cause the six kinds of earth tremors and move all the devas;
from the merging of the different to the penetration of the obstructed, his supernatural powers may be said to be supremely great.

Yet, as for being unable to fully describe the virtues of this sutra, it is because all the profound and wondrous merits of the Tathāgata are concentrated within this sutra, and thus they cannot be exhausted. △ Second, praising its secret and wondrous nature.
To summarize: all that has been proclaimed and clearly expounded in this sutra—namely, all dharmas which are those attained at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
sovereign spiritual powers which are manifestations in accordance with the nature (dharmatā);
the secret treasury which is the dharma that cannot be pointed out; and the profoundly deep matters which are the mind—[are all herein revealed].
That which cannot be transmitted is all exhausted within this sutra; therefore, its merit is beyond description.
△ Third, the formal exhortation for circulation:
"For this reason, you [all]... until... all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa herein."
The passage beginning with "One should know that in this place" clarifies that the Buddhas, from the beginning to the end of their cultivation and realization, never depart from this Dharma;
therefore, wherever it is found, it should be revered. 4. Reiteration through Verses (in three parts): First, verses praising its excellence by manifesting its supernatural power.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world... (down to) the earth shakes in six ways.
This verse describes the manifestation of the tongue, the emission of light, the manifestation of sound, and the shaking of the earth.
From "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" (up to) "one cannot find its limit," the verse concludes by manifesting the virtues of the sutra.
△ Second, the verse praises the sublime mystery:
"Those who can uphold this sutra" (up to) "they teach and transform all bodhisattvas."
The path to attaining Buddhahood, the principle of manifesting emanations, and the methods of teaching and transforming beings—all do not depart from this.
△ Third, a verse on the formal entrustment for circulation:
"Those who can uphold this sutra... shall also cause them to attain joy."
The Way has obtained its transmission and is called the Buddha-mind.
From "All Buddhas sit at the site of enlightenment" up to "all things are without obstruction":
if one can uphold this sutra, then all will be thoroughly understood and one will encounter the source at every turn; what further obstructions could there be?
From "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata" up to "ultimately abiding in the One Vehicle," the above all praises and exhorts the virtue of propagating [this teaching].
Below is the concluding exhortation: "Therefore, those who possess wisdom... shall certainly have no doubt."
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Two: Entrustment.
△ Second, the entrustment for circulation, which has two parts. First, the introductory statement:

to commit [the teaching] to others through speech is called "entrustment" (zhù); to bind [the teaching] to others through the Dharma is called "cumulative charge" (lèi). This is intended to ensure that the wondrous Dharma is transmitted and continued for the benefit [of all].

It reaches infinity. Therefore, it is said that the entrustment (*parindanā*) constitutes the transmission for its circulation. Now, as to why the entrustment is spoken of so abruptly before the assembly has concluded:
this sutra establishes its fundamental nature through wisdom and perfects its virtues through practice.

Having previously opened up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to clarify the Great Matter, the method for establishing the fundamental nature is already complete; thus, the entrustment is spoken of to clarify the Buddha’s [intent].

The Buddha’s essential instruction for bestowing his hand ends with this alone. Those who hereafter seek to perfect their virtue through practice must only embody these prior teachings and extend them into action;
there is no other dharma. Since there is no other dharma, it is appropriate that he entrusts [the teaching] to you at this point.
The *Avataṃsaka* consists of thirty-nine chapters, which unfold the stages of cultivation and progress up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), concluding with the Tathāgata.
The "Chapter on Manifestation" consists of only thirty-seven sections, after which the entrustment for circulation is immediately given.
Subsequently, the two chapters on Samantabhadra’s Constant Practice and Sudhana’s Southern Journey are taught. This is because the preceding methods have already been fully prepared;

what follows merely builds upon the former to perfect the virtues of practice, as there are no further distinct dharmas. Furthermore, the preceding section reveals the realm of wisdom, thereby distinguishing it from deluded emotions and making it manifest.

[The Master] explains: This subsequently demonstrates the sphere of practice (*caryā-viṣaya*). Because one desires that the understanding culminate in practice, it is distinguished here. As for what is called the sphere of practice:
there is no further discernment or manifestation, nor any further intellectual interpretation; there is simply the total application of the whole being. The *Guan* says:
"If one does not thoroughly clarify the preceding understanding, there is no way to proceed to accomplish the subsequent practice. Furthermore, one must forget and sever the preceding understanding.
Only then can one enter the realm of practice. Therefore, practice is accomplished through understanding;

when the arising of practice is severed from understanding, the subsequent realm of practice transcends what words can reach, what understanding can attain, and is not something that can be transmitted even through formal entrustment.

Students should advance beyond this. Later, when Śīlagupta translated this sūtra, he moved the section on the entrustment (*parindanā*) to the end of the volume, thereby losing the essential intent of the *Avataṃsaka*.
II. Explanation of the Text, in six parts: First, the World-Honored One’s Entrustment.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [repeatedly] rubbed their heads until all sentient beings universally heard and knew it;
this was done to demonstrate his earnest diligence. The various secret teachings, such as the *Śūraṅgama*, are called "Buddha-Topknot" (*uṣṇīṣa*), signifying the unsurpassed Dharma.
When the Buddhas bestow predictions and entrustments, they always rub the crown of the head, signifying the conferral of the unsurpassed.
This is the Dharma. As for the immeasurable bodhisattvas who immediately surged forth from the earth: △ Second, showing the practice of circulation.
Why is this so? (Up to: "instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening."
The reason for causing them to widely proclaim this Dharma is to enable them to learn the three practices of the Tathāgata and bestow great Dharma benefits upon all sentient beings:
first, the practice of great compassion, which provides equal relief and succor; second, the practice of being free from stinginess, which exhausts both internal and external wealth;
and third, the practice of fearlessness, which does not shrink from toil or difficulty. Only in this way can they [benefit] all...
Sentient beings possess three kinds of wisdom: Buddha-wisdom is free from the views of the two vehicles; Tathāgata-wisdom is free from the views of bodhisattvas;
and Self-existent Wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna) is free from all grasping at realization and is not awakened through others. It penetrates the single vehicle of true wisdom.

These are merely different names according to their respective qualities and functions. To have faith in the Tathāgata’s wisdom means to be able to believe in the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) and to incline toward the One Vehicle.
Regarding "those who ride [the vehicle]": for their sake, one should preach this sutra so that they may attain the Buddha-wisdom and not remain stuck in the two vehicles.
"Other profound and wondrous dharmas" refers to the provisional and gradual teachings. They are also called "profound and wondrous" because these dharmas all constitute the single Buddha-vehicle.
△ Third, the conclusion and exhortation to perfect practice.
If you are able to act in this way, you will have already repaid the kindness of all Buddhas;
this is what is meant by "offering this profound mind to the lands as numerous as motes of dust. △ Fourth, the assembly receives the command.
At that time, the various Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas [requested] until they said, "We pray that you have no further concern.

The Buddha entrusted them three times to demonstrate his diligence; the assembly responded three times in turn to demonstrate their reverence. △ Fifth, the dispatching of emanations and the leaving behind of the stūpa.
At that time, from the words "Śākyamuni Buddha" until "the stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna was restored to its former state," [it is said that] he caused his emanated bodies to each return.
This shows that when the Dharma is transmitted, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) subsequently becomes hidden.

As for leaving the jeweled stūpa as it was, it is because the subsequent teaching has not yet been completed; there is still a need for perfect realization. △ Sixth, the assembly attains the joy of the Dharma.
When these words were spoken, [from "at that time" until] all who heard what the Buddha taught were filled with great joy.

First, they rejoiced that the emanated being had been sent to reach the Way of Manifestation and Concealment; second, they rejoiced that the stūpa was left behind so that they might again hear the Dharma.

*Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Six, Part Three.
By the Bhikṣu Jiéhuán of Kāiyuán Lián Monastery in Wēn’lǐng. Explanation.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Three: The Past Deeds of Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja. Part Three:
The Propagation through Austerities, in two sections. First, the introductory narrative:

In the past, Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja was the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana. For the sake of the Dharma, he practiced rigorous asceticism, burning his body and setting his arms on fire. Regarding this, Śākyamuni...
Among all the teachings of the Dharma, there is none among gods or humans who can equal one who upholds this sutra.
Now, its original cause is revealed so that people may aspire to it and together honor this path; therefore, it is titled "The Original Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
To circulate it through ascetic practice refers precisely to the difficult practices and austerities questioned by Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña. Observing this sutra through wisdom, I [perceive]...
Through the practice of the three dimensions, one accomplishes virtue. The preceding realm of wisdom serves to dispel emotional attachments and manifest understanding;
the subsequent realm of practice seeks to bring that understanding to its consummation through application.

This is exemplified by the self-immolation of Bhaiṣajyarāja, the responsive manifestations of Gadgadasvara, the universal gateways of Avalokiteśvara, the conversion of the heterodox by Prabhūtaratna, and the exhortations of Samantabhadra—all of which demonstrate the practice of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The objective realm causes one to forget emotions and sever conceptual understanding, so that through following practice, one awakens and enters [enlightenment].

Therefore, when this "Medicine King" chapter was being preached, eighty thousand bodhisattvas attained the liberation of all languages; thus, it is through ascetic practice that the virtue of perfect penetration is accomplished.
When the "Expedient Means" chapter was being taught, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue attained the Dharma-flower Samādhi; thus, through wondrous practice, he perfected the virtue of the true mark.
When the "Universal Gate" chapter was being taught, an assembly of eighty thousand gave rise to the unequaled mind.

Thus, through perfect conduct, one accomplishes the most supreme virtue. When the "Chapter on Dhāraṇīs" was preached, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the "Chapter on King Adorned" (*Vyūharāja-parivarta*) was preached, eighty-four thousand people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).
This further demonstrates how spiritual power and the power of truth assist in the perfection of virtuous conduct, even unto the preaching of the exhortation.

At the time of the "Chapter on the Arising of the Resolve," bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*, and bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust perfected the path of Samantabhadra;
thus, through constant practice, they accomplished the virtue of non-virtue. Indeed, one who can reach this depth has fully realized and exhausted the wondrous practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Therefore, it is here that the assembly concludes. Now, as for beginning with ascetic practices and concluding with constant practice: it is because [the former] is the entryway and [the latter] is the ultimate destination.
If one wishes to cultivate virtue through practice, there is no way to achieve profound realization without a refined mind and arduous resolve.

Therefore, it is only through refinement and hardship that one subsequently attains subtlety; only after attaining subtlety can one become perfect; and only after becoming perfect can one truly accord with the constant practice of Samantabhadra.
This is also the sequence of the teaching. Part Two: Explanation of the Text (twelve sections). First, the Inquiry of King Śakrābhilagna.
At that time, from the Bodhisattva Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña down to this assembly of śrāvakas, all heard [this teaching] and rejoiced.
This chapter is initiated by Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña in order to clarify the causes for his sovereign mastery in propagating the sutra throughout past lives.
△ Second, the Buddha reveals his past causes, in three parts. First, the Buddhas who were his teachers:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Sudhana-rāja-putra), [and so forth], up to the assembly of seventy-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* great śrāvakas.
The true light of wisdom illuminates both the hidden and the manifest without being encumbered by external objects; therefore, he is named Sun-Moon Pure Bright Virtue.
His retinue of Dharma companions fully embodies the essence of the Three Vehicles.
The Buddha’s lifespan was forty-two thousand kalpas... [up to] she made these offerings.

The daughter had five obstacles and [was subject to] the four realms of existence, all of which made it difficult for her to repay [his kindness]. The tree was at a distance of one arrow-shot from the terrace;
this speaks to the vastness of its shade.
At that time, that Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra for the sake of all sentient beings (up to this point).
The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-sūtra* begins from here. △ Second, attaining the Way by means of the sūtra.
This Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Form-Bodies after practicing with single-minded diligence for twelve thousand years.

As for the manifestation of all form-bodies, they appear without departing from the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). The statement that he completed twelve thousand years refers precisely to the faculties.

The twelve sense bases of the sensory dusts are perfectly interfused and mutually illuminating. When one reaches the stage where meritorious practice is fulfilled, through this perfect interfusion and mutual illumination, one attains their true nature (*dharmatā*).
Thus, one knows that every root and every object—every phenomenon of form—is manifested from the single true reality (*eka-dharmatā*).
By means of this, one fuses all roots and objects with the single true reality, such that they manifest within any single root or object.
All phenomena of form interpenetrate, harmonize, and encompass one another in infinite layers; this is called "filling twelve thousand years" and attaining the Samādhi of Manifesting All Form-Bodies.
This is precisely the sphere of practice for realizing the true nature (dharmatā) deeply.
The *Avataṃsaka* frequently cites eons exceeding measure to directly clarify this: through limitless wisdom and compassion, one cultivates such practices, never [failing].
The mind of limitation. All such cases follow this pattern when they exceed the prescribed measure. △ Third, the observance of ascetic practices has three parts.
First, offerings through supernormal power.

This sūtra, however, brings about sudden awakening where all veils are simultaneously exhausted; it is perfectly integrated, vast, and penetrating, like the brilliance of the moon. △ Fourth, the removal of darkness.
Furthermore, just as the Sun Deva is able to dispel all darkness—up to being able to shatter the darkness of all that is unwholesome—when the sunlight emerges, it does not coexist with the gloom.
When people attain right wisdom, all darkness is naturally eliminated. △ Fifth, the Most Honorable.
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings [and so forth]... it is the most honored among all sūtras.
The previous statement referred to the "supreme division of illumination," while this statement refers to the "most honored illuminating majesty and virtue. △ Six: Comprehensive Subsumption.
Furthermore, just as Śakra is the king among the gods, so too are the teachings of the Three Vehicles honored according to the capacities of sentient beings, yet they cannot encompass one another.
This sutra unifies the three vehicles into one, serving as the orthodox standard for all sutras. △ Seventh, it acts as a protector.
Furthermore, he is like Mahābrahmā (up to) the father of those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta.
Mahābrahmā is the lord of the Sahā world; "father" means being one’s refuge and support. △ Eighth, superiority in the vehicles.
Furthermore, among all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), [the practitioner of the *śrāvaka* vehicle] is also the foremost.
Among those who have not yet left the stage of ordinary persons regarding the four fruits of the path, the *pratyekabuddha* is the foremost because his faculties (*indriya*) are sharp.
While sentient beings have not yet left the state of ordinary persons, the *sūtra* is the foremost because its vehicle (*yāna*) is superior. △ Nine: Advancement.
Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, [he is] the most supreme.
Previously, he was ranked first among ordinary beings; here, he is ranked first among the three vehicles; subsequently, he is ranked first in the stage of Buddhahood.
This thus represents a progressive manifestation of excellence. △ Ten: Perfect Manifestation.
Just as the Buddha is the sovereign king of all dharmas, so too is this sutra the king among all sutras.
To summarize it thus is to fully manifest its supreme excellence. Indeed, the manifestation of this sutra’s supreme excellence can be exhausted in these words alone.
The reason for necessarily citing these various meanings is to clarify that the wondrous Dharma is supreme in every place according to the capacities of sentient beings.
△ Seventh, the extensive manifestation of its superior merit, in three parts. First, the general heading.
Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā: "Rāṣṭrapāla, this sutra can save [beings]... fulfilling their aspirations.
△ Second, clarification by analogy:
"It is like a pond of cool water... like a torch that dispels darkness."
A lamp can produce illumination but cannot eliminate darkness. △ Third, the combined manifestation:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this (up to) being able to untie all the bonds of birth and death.
The various sufferings, illnesses, and fetters of sentient beings all arise from delusion and ignorance; once one can open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they will all be left behind.
△ Section Eight: Extensively Revealing the Superior Benefits (in five parts). First: The Benefit of Writing and Maintaining.
If a person hears this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, [the merit] they obtain is so vast that one could not measure its limits by calculating its quantity.
△ Second, the benefit of making offerings:
If one copies this sūtra scroll, the merit obtained is likewise immeasurable.
From *campaka* onwards, all are names of flowers; these are used to infuse and create scented oils. △ Third, the benefits of hearing this chapter:
"O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there is anyone who hears [this]... (up to) ...all such women shall never again receive a female body after this life."
Because it serves as the true cause, its merits are boundless. A woman is able to maintain [this teaching] and exhaust all obstructive outflows. △ Fourth, the benefit of diligent cultivation:
"If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, during the final five hundred years... (up to) "...distressed by various defilements."
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: "In the first five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, liberation will be firm;
in the second five hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm; in the third, learning will be firm; in the fourth, merit will be firm;
and in the fifth, strife will be firm—this is the final five hundred years. When strife is firm, it is difficult to find roots of goodness."

Therefore, although even women can attain supreme merit—this statement, while highlighting excellence through the inferior, implicitly includes men as well—greed, hatred, and delusion constitute the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), while pride, envy, and so forth are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Once born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*), that upon which one relies consists of pure karma, and those with whom one associates are virtuous people; thus, there are no defiled afflictions.

Attaining the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), such that even a thousand Buddhas speaking together could not exhaust its description;
wherein mind and phenomena are both quiescent yet capable of illuminating and functioning—this is called the Bodhisattva’s supernormal powers and the realization of the non-arising of dharmas.

Because the mind is quiescent and the faculties are pure, one is able to see many Buddhas. This is the state where the merit is perfected and wisdom is fulfilled for a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka*, wherein the objective realm and the subjective mind are [in perfect harmony].
They interpenetrate one another. One can see many hundreds of Buddhas, up to many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas; the same applies to their intentions.

It is not because they are conditioned merits that they cannot be burned or swept away; rather, it is because they accord with the virtue of the true mark (*dharmatā*) that it is said they cannot be exhausted.
You have now been able to destroy the various demonic marauders and shatter the army of birth and death; all other enemies have been utterly crushed.

This praises the wondrous power of the *dharmakṣānti* (patience with the Dharma) you have attained. The "demonic marauders" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and so forth.

The "army of birth and death" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*), and so forth. "Marauders" implies inflicting harm, while "army" implies launching attacks. As for the "other enemies," they are...
The delusions and karmic actions that arise in accordance with one's inclinations toward objects are all utterly destroyed by the attainment of this patience.
Son of good family, among the hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, there is none who is your equal.
The above are all the words of remote praise from the Buddhas.
"Sudhana-puṣpa, this bodhisattva has accomplished such power of merit and wisdom.
This concludes the benefit of diligent cultivation. △ Fifth, the benefit of sympathetic joy.
If there are those who hear [this] (up to) the merit they obtain as described above:
by reciting the title of this sutra once, a lotus flower will emerge from their mouths; by being able to rejoice in it once, the fragrance of the Dharma will abide within their bodies.

The seeds of goodness will not perish, and the accomplishment of merit will manifest of itself. "As described above" refers to the "Chapter on Rejoicing. △ Ninth, the conclusion that clarifies the flow [of the teaching].
[He] spread [it].
Therefore, O Śrīgarbha, from [this point] until the illness is immediately extinguished, one neither ages nor dies.

The power of true knowledge and vision repels the diseases of delusion and craving; this is the excellent medicine. When the diseases of delusion and craving are eliminated, then birth [is transcended].
When the conditions for death are severed, one suddenly realizes the true and eternal; how, then, could there be further aging and death?

This is like the wisdom of *prajñā*, which can illuminate the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and cross over the perils of suffering, free from aging and death. △ Tenth, causing respect for those who uphold [the teaching].

"O Rājapadmavṛṣabhitā, if you see anyone [from the point 'if you see' up to] 'you should thus give rise to a mind of reverence,' scatter flowers and form mental recollections, etc., so as to cause them to give rise to a mind that regards them as the Buddha. Regarding 'taking grass':
when the Buddha attained enlightenment, he took auspicious *śara* grass to serve as his seat. 11. Hearing the Chapter and Accomplishing Practice.

When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja" was being preached, up to the point of the *dhāraṇī* of speech, the one named Priyadarśana immediately attained the samādhi of manifesting the body upon hearing the sutra; and after his self-immolation by fire, he immediately attained the *dhāraṇī* of speech.
This was because, having realized the Dharma-body and transcended all marks and views, he had profoundly and perfectly accorded with the wondrous perfection. And...
That he burned his arm enabled the Śrāvaka to attain the Samādhi of Manifesting the Present Body;

that he now recounts this past event enables the Bodhisattva to attain the Dhāraṇī of Understanding Languages. This was likely because, by awakening to the matter of burning his body and burning his arm, he was likewise able to leave behind all attachments to views and penetrate the wondrous perfection.
This is what is meant by achieving the virtue of perfect penetration through ascetic practice.

Furthermore, those who have attained both samādhi and dhāraṇī manifest their bodies through samādhi, assuming various forms according to the species of beings they encounter, and employ dhāraṇī of speech to preach the Dharma according to the species of beings they encounter.
These two qualities are constantly in need of one another and are both realized through the wondrous Dharma.
Therefore, when the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" was being taught, the assembly of bodhisattvas also attained these samādhis and dhāraṇīs.
Dharani. △ Twelve: The Concluding Praise of Prabhūtaratna.
From "The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna within the jeweled stupa" (up to) "...benefiting immeasurable all sentient beings."
Without having previously accomplished the virtue of mastery in hearing and retaining [the teachings], one cannot initiate this benefit.

Chapter Twenty-four: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Part Four: The Propagation through Sublime Practice. Section One: Stating and Narrating the Title of the Section.
Ghoṣadatta (Wonderful Sound) deeply realized the sublime Dharma and was able to expound it with a wondrous voice according to the needs of others, thereby circulating this Path.
Although his name is "Wonderful Sound," his true manifestation is "Sublime Conduct.

Observing the causes he planted in the past, when he offered music and presented an alms bowl to the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararāja (King of Cloud-Thunder Sound), he aspired to possess a wonderful voice for preaching the Dharma and to manifest sublime conduct in accordance with the needs of beings.
Therefore, it was reported that the Buddha of the Past, Jñānakūṭa, possessed such supernormal powers as these.

Now, to enable students to embody his wondrous practice and to expound this Way by preaching the Dharma according to the needs of others, the "Chapter on Wondrous Sound" is taught as the circulation of this wondrous practice.
Indeed, by embodying wondrous sound, one does not become obstructed by verbal expressions; by being able to respond according to the occasion, one does not confine oneself to the traces of the mind.

To be neither stagnant nor limited is what constitutes wondrous practice (*caryā*). Following this, there are further the perfect practice (*pariniṣpanna-caryā*) and the constant practice (*nitya-caryā*).
Those who speak of these after the aforementioned ascetic practice (*duṣkara-caryā*) do so because they intend to establish virtue through practice;

one must first refine the mind and exert the will before attaining the wondrous, attain the wondrous before being able to achieve perfection, and achieve perfection before truly conforming to the constant practice of Samantabhadra. Thus it is said.
As explained previously. △ Second, the explanation of the textual meaning has nine parts. First, the explanation of the Honored One’s light-summoning:
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [to] the worlds of all Buddhas."

When convening assemblies or summoning the emanated bodies, he merely emits light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. Now, in summoning Gadgadasvara, he simultaneously emits light from the uṣṇīṣa.
This is because the uṣṇīṣa constitutes the mark of the invisible crown; it is the light of the supreme fruit.

Since he is about to proclaim and demonstrate the practice of wondrous perfection—the very form of the conduct of the ultimate fruit—he summons [Gadgadasvara] by means of the light of that ultimate fruit.
The Buddha possesses ninety-seven marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), of which the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of his head is one.
Beyond this number, there is a world that universally illuminates his realm.
The *Avataṃsaka* and the lands from which the Bodhisattvas come represent the practices they have performed; the Buddhas whom they originally served represent the fruits they have realized.
"Pure Light Adornment" (*Vimalaprabhā-vyūha*) refers to practice based on wisdom; "Pure Flower Prior Wisdom" (*Vimalakusuma-pūrvajñāna*) refers to wisdom based on practice.
Wisdom and practice adorn one another, such that cause and effect are integrated as a single essence. Wondrous sound and wondrous practice depend upon this.
Manifestation. △ Second, the Mysterious Response of Sublime Sound, in seven parts. First, the Sūtra Master’s description of his virtues:
"At that time, in the land of Universal Pure Light Adornment... [up to] all great samādhis."
By planting roots of virtue and making offerings to the Buddha, one achieves profound wisdom; this is what is meant by being "fully endowed with both merit and wisdom.

Regarding *samādhi*, here it is translated as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*). The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: "As for 'the right reception within *samādhi*,' this refers to the dharmas experienced within right concentration, distinguishing them from erroneous experiences.
It does not mean that the Sanskrit term *samādhi* is here translated as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*). Therefore, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says: "Samādhi and..."
"Samādhi of Right Reception. As for the "Exquisite Banner Mark," it means to subdue the heterodox and manifest the orthodox, yet not dwell in marks.

The "Lotus Samādhi" involves entering deeply into the One Vehicle and realizing all true marks (*dharmatā*). The "Samādhi of Pure Virtue" means that among all virtues, true purity cannot be defiled by anything.

The "Samādhi of the Play of the Constellations" means that fundamental wisdom is sovereign and free from any obstruction or attachment. "Without conditions" means to illuminate while remaining eternally [unconditioned].
Quiescence: the seal of wisdom integrates with all phenomena; understanding all languages means realizing that they are all true teachings;
gathering all merits means the perfection of the myriad virtues; pure samādhi leaves not even a speck of dust to stand upon;

sporting with supernatural powers, transformations and manifestations are sovereign; the torch of wisdom is able to shatter the darkness of ignorance; and the King of Adornments universally encompasses the sublime.
As for their practices: Pure Radiance attained the illumination of wondrous wisdom; Pure Treasury attained the treasury of the Dharma-eye;

Incomparable means that which is not reached by the two vehicles; Sun-Spinning means the circular illumination of the great trichiliocosm. He attained such samādhis as these, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This refers to their mutual penetration and harmonious integration, which are infinitely layered; all of these are possessed by Wondrous Sound.

Because he possesses these, he is able to accomplish wondrous practices and circulate the wondrous Dharma. △ Second, the manifestation of Wondrous Sound’s origin has two parts. First, his address to that Buddha.
The light of Śākyamuni Buddha illuminated their bodies [extending] to Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva;
these were all the assembly of the Dharma on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
At that time, the Buddha Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom [extended his praise] to the Tathāgata’s adornment of merit and wisdom.

In the Sahā world, the Buddha’s body conceals its excellence and manifests inferiority; compared to the superior body of Prabhāvyūha, [the disciples] give rise to thoughts of inferiority within their discriminating minds.
Yet, according to the Tathāgata’s correct vision, there is fundamentally no distinction between difference and sameness.

Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña informs them of these differing manifestations, while Gadgadasvara replies by means of the Tathāgata’s three virtues, demonstrating that there is no thought of inferiority. These are the three virtues.

Regarding the statement that "all are called Tathāgatas": this means that whatever power, spiritual transformations, and adornments I now employ are all modeled upon the virtues of the Tathāgata and emerge from the path of suchness.
Thus, regarding all phenomena, there is nothing that does not accord with reality.
How, then, could there be any distinction between superior and inferior? For this reason, I manifest various forms and preach various teachings.

Yet his supernormal powers and wisdom were not diminished in the least; they remained exactly as they were. △ Second, the manifestation of these omens: Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara did not rise from his seat... From this we know they are mutually the beginning and the end. Now, one who wishes to embody the Dharma of the former must necessarily incorporate both practices; from the wondrous to the universal, there is a beginning.

Only after reaching its conclusion is it fully perfected. Therefore, following the *Sūtra of Sublime Sound*, the *Universal Gate Chapter* (*Pumen pin*) is taught for the purpose of circulating the practice of perfection.

Mañjuśrī told him: "If you give rise to attachment toward even a single good quality, or consider a small amount of merit to be sufficient, you will be unable to skillfully initiate the practice of vows, nor will you be able to thoroughly investigate all dharma-gates. It was because of this that Sudhana achieved perfection.

Upon entering the *asaṃkhyeya* dharma-gates, one immediately beholds Samantabhadra. Samantabhadra addresses him, saying: "Throughout kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, I have practiced the bodhisattva path seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
I have attained the ultimate, equal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and further attained the unsurpassed Form-body (*rūpakāya*)."
Entering all lands and pervading all places, he manifests in response to the capacities of beings.
By means of this, Sudhana fulfills the ocean of Samantabhadra’s vows and practices; he becomes equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas.

All of these constitute the final exhortations that cause him to attain the *vimalacakra-dhāraṇī* (the billion-fold revolving dhāraṇī) and to be endowed with the path of Samantabhadra. △ Fourth, the summary of the Dharma.
[The assembly] understood.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, [the assembly] received and upheld the Buddha’s words, paid homage, and departed.
*The Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*, Fascicle Seven, Part Two (End).
